Authors: Kasa A.; Koranteng R.
Title: Employee cybersecurity awareness impact on cybersecurity posture of business organizations in Canada
Abstract: This study investigates the impact of employee cybersecurity awareness on the cybersecurity posture of business organizations in Canada, as the prevalence of cyber threats, such as ransomware, phishing, and data breaches, continues to rise. The study adopts Servant Leadership (SL) theory as the analytical framework, with particular emphasis on SL’s attributes of employee empowerment, training, and organizational culture as factors in building resilience against cyber threats. A systematic literature review (SLR) methodology was employed, drawing on peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 from databases including Google Scholar, Scopus, and Web of Science. The review process followed PRISMA guidelines, with rigorous application of inclusion and exclusion criteria, data extraction, and quality appraisal using the AMSTAR and CASP tools, resulting in 30 articles for the SLR. The findings reveal that organizations with strong servant leadership attributes, employee empowerment and training, combined with a cybersecurity-conscious culture, enhance employee cybersecurity awareness and training. The study further found that clear and consistently enforced policies are critical for guiding employee behaviour and fostering long-term adherence. The study recommends adopting targeted role-based and scenario-driven training approaches on cybersecurity for employees to improve their knowledge retention and threat response to cyberattacks for strengthening organizational cybersecurity posture in Canada. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Limited 2026.

Authors: Sui X.; Chen T.; Liu G.
Title: Business-oriented branding strategies, consumer perceptions, and marketing potential in green tourism
Abstract: Effectively promoting green tourism in China demands a comprehensive understanding of the key factors influencing consumer behavior, as well as the marketing strategies that support sustainable development. This involves not only addressing the environmental and economic aspects of tourism but also acknowledging the cultural and social dimensions that shape consumer preferences and motivations. Additionally, the rapid advancement of digital technologies presents new opportunities to enhance green tourism through innovative solutions. This study aims to identify and analyze these factors and business-oriented strategies, employing fuzzy analytical hierarchy process (FAHP) and fuzzy technique for order preference by similarity to ideal situation (FTOPSIS) methodologies to prioritize their importance. Results of FAHP revealed that environmental impact (EB1) is the most critical factor, emphasizing the necessity of robust environmental management practices. Marketing strategies (EB3) and government policies (EB4) were identified as the second and third most important factors, highlighting the significance of effective promotional efforts and regulatory frameworks in fostering green tourism. FTOPSIS analysis ranked stakeholder engagement programs and digital marketing for sustainable brands as the top strategies for optimizing green tourism, highlighting the importance of inclusive planning processes and the power of digital platforms in promoting eco-friendly travel. The study also identifies several policy implications, including the need for strengthening environmental regulations, incentivizing sustainable practices, enhancing consumer awareness, and fostering stakeholder collaboration for sustainable development. © The Author(s) 2025.

Authors: Wang Y.; So K.K.F.; Li X.R.
Title: Influencing social media engagement: integrating insights from survey and eye-tracking research
Abstract: Purpose – Hospitality and tourism brands face the challenge of effectively building customer engagement (CE) on social media. Drawing on social psychology theories of influence, this study aims to examine how reciprocity and social proof affect hotels’ Facebook CE performance and tests the moderating effect of gender on these relationships. Design/methodology/approach – Data were collected from 360 participants in an online experimental survey (Study 1) and from 110 participants in a subsequent eye-tracking study (Study 2). Findings – Results reveal that the impact of influence tactics on online CE performance varies by gender and across measures, including behavioral intention, attention and trust. Overall, the eye-tracking study’s findings align more closely with the research hypotheses regarding attention. Research limitations/implications – Results suggest that the effectiveness of engagement tactics depends on specific business goals, offering valuable insights for designing targeted social media strategies and future research. Originality/value – This study advances understanding of firm-led CE strategies in hotel brands’ social media by exploring the interplay of reciprocity, social proof and gender. The findings advocate for methodological designs that incorporate objective data in future CE research. © 2026 Ying Wang, Kevin Kam Fung So and Xiang (Robert) Li.

Authors: Wolf P.; Fabian S.D.
Title: A perspective from the future: How scenarios can inform blockchain investment and implementation decisions
Abstract: Conflicting predictions about the prospects of blockchain adoption make it difficult for strategists to decide whether to invest in blockchain applications and undertake the associated business process innovations. This challenge is intensified by a temporal dilemma: while such decisions are made with a long-term horizon in mind, the available information largely reflects present-day conditions and assumptions. To address this problem, this paper introduces the concept of aligning the timeframe of decision-making with the timeframe from which strategic information is derived through the use of far-future scenarios. The paper contributes to blockchain decision-making research by introducing a scenario-based perspective (from the future) that complements the dominant reliance on forecasting approaches and predictive models (on the future). Empirically, we analyse scenarios of far-future life-worlds with blockchain applications developed by 83 young future strategists. The analysis identifies ten ideal types of future life-worlds and demonstrates how far-future scenarios can support present-day decision-making regarding blockchain investment and implementation. The findings reveal four ways in which far-future scenarios contribute to strategic decision-making: (1) by identifying critical conditions for blockchain adoption, (2) broadening perspectives and revealing blind spots, (3) supporting backcasting from desirable futures, and (4) generating novel ideas for innovation. Thereby, the paper contributes to the strategic decision-making and foresight literature by demonstrating how far-future scenarios can bridge the temporal gap between present-day decision-making and future-oriented information, enabling decision-makers to adopt a broader perspective that encompasses the full spectrum of opportunities and threats emerging across alternative futures. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Alsalemi A.H.; Ahmad R.; Yusof N.A.M.
Title: Strategic Adaptation and Resilience During Armed Conflict: Cost Leadership and Informal Partnerships in the Hotel Sector of Ibb, Yemen
Abstract: Hotels operating under protracted armed conflict face persistent operational disruptions that differ fundamentally from the temporary shocks typically examined in hospitality crisis research. Yet limited empirical attention has been given to how cost-oriented strategies interact with locally embedded adaptive mechanisms to sustain hotel operations when formal institutional support and conventional recovery pathways are constrained. Addressing this gap, this study examines how hotels in Ibb, Yemen, use cost leadership and informal partnerships to maintain business continuity during prolonged armed conflict. A qualitative case-study design was employed, drawing on semi-structured interviews with 20 hotel managers from three- and four-star hotels. The data were analyzed thematically following Braun and Clarke's six-phase approach, supported by NVivo, with triangulation, member checking, and contextual analysis used to strengthen the trustworthiness of the findings. Six interconnected themes emerged: operational disruptions, cost leadership strategies, internal organizational adjustments, effectiveness and morale, informal networks and partnerships, and crisis-related learning. The findings show that hotel survival depended not simply on reducing costs, but on combining operational retrenchment including service simplification, local procurement, workforce flexibility, and energy-saving practices with adaptive pricing, localized resource mobilization, and informal partnerships with NGOs and community actors. The study contributes to crisis-management and hospitality-resilience research by showing that, under prolonged conflict, cost leadership functions less as a conventional competitive positioning strategy and more as an operational survival mechanism embedded within locally coordinated adaptive responses. Practically, the findings highlight the importance of flexible cost structures, local supply networks, community partnerships, and decentralized adaptation for hospitality organizations operating under sustained institutional and infrastructural disruption. © 2026 John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

Authors: Muhammad Kakale M.; Pinelli N.
Title: Impacts of artificial intelligence on healthcare business models and outcomes
Abstract: Purpose – This study aims to identify what the interaction between artificial intelligence (AI) and business models (BMs) can have on healthcare (HC) outcomes and experience and also what the ethical considerations are for AI implementation in HC. The study proposes an exploratory method using data collected from HC professionals. It aims to fill the identified gaps and contribute to theory and practice. Design/Methodology/Approach – This study used an exploratory methodology based on open-ended essay questions designed on prolific.co and collected data from 29 HC professionals. These include experts in the use of AI in HC, and a content analysis was used to analyze the data. Findings – The results showed that using AI in HC can lead to the standardization of HC services, leading to improved access to quality care with reduced cost. It revealed that AI can increase HC efficiency by automating services and increasing innovations and discoveries. But there are some ethical concerns hindering the adoption of AI HC, including data privacy, bias in algorithms and liability issues. Research limitations/implications – The sample size and the lack of including the opinions of patients are the major limitations of this study. Future studies are encouraged to improve in this direction. Practical implications – This study will promote and facilitate the wider acceptance and implementation of AI in HC. It will also enable policy and decision-makers to address ethical issues hindering the adoption of AI in HC. Originality/Value – This study has filled an important research gap by revealing how AI is impacting HC BMs and outcomes. The study will facilitate the adoption of AI in HC. © 2025 Mus'ab Muhammad Kakale and Nicola Pinelli

Authors: Gariba M.I.; Odei S.A.; Arthur E.E.; soukal I.
Title: Driving circular economy transformation through technological innovation: the moderating role of regulatory environment, human capital, and technological capacity
Abstract: Addressing the urgent issues of climate change, resource scarcity, and environmental deterioration necessitates a shift toward a circular economy. However, there is a lack of research on the circumstances under which technological advancements influence the circular economy. This study explores the connection between technological innovation and the circular economy in the context of OECD economies, emphasizing the moderating effects of regulatory environment, human capital, and technological capacity. Utilizing the endogenous growth theory, we develop and evaluate a model using annual data from 37 OECD countries comprising 692 country-year observations from 2000 to 2022. Employing a panel fixed-effects regression model with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors, instrumental variable estimation, and quantile regression, our findings based on the instrumental variable model indicate that technological innovation is positively and significantly associated with the circular economy indicator, indicating deteriorating circular performance as patenting activities increase. Although the quadratic term is negative and statistically significant, the marginal effects remain positive across the observed range, revealing a concave relationship in which the adverse environmental effects of technological innovation persist but diminish in magnitude at higher levels of technological innovation. The results further show that technological capacity positively moderates the relationship between technological innovation and the circular economy, whereas human capital has a negative moderating effect. Finally, environmental regulation strengthens the positive impact of technological innovation on a circular economy. The findings differ across the fixed effects and quantile regression models, highlighting the context-specific nature of the results and the importance of addressing endogeneity and distributional effects. Our results contribute to the theoretical understanding of the interplay between technological innovation and the circular economy, underscoring the significance of contextual factors. Practical implications for policymakers and businesses include prioritizing funding programs and incentives for sustainable technologies, monitoring innovation efforts, and creating a supportive regulatory landscape that encourages circular economy practices, while minimizing bureaucratic barriers. © The Author(s) 2025.

Authors: Scafarto F.; Poggesi S.; Mari M.
Title: Work–family conflicts, burnout and life satisfaction: an observational study
Abstract: Purpose – This study explores the interplays among Work–Family Conflict (WFC), burnout and life satisfaction in the case of Italian entrepreneurs and employees, as moderated by parental demand and social support from partner. Design/methodology/approach – Grounded in the Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, a complex theoretical model was developed and tested. The study employed a quantitative approach, analyzing survey data from two distinct samples of workers: 140 entrepreneurs and 371 employees. The relationships were assessed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to compare the structural paths between the two groups. Findings – Family Interference with Work (FIW) was found to significantly increase burnout, in its two dimensions of disengagement and emotional exhaustion, only among entrepreneurs. Conversely, Work Interference with Family (WIF) impacted emotional exhaustion in both groups but influenced disengagement only among employees, partially supporting a “matching-domain” effect. For both employees and entrepreneurs, disengagement emerged as a stronger predictor of life satisfaction than emotional exhaustion. However, emotional exhaustion was a valid antecedent of life satisfaction only for employees. Moreover, social support from partner buffered the negative impact of disengagement on life satisfaction for employees but failed to mitigate the impact of emotional exhaustion, while parental demand exerted no significant moderating effect in either group. Research limitations/implications – This study advances the understanding of WFC, burnout and satisfaction within the Italian business and entrepreneurship landscape, while advocating for further cross-cultural validation. Practical implications – This research offers actionable insights to employees, entrepreneurs and policymakers. The findings can inform the development of targeted coping strategies and support systems designed to reduce the strains of WFC, mitigate the risk of burnout and poor life satisfaction. Originality/value – This study extends the empirical literature on WFC by offering a nuanced, comparative analysis of the consequences of WFC on burnout and life satisfaction. By contrasting the distinct “resource ecology” of entrepreneurs and employees and examining key conditional effects, it provides a more precise understanding of how occupational roles shape the interface between work and family life and the dynamics of resource depletion and conservation among the groups. © Francesco Scafarto, Sara Poggesi and Michela Mari

Authors: He D.; Wei L.; Wang J.; Cao C.C.; Tok D.
Title: Handmade brands and product variety perception: The “handmade = small variety” belief
Abstract: Handmade brand positioning has become increasingly popular in recent years and is often believed to elicit positive reactions from consumers. However, consumers may not always view handmade brands positively. This research explores consumers’ perceptions of handmade brands and reveals a potentially negative consequence of handmade brands. Through five preregistered studies and two supplementary studies reported in the Web Appendix, we demonstrate that consumers perceive handmade brands as offering a smaller product variety than non-handmade brands, a phenomenon we term the “handmade = small variety” belief. This belief occurs mainly because consumers perceive handmade brands as having a smaller business size than non-handmade brands. Additionally, we demonstrate that the “handmade = small variety” belief is weakened when the business size is very large and when the production complexity is high. We also show the downstream implication of this belief: consumers are less likely to choose a handmade brand over a non-handmade brand when they have a shopping goal of exploring a wide variety of products, compared to when they do not have such a goal. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025.

Authors: Khan M.S.; Charissis V.; AlTarteer S.; Kabli T.; Naseraldin A.
Title: Communicating servitisation offers for mitigating weather-related risk for the construction industry through a simulation based serious game
Abstract: Climate change is a pressing global challenge that significantly impacts the day-to-day operations of various sectors, including the construction industry. The construction sector, in particular, experiences severe consequences due to the unpredictability of weather conditions. This unpredictability poses significant challenges for effective planning, risk management, and obtaining appropriate insurance coverage for construction projects. Servatization is transforming business models across many sectors, including the financial sector, where parametric insurance products are being introduced as Digitally Enhanced Advanced Services (DEAS) to facilitate weather risk management for the construction industry. While these services aredesigned to enhance accuracy and streamline the operations and processes, their complexity often makes them difficult for end users to understand and evaluate. As a result, limited exposure and understanding of servitisation offerings can negatively impact the uptake of the service. This research collaborated with real-life servitisation designers - (EHAB) within the construction industry to capture the key factors impacting the communication and understanding of servitisation offer. Based on these insights, it then designed & developed a prototype simulation based serious game to communicate the servitisation offer to end users. The serious game enables users to experience weather-related risks and the operational logic of parametric insurance through interactive, simulation-based gameplay, allowing long-term impacts to be explored within a short game cycle.Quantitative methods was used to evaluate the effectiveness of simulation-based serious games, involving 50 participants from the construction sector. The evaluation focused on perceived usefulness, ease of use, engagement, and overall user experience. The results indicate positive user perceptions and suggest that serious games can provide an effective and engaging medium for communicating complex servitisation offerings related to weather risk management in construction. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Basson R.; Fortuin G.S.; Malan N.; Patterson M.; Pietersen L.-A.
Title: Developing citizenship competencies in accounting students through experiential learning: An action research study
Abstract: Calls for more socially responsible professionals underscore the need for accounting graduates to possess citizenship competencies for meaningful engagement with diverse stakeholders in an increasingly globally connected business landscape. Few studies explore pedagogical approaches to develop such competencies in accounting students, especially in complex post-colonial contexts. Addressing this gap, this study explores how community-based experiential learning can be optimised to develop citizenship competencies. Action research was employed across two cycles of an experiential learning programme at a South African university, designed using Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory and framed by Pless, Maak and Stahl's model for responsible leadership development. A triangulated dataset comprising reflections and peer- and self-evaluations, supported by questionnaires, were analysed using thematic analysis, descriptive statistics, and non-parametric statistical tests. The action research approach facilitated iterative refinements, to which strengthened perceptions of competency development between cycles were likely attributable. Based on these findings, the study provides empirically grounded recommendations for community-based citizenship development, including academic transcript recognition, rubric-based assessments, and scaffolded, structured reflections. Experiential designs should incorporate sustained engagement through repeat visits, enabling participants to observe the tangible impact of their involvement and thereby fostering greater social responsibility. Intentional experiential exposure to unfamiliar community contexts, including diverse cultural and socio-economic backgrounds, enhances a broad spectrum of citizenship competencies, notably empathy and social awareness, but also extending to tolerance and adaptive communication skills. The insights from this study support professional programme development that seeks to deliver socially responsible graduates who can contribute to the public interest beyond technical expertise. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Greven A.; Poblocki J.; Fischer-Kreer D.; Maus C.; Brettel M.
Title: Serendipity and innovation in new ventures: The moderating role of primary investor type
Abstract: Rather than pure luck or a fully planned search, opportunities in new ventures frequently emerge from serendipitous discoveries. While research has emphasized the antecedents of serendipity, empirical evidence on its innovation outcomes remains scarce. Drawing on social cognitive theory, we argue that serendipity’s value depends on environmental conditions, which shape whether unexpected discoveries are recognized and translated into venture-level action. Analyzing survey data from 386 founders and CXOs of new ventures in Western and Northern Europe, we find that serendipity is positively associated with innovation radicalness and speed. These relationships are contingent on investor type: Compared with bootstrapped ventures, the positive associations are weaker in ventures backed by venture capitalists, business angels, or family and friends. These findings advance our understanding of serendipity’s contingent value in early-stage entrepreneurship and highlight investor dynamics as a boundary condition shaping innovation trajectories. Authors: Tirdasari N.L.; Dhewanto W.; Arief N.N.
Title: The rationales behind family business digitalization
Abstract: Purpose – This study aims to explore the factors influencing digital adoption within family businesses, highlighting its role in ensuring operational continuity, competitiveness and long-term viability. Design/methodology/approach – A qualitative multiple-case study incorporated in-depth interviews with representatives from 13 family businesses across diverse industries. Data were analysed using thematic coding and cross-case analysis to identify key themes and rationales behind digital adoption. Findings – This study identifies nine primary rationales for digital adoption: agility, collaboration, competitiveness, cost efficiency, productivity, innovation, sales orientation, time savings and operational streamlining. This study proposed a conceptual model to illustrate these forces. Research limitations/implications – The findings enrich existing literature on family business digitalization by identifying key drivers and proposing a conceptual framework. Given its geographic focus, scholars should cautiously generalize findings. Practical implications – Family business practitioners can leverage the identified forces to adopt digital technologies strategically, enhancing operational efficiency and market relevance. Social implications – Digital adoption supports family business sustainability, job creation and long-term economic contributions. Originality/value – This research provides actionable insights into digital adoption rationales for the family business operating within a developing economy. © 2026 Nyayu Lathifah Tirdasari, Wawan Dhewanto and Neneng Nurlaela Arief.

Authors: Pettersson K.; Hoffmann K.; Mahlendorf M.D.
Title: Sales forecast accuracy and adjustment costs
Abstract: Managers’ forecasts about future sales are at the core of managerial decision-making. Using a monthly business survey, we study managers’ directional sales forecast accuracy three months ahead. Managers incorrectly predict the direction of sales changes in 42 % of their forecasts. In exploratory analyses, we find that firms with better educated and more tenured CEOs make better forecasts. In our main analyses, we investigate how sales forecast accuracy is related to adjustment costs. We find that SG&A costs increase less per dollar of sales increase in firm-years with high accuracy. The results hold after controlling for different proxies related to long-term cost structure. Accordingly, the empirical evidence is consistent with the explanation that our findings primarily reflect short-term dynamics, wherein SG&A expenses rise disproportionately when firms must make ad hoc adjustments in response to unexpected changes in sales. When focusing on within-firm variation of forecast accuracy, the associations with adjustment costs are only significant for firms with low average accuracy. Additional cross-sectional analyses are consistent with the interpretation that forecast accuracy matters more for larger firms and firms with higher demand volatility. Finally, firms with higher forecast accuracy have a lower cost-to-sales ratio and higher gross profit margins. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Mehran J.; Kristensson P.; Shams P.
Title: Customer-perceived supplier innovativeness in B2B services: evaluative cues across ecosystem interactions
Abstract: Purpose – In business-to-business (B2B) contexts, innovativeness is often conceptualized as a firm-internal capability reflected in research and development investment, technological advancement and process improvements. This study examines how business customers evaluate supplier innovativeness in B2B service ecosystems and identifies the cues that shape such evaluations beyond innovation outputs or capabilities alone. Design/methodology/approach – The study adopts an abductive qualitative multiple-case design. Empirical material comprises six in-depth interviews with boundary-spanning informants across five innovation-intensive B2B firms, complemented by secondary data. Data were analyzed through iterative coding and comparison within an abductive analytic logic. Service-dominant logic and service ecosystem theory are used as sensitizing lenses. Findings – Customers evaluate supplier innovativeness through observable patterns of action embedded in interaction and coordination practices. These evaluations draw on three interrelated cue clusters: (1) credible enactment of innovation intent, (2) transparency in resource integration and coordination and (3) contributions to ecosystem arrangements that support customer value creation. Combined, these cues form a role-based evaluative frame that customers use while interpreting innovativeness across recurring interaction configurations. Practical implications – Managers can strengthen customer perceptions of innovativeness by making innovation-related practices more transparent, selectively enabling customer involvement and coordinating collaboration across relevant ecosystem actors. Originality/value – This study contributes an empirically grounded perspective on customer-perceived innovativeness in B2B services and develops a role-based framework conceptualized as a co-creation continuum that captures how customers draw on different evaluative logics when assessing supplier innovativeness. © Javaneh Mehran, Per Kristensson and Poja Shams

Authors: Blanco-Mazagatos V.; Temprano-García V.; Pérez-Fernández H.; Delgado-García J.B.
Title: Ability and willingness as jointly sufficient conditions for the family effect on family firm economic performance: a configurational approach
Abstract: Family business research remains inconclusive about how family influence affects the financial performance of family firms. Drawing on agency theory and the resource-based view, most studies examine family involvement in ownership and management, which reflects the family’s ability to make decisions. Other studies emphasize the family’s willingness to pursue specific objectives, particularly those related to socioemotional wealth. However, particularistic behavior in family firms cannot be explained solely by ability or willingness. Building on this reasoning, we propose that both ability and willingness are necessary but individually insufficient conditions for explaining family firm performance. We further argue that their joint presence constitutes a sufficient condition. Using a sample of 141 family firms, our results identify seven configurations combining measures of ability and willingness that are associated with high financial performance, thereby supporting our arguments. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Saâdaoui F.; Rabbouch H.
Title: Shaping sustainable investment through digital technologies: Strategic perspectives for the transformation era
Abstract: This paper examines the importance of technological infrastructure in influencing sustainable investment, with particular reference to gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) and foreign direct investment (FDI). We use principal component analysis (PCA) and data envelopment analysis (DEA) to uncover the structural interdependences among digital readiness, innovation capacity and macroeconomic stability. Countries that are identified as DEA-efficient, with high internet penetration, extensive mobile uptake and strong high-tech exports, are consistently receiving greater investment. Inflation impacts economies in different ways, it prevents capital accumulation in less efficient economies and it helps promote investment in more efficient economies. This highlights the importance of context sensitive macroeconomic strategies. Unemployment is still a big hurdle to sustainable investment, limiting GFCF and FDI especially in economies with structural rigidities. The outlier analysis identifies Vietnam, China and Malta as examples of ICT-driven investment resilience, while Sudan illustrates how structural and labor-market constraints can impede capital accumulation despite moderate digital progress. A robust digital infrastructure, innovation capacity and a stable macroeconomic and labor-market are essential to sustain competitive investment strategies. This alignment of factors strategically promotes inclusive growth and long-term investment resilience in countries. It provides actionable guidance to policy makers and business leaders to advance sustainable economic development. © 2026

Authors: Ramírez-Orellana A.; Tejero C.B.G.; Garvey A.M.; Gonzalo-Angulo J.A.
Title: EU Taxonomy eligibility, sustainability performance and systematic market risk in the airline industry
Abstract: Air transport constitutes a complex sector to address from a sustainability perspective because of its high technological requirements and the significant volume of emissions associated with its activity. Since the introduction of the EU Taxonomy, aviation has been recognised as a transition activity, reflecting its potential role in the progression towards more sustainable business models. This study examines whether EU Taxonomy eligibility and sustainability performance are associated with systematic market risk in the airline industry. Using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and 156 pooled firm-year observations from 39 listed airlines over 2021–2024, this study examines the direct and indirect associations among EU Taxonomy eligibility, measured through eligible CapEx, sustainability performance, and systematic market risk, proxied by market beta. In addition, the moderating role of ESG Controversies Score in the relationship between sustainability performance and systematic market risk is analysed, while controlling for firm size. The results show that greater eligible CapEx and stronger sustainability performance are associated with lower systematic market risk. Sustainability performance partially mediates the association between EU Taxonomy eligibility and market beta. In addition, the ESG Controversies Score is negatively associated with systematic market risk and significantly moderates the sustainability performance-risk relationship. The negative interaction indicates that sustainability performance is more strongly associated with lower market beta when firms have a more favourable controversy profile and lower exposure to negative ESG events. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Suryo M.B.; Hakam D.F.
Title: Transportation energy transition development scenario planning 2060: Case study of Indonesia
Abstract: Indonesia's road transportation sector accounts for 36.11% of total national energy consumption and emitted approximately 160 Mt of CO₂ in 2023 yet remains almost entirely dependent on fossil fuels. This study develops a LEAP-based energy shift model to project Indonesia's road transport energy consumption, fuel mix, CO₂ emissions, and infrastructure investment across four scenarios from 2024 to 2060, grounded in the newly enacted National Energy Policy KEN PP No. 40/2025. The four scenarios are Business-as-Usual (BAU), Accelerated Energy Transition (AET), Net Zero Transport (NZT), and Best Practice (BP). Modal energy shares are anchored to ICCT's 2023 base-year splits, and baseline total energy follows the KEN 2025 lower trajectory, peaking at 78.30 MTOE in 2030 before declining to 58.23 MTOE by 2060. Results show that BAU and AET fall short of net-zero alignment, with 2060 emissions of 101.66 MMT and 57.68 MMT respectively and fossil fuel shares remain at 58.25% and 33.00%. NZT achieves 15.22 MMT by 2060, an 85.0% reduction versus BAU, with zero-emission fuels covering 87.43% of total road transport energy. BP reaches 4.04 MMT at a 96.0% reduction, with zero-emission fuels at 96.28% and total energy declining to 30 MTOE. Cumulative CO₂ savings relative to BAU reach 2518.71 MMT under NZT and 3412.95 MMT under BP. Infrastructure investment for NZT and BP amounts to USD 273.75 billion and USD 265.18 billion respectively, with BP falling below NZT after 2053 due to earlier infrastructure saturation. The findings confirm that NZT and BP are the only viable pathways for NZE 2060 alignment, and that achieving either requires legislated ZEV sales mandates toward 100% by 2045, front-loaded charging and hydrogen refueling investment, and coordinated power sector decarbonization. © 2026

Authors: Zeng Y.; Liu Y.; Mei L.
Title: Curriculum greenwashing in business statistics education: Institutional decoupling in responsible management education
Abstract: Business schools increasingly state commitments to responsible management education (RME), yet institutional commitment may not be consistently reflected in pedagogical change. This study examines curriculum greenwashing as a possible divergence between RME language in curriculum artifacts and corresponding evidence in teaching practice and student learning, without assuming deliberate intent. Drawing on institutional theory and decoupling, we test whether signatory status in the Principles for Responsible Management Education (PRME) is associated with declarative, procedural, and consequential integration in undergraduate business statistics courses. Longitudinal multilevel data were collected from 215 students and 45 faculty members across 30 institutions across three waves. PRME status was positively associated with RME content in syllabi, whereas associations with reported teaching and student learning gains were not detected. Faculty-reported practices were positively associated with student learning gains. The PRME status × faculty quantitative teaching self-efficacy interaction was positive but did not reach conventional statistical significance; exploratory probing indicated a positive PRME association only at high self-efficacy. The study contributes a three-level audit framework for evaluating how institutional RME commitment is reflected across curriculum representation, reported teaching practice, and student learning, while underscoring the value of evidence beyond syllabus language alone. © 2026

Authors: Fakfare P.; Worrachananun M.; Lee J.; Lee J.-S.
Title: Embodied cognition and the luxury hospitality experience of in-flight wine in premium cabins
Abstract: This study explores how first- and business-class passengers experience in-flight wine as luxurious, even though flying reduces taste and smell. Drawing on embodied cognition theory, we argue that passengers do not simply judge wine by its quality. They build a sense of luxury by noticing how the airline tries to compensate for sensory limits, by feeling that the service fits their bodily experience, and by responding emotionally. We surveyed 500 premium-cabin passengers and used two analytical approaches: structural equation modeling and necessary condition analysis. The results show two related paths to luxury: a cognitive path, in which the service feels consistent with the passenger's bodily state, and an affective path, in which the service creates positive emotions. For first-class passengers, both paths had to reach a minimum level for luxury to emerge. For business-class passengers, the cognitive path was more important, and positive emotions were less essential. These findings help airlines design in-flight wine service that still feels luxurious despite the sensory challenges of air travel. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Liang Y.; Chen R.; Zeng Y.; Yin S.
Title: Beyond participation: Creativity and entrepreneurial mindset across instructional modes and learner-level digital conditions in entrepreneurship education
Abstract: Entrepreneurship education is often examined as a uniform educational exposure, although its associations with student development may depend on instructional mode and learner-level digital conditions. This study compares six entrepreneurship education formats and examines their associations with two self-perceived outcomes—creativity and entrepreneurial mindset—while assessing whether these relationships vary by perceived digital literacy and functional social media use. Drawing on survey data from 1181 graduating students at a multidisciplinary university in Guangdong, China, we use propensity score matching to improve comparability between participants and non-participants on observed characteristics and estimate interaction models to assess conditional relationships. The results indicate that entrepreneurship education is more consistently associated with entrepreneurial mindset than with creativity. Business plan competitions, training programs, and practical workshops generally show comparatively strong associations, particularly relative to entrepreneurship courses, although public lectures are also notably associated with entrepreneurial mindset. Perceived digital literacy displays a selective and format-dependent moderating relationship with creativity but does not consistently moderate the relationship with entrepreneurial mindset. Functional social media use shows no stable moderation in the primary binary models, while supplementary continuous-measure models reveal some operationalization-sensitive patterns. These findings indicate that entrepreneurship education is best understood as a heterogeneous set of learning experiences whose associations with student development vary across instructional modes, developmental outcomes, and learner-level digital conditions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Bzhalava L.; Makkonen T.; Šipikal M.; Omorede A.; Hassan S.S.
Title: Detecting promising green ventures with foresight and data mining
Abstract: There is growing consensus on the need to decouple economic growth from environmental degradation, with radical innovation playing a critical role in addressing environmental challenges. Green ventures are key drivers of such innovation, yet decision-makers lack systematic tools to identify ventures with transformative potential. This study advances computational foresight by integrating weak signal detection with venture-level performance analysis to identify promising green ventures and anticipate pathways of transformative green innovation. Using Crunchbase metadata, we identify strong and weak signals in green venture business descriptions (2013–2018) and link them to individual venture performance in 2019–2024. We further apply LDA topic modelling to examine how weak signals evolve into structured business opportunity domains. The results show that strong signals play a limited, context-specific role, primarily supporting early-stage funding, while weak signals exhibit heterogeneous and generally attenuated effects. Weak signals consolidate into distinct domains, with Sustainable Finance & ESG Platforms emerging as the most scalable pathway, whereas Green Mobility and Sustainable Consumption face greater commercialization challenges. Geographic variation further highlights differences in entrepreneurial ecosystem specialization and scaling dynamics. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Balducci B.; Pang B.; Hu L.; Li C.; Wang W.; Shang Y.; Marinova D.; Gordon M.
Title: Leveraging audio data: A guide to understanding customer-firm conversations
Abstract: Although technological advancements enable communication through diverse mediums, conversations involving back-and-forth dialogue remain a central way in which firms interact with customers. Yet technical barriers, high subscription costs, and data security concerns hinder the extraction of insights from customer-firm conversations. To address these challenges, we create a methodological framework and end-to-end automated program, AudioMatic, designed to process audio recordings of conversations between business agents and customers. This paper details AudioMatic’s workflow, provides access to the corresponding code, and demonstrates its effectiveness using 3,900 sales prospecting calls. A logistic regression-based machine learning model trained on salespersons’ verbal and vocal features extracted via AudioMatic accurately predicts conversation outcomes with 88.08% accuracy. Follow-up analyses further reveal that salespersons’ vocal features account for 39.2% of the model’s predictive value. Overall, AudioMatic enhances the accessibility of audio analysis, highlighting both the practical and theoretical potential of integrating conversational audio data in research and practice. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025.

Authors: Karsas G.
Title: Six steps for a modern digital strategy
Abstract: In today’s rapidly shifting financial landscape, digital transformation is no longer a destination; it is a continuous journey. Financial institutions must evolve from reactive upgrades to proactive digital strategy planning. At Travis Credit Union, a six-step framework was implemented to advance meaningful and sustainable progress in digital initiatives, reflecting this philosophy. This paper outlines that framework and offers practical guidance for financial organisations seeking to modernise with intention and purpose. The main insights from this paper include a modern framework for digital strategy and insights into conducting a digital audit, aligning internal capabilities with industry trends and fostering organisational buy-in. Readers will gain actionable strategies to initiate and sustain digital maturity, tailored to the needs of financial institutions. Authors: Lee J.; Park S.; Lee J.
Title: A study on the monitoring of technology innovation through patent analysis
Abstract: These days, innovation cycles are becoming shorter, and market competition has grown increasingly intense. Therefore, it is essential for companies to adopt strategic R&D approaches to remain competitive. This study proposes a systematic approach to technology monitoring (TM). While previous TM studies have employed scientific analysis methods based on different types of patent information, their interpretations have often relied heavily on the subjective judgments of analysts. To mitigate such subjectivity, several methods have been proposed using patent classification schemes; however, they still remain dependent on expert interpretation. The present study introduces a technology monitoring methodology based solely on the Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC), the most recent and fine-grained patent classification system established in 2013. To demonstrate the utility of the proposed methodology, we apply it to the domain of electric vehicle (EV) battery charging technologies. Patent data were collected from WIPS ON, a major commercial patent database in Korea, and 2498 CPC-classified patents filed between 2013 and 2023 were analyzed. The Bass diffusion model was used to identify stages of technological innovation. To identify core technology clusters, UMAP (with cosine similarity, min dist = 0.5, and n neighbors = 50) and DBSCAN (with Euclidean distance, eps = 15, and min samples = 4) were employed, achieving a silhouette score of 0.781 for three clusters. Association Rule Mining (ARM) was then conducted to identify the technological patterns within each cluster, thereby revealing temporal shifts in EV charging technologies. Notably, this study finds that patent data not only capture technological characteristics but also reflect strategic business directions, suggesting that structured patent metadata, such as CPC codes, can serve as an insightful resource for future-oriented decision-making in innovation management. © The Author(s) 2025.

Authors: Choi J.O.; Shahi A.; Kwon W.
Title: Modularization Barriers and Barrier Breakers in Capital Projects
Abstract: Modularization is an execution strategy that transfers work from the project site to an offsite location for improved project performance. It is expected to have significant growth and wide acceptance, leading to enhanced productivity and competitiveness of capital projects. However, many practitioners in capital projects are still unfamiliar with modularization and resist changing from a traditional approach. The implementations have been limited to lower levels of modularization (e.g., prefabs or pipe racks) and lower extents of modularization. Although previous research has investigated barriers to modular/offsite construction in residential and commercial sectors, there is a lack of studies identifying barriers specific to capital projects (including but not limited to petrochemical plants, manufacturing plants, power generation facilities, and mining operations). Thus, this study focuses on identifying barriers to modularization implementation and proposing solutions to break these barriers in capital projects. First, 33 barriers were identified through iterative sessions with the Construction Industry Institute (CII) Research Team (RT-396), a panel of 15 subject matter experts averaging more than 15 years of modularization experience and 28 executed modular studies/projects. Subsequently, a survey based on these barriers was distributed to CII member companies, gathering data from experts affiliated with globally leading owner and contractor organizations, who possess an average of 23 years of industry experience and 11 years of specific modular expertise. The results identified nine top-rated barriers: (1) requirement of early scope/design freeze; (2) unavailability of vendor data; (3) noncompelling business cases; (4) exclusion of modularization from initial design; (5) incompatible project delivery methods; (6) owner reluctance; (7) lack of final drivers; (8) insufficient early fabricator involvement; and (9) lack of project standardization. These findings contribute to the management-in-engineering body of knowledge by showing that modularization adoption in capital projects is constrained primarily by front-end managerial and organizational conditions rather than by technical concerns alone. The comparative analyses and expert-derived specific "Barrier Breakers"strategic solutions developed to overcome each of these nine top-ranked barriers provide actionable guidance for diverse practitioners regarding early decision making, project delivery alignment, and supply-chain integration.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Authors: Lin S.; Lin J.
Title: Understanding the interplay of digital technology resources, digital technology–business alignment and government digital support to shape digital business capability: A multi-method approach
Abstract: Grounded in the resource-based theory, this research investigates how tangible, human, and intangible digital technology (DT) resources shape the digital business capability of organizations. To capture both linear and configurational effects, a multi-method approach integrating partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) was employed. The outcomes of PLS-SEM indicate that digital technology infrastructure and digital employee skills significantly enhance digital business capability, whereas digital organizational culture alone does not exert a direct effect. DT–business alignment weakens the positive influence of digital technology infrastructure, suggesting that overly rigid alignment may constrain the benefits of digital investments. Complementing these findings, the fsQCA results identify multiple equifinal resource configurations through which firms can develop digital business capability under different levels of DT–business alignment and government digital support. Overall, this study advances theoretical understanding of how digital resources collectively contribute to capability formation and offers practical guidance for firms seeking to allocate resources strategically and strengthen their competitive advantage. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Hruby J.
Title: Participation, engagement, and competency development in multicultural virtual management education: Multi-source evidence from an 8-week program
Abstract: This study examines how behavioral participation, peer-assessed engagement quality, and team psychological safety relate to performance and competency development in a multicultural virtual management education program. Drawing on experiential learning and student engagement theories, we use a six-source mixed-methods design based on an eight-week virtual International Business Strategy course with undergraduate students from Mexico, Germany, and 11 other countries, organized into eight, cross-national teams. We propose a participation–engagement–learning (PEL) framework that distinguishes participation intensity as a behavioral condition, engagement quality as a relational process, and competency development as an outcome. The findings show that individual participation strongly predicts individual course grades but not the independent team performance. Matched pre- and post-analyses indicated significant gains in cultural intelligence and global leadership self-efficacy. Team psychological safety and peer-assessed engagement quality were positively associated with post-program competency outcomes, whereas participation intensity was not directly associated with these self-reported outcomes. Reflection reports suggest that students experienced identity disruption, collaborative meaning making, and leadership schema reconstruction, helping explain how relational engagement supported learning. This study contributes to management education research by demonstrating that participation, engagement, and development should not be treated as interchangeable indicators of learning. For management educators, the findings support multi-source assurance-of-learning systems that combine behavioral, relational, and developmental evidence. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Flego C.; Tei A.
Title: Boosting accessibility and inclusiveness in tourism and cultural heritage sites: benchmarking best-practices
Abstract: Purpose – “Accessibility” and “inclusiveness” are pivotal factors influencing the socio, environmental and economic dimensions of tourism attractions and heritage sites. Despite their high impacts and related spillover effects, comprehensive strategies and tools for assessing, monitoring and optimizing their effects have not been defined yet. Design/methodology/approach – A systematic literature review technique has been used in order to identify, evaluate and synthesize the available literature in both fields of tourism and cultural heritage. It has been essential for framing the concepts of “accessibility” and “inclusiveness”, identifying the main methods and practices employed to measure and evaluate them, and proposing a set of universal actions. Then, it classifies the best-case studies at the global scale. Findings – This research confirms that best practices leveraging accessibility and inclusiveness in tourism and cultural heritage actively involve local communities in the economic and social discussions, supported by long-term planning and sustainable policy frameworks. In this context, collaboration and communication among all stakeholders – such as citizens, local businesses and public authorities – play a central role. Moreover, the establishment of a continuous action-oriented system for monitoring and evaluating social, economic and environmental impacts is demonstrated to be essential. Such systems are key to developing long-term strategies, particularly for the preservation and conservation of social and natural environment. Originality/value – This paper fills the literature gap proposing a set of strategies enhancing accessibility and inclusiveness in tourism and cultural heritage. This research may be employed by local and international regulatory agencies to extend their socio-economic perspective, reducing the related environmental impacts. In this way, it would overcome the actual fragmentation, facilitating global justice and equality. © 2025 Clio Flego and Alessio Tei

Authors: Fu L.; Boehe D.; Heyden M.L.M.
Title: CSR focus under competitive pressure: The role of national institutions
Abstract: How does competitive pressure shape CSR strategy, and does this relationship vary across national institutional contexts? We challenge the prevailing binary framing that competitive pressure either promotes or suppresses CSR by arguing that competition reshapes how firms configure their CSR portfolios, not merely how much they engage. We introduce CSR focus strategy: a firm's selective emphasis on specific CSR dimensions while deliberately de-emphasizing others, allowing simultaneous differentiation and cost-economization through CSR under some conditions. Employing multilevel linear modeling (MLM) on a global dataset of 41 countries comprising 2294 firms from 2002 to 2020, we demonstrate that competitive intensity drives adoption of CSR focus strategy. Critically, this effect is contingent on national market-supporting institutions and firm size, where CSR focus strategies are most pronounced in institutionally weaker environments characterized by limited property rights protection and among smaller firms with limited stakeholder relational capital and opportunities. Further analyses reveal two subtypes, namely CSR excellence and CSR distinction , reflecting different portfolio configurations under competition. By establishing that institutional context shapes firms' CSR portfolio configuration under competition, our study advances international business research and reconciles opposing theoretical positions in the competition-CSR debate. Collectively, these findings extend the emerging portfolio-based view of CSR into the cross-country competitive domain. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Wu Y.; Lu X.; Lin C.
Title: How generative artificial intelligence reshapes students’ interdisciplinary cognitive structures: Implications for management education
Abstract: Management education increasingly asks students to work across disciplinary boundaries when addressing complex business problems. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may support this work by scaffolding information search, problem framing, and cross-functional reasoning, but it also raises concerns about uncritical reliance and reduced independent evaluation. This study examines a pedagogically tuned GenAI intervention as a cognitive mediator in team-based management learning. In a mixed-methods randomized controlled trial, 84 MBA students assigned to 28 teams solved an ill-structured strategic case with either a customized GenAI partner or traditional search resources. The analysis combined rubric-based evaluation of final team reports, team-level epistemic network analysis (ENA) of collaborative discourse, and post-task interviews. AI-supported teams produced higher-quality strategic reports, with higher scores especially for interdisciplinary integration and innovation. ENA showed that these teams also displayed more densely connected discourse patterns linking information retrieval, cross-disciplinary reasoning, integrative synthesis, and critical evaluation. Interview data suggest that the AI partner helped teams move some low-level information-foraging work into a more evaluative and synthetic discussion mode. Rather than supporting generic GenAI use, the results highlight the value of human-in-the-loop tasks that combine scaffolded inquiry, peer discussion, and assessment of reasoning processes alongside AI-assisted products. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Zakaria Z.; Mokhtar N.; Abu Talib N.Y.; Ahmad H.; Mamat S.
Title: Perceived value of experiential learning among accounting students: insights into transferable skills, critical thinking, and deep learning
Abstract: Experiential learning has been widely acknowledged as a contemporary approach to teaching accounting courses. This study advances teaching excellence in accounting education by examining the students’ perceptions of the value of experiential learning and identifies areas for improving its implementation for the Business Finance course under the undergraduate accounting degree. Data was gathered through client interviews, student focus groups, and a questionnaire survey. Drawing on Kolb’s theory and the constructivist approach to experiential learning, this study demonstrates that students’ perceptions of the value of experiential learning are based on their interactions with clients, classmates, and teachers, which allows them to acquire new experiences and refresh their preexisting conceptual schema. The results confirm the findings of existing studies that experiential learning improves deep learning, critical thinking, and the development of transferable skills, as well as exposes them to the subtleties of solving real-world business issues. Extending prior research, this study contributes to the literature on teaching excellence by showing how experiential learning fosters students’ conscience, such as self-awareness of empathy, patience, integrity, self-confidence, persistence, and building trusting relationships as core principles in the financial decision-making environment. These qualities are essential for developing virtuous conduct and self-governing accountants, which society needs. This study also notes that meticulous planning is the key element that influences the effectiveness of experiential learning. The results of this study could be of interest to accounting educators in developing teaching excellence in the business finance course to produce graduates who are prepared for the workforce as expected by employers and other stakeholders. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Mindzak J.; Mindzak M.
Title: Robert's Rules: The accounting classroom as a business meeting
Abstract: This paper details the incorporation of Robert's Rules of Order into a university-level course. Robert's Rules of Order is a formal system of parliamentary procedure and a normative guide to conducting meetings and group decision-making with the intention of accomplishing goals fairly. This pedagogical strategy was selected to more accurately resemble a business environment—specifically with respect to the manner by which meetings and decisions are often conducted in a diverse range of organizations—including, but not limited to the business community. In this study, Robert's Rules were integrated into an upper-level accounting course to examine how structured decision-making processes can shape student engagement, communication, and professional behavior in a higher-education setting. This paper seeks to gain insights and develop learning strategies in integrating Robert's Rules on teaching and learning in a higher education accounting classroom setting. Using an action-research orientation, the approach revealed several benefits related to participation, collaboration, and the development of transferable skills. Overall, this method demonstrated positive results, while also assisting in the development of professional behaviours. The findings indicate that, when paired with complementary pedagogical approaches such as flipped instruction, Robert's Rules can provide a practical framework for supporting active learning and strengthening students' preparation for professional environments. © 2026

Authors: Jepson A.; Stadler R.; Garrod B.; Page S.
Title: Family holidays with autistic children: An exploratory study of parents’ emotion work due to service delivery failure
Abstract: There is growing recognition that autistic children face significant emotional challenges during a family holiday. Interviews with parents of autistic children in the UK and Ireland were undertaken to explore parents' perceptions of the role of emotions in service delivery failure. Inductive latent analysis found four types of service delivery gap, each associated with uncertainty about who is responsible for managing emotions: this is termed ‘emotion work’ when undertaken by parents and ‘emotional labour’ when it is performed by staff. The findings suggest that there is a need for a more complete understanding of the use of emotions in recovery after instances of service delivery failure, particularly with regard to distinguishing between the concepts of emotion work and emotional labour. An important implication is that tourism businesses may need to adapt their service provision through staff training and development schemes that recognise the importance of emotions in supporting autistic children. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Iqbal M.Z.; Khan T.; Kamran M.; Qureshi S.K.; Alkhoraif A.A.
Title: Clear the fog: Academic confidence, critical thinking, and career decision ambiguity tolerance among business students
Abstract: Drawing upon Social Cognitive Career Theory, this study examines if academic behavioral confidence improves business students' ability to tolerate ambiguity in career decisions, with critical thinking disposition acting as a mediating factor. The survey involved two samples of business and management students from one country in Asia and one in Europe (N = 1707 participants). The data were analyzed using the partial least squares structural equation modeling approach (PLS-SEM). Students' academic behavioral confidence is positively associated with their tolerance for ambiguity in career decisions, both directly and through their critical thinking disposition. Findings were consistent across samples. Current research on Social Cognitive Career Theory has concentrated on self-efficacy, overlooking the influence of cognitive skills in transforming confidence into ambiguity tolerance. To fill this gap, the study advances Social Cognitive Career Theory by showing that critical thinking disposition is a cognitive mechanism that connects students' academic behavioral confidence to their ability to cope with uncertainty in career choices. Moreover, the study incorporates critical thinking from educational psychology into career theory, highlighting its importance in addressing modern career challenges, including the gig economy and nonlinear career trajectories. Overall, the findings offer important implications for management educators seeking to enhance students’ career readiness. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Milani R.; Ghirotto L.; Setti I.
Title: Workplace learning in times of uncertainty: exploring how leaders learn under the lens of learning agility
Abstract: Purpose – The uncertainty of today’s business environment requires leaders to acquire new skills continuously and remain adaptable to change. This qualitative study aims to examine how leaders experience learning in the ever-changing workplace and the agile learning strategies they develop to navigate uncertainty. Design/methodology/approach – This study builds upon the literature on learning agility and learning organization. Participants were purposively sampled from banks in several Central and Eastern European countries, Italy and Egypt. The authors conducted semi-structured interviews with 29 senior managers and used reflexive thematic analysis. Findings – The analysis yielded an overarching theme, “learning what to do when you do not know what to do, ” and two themes: “signifying learning from mistakes” and “learning a resilience capacity. The findings highlighted the complex interplay among mistake tolerance, reflective practices and resilience strategies in the daily learning experiences of leaders. Originality/value – Although there is considerable literature on leaders’ roles in fostering a learning culture, qualitative research incorporating their perspectives is limited, particularly in rapidly changing contexts. Understanding leaders’ learning experiences is vital for rethinking workplace learning and development. This study uniquely captures a diverse range of perspectives from leaders across different roles, business functions, geographical regions and cultural backgrounds. © 2026 Roberta Milani, Luca Ghirotto and Ilaria Setti

Authors: Blauhut C.; Ungerer C.; Reuther K.; Dahle Y.
Title: Fit matters - support configurations and sustainability venture survival
Abstract: The growing urgency of solving worldwide societal and climate change issues through viable business models has intensified research on entrepreneurship support. Despite the expansion of entrepreneurship support, little is known on how different support configurations interact with sustainability venture orientation and founder characteristics to shape survival outcomes. We reposition venture survival as a critical precondition for long-term sustainable impact and introduce a framework for context-sensitive support design that treats venture orientation - distinguishing social from ecological orientation - as a central contextual condition shaping support effectiveness. Addressing the limited attention on heterogeneity and configurational causality in venture survival research, we employ a configurational approach using qualitative comparative analysis (QCA). Based on a sample of 262 Norwegian ventures and interviews with entrepreneurship support organizations, we show that survival is associated with selectively combined and orientation-aligned support bundles, whereas expansive multi-type support configurations are, in some cases, linked to non-survival. Depending on venture orientation (social vs. ecological), education, and support bundles, we identify distinct configurations associated with both survival and failure, revealing causal asymmetry. Our findings highlight the double-edged nature of entrepreneurship support: while targeted configurations aligned with venture orientation appear to sustain problem-solving and persistence, overly extensive support bundles may crowd out agency and diffuse attention. By demonstrating that support effectiveness depends on configurational alignment rather than additive intensity, this study challenges the assumption that more support is inherently beneficial and advances a context-sensitive perspective on sustainability entrepreneurship support design. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Veloso P.R.S.; López L.M.; Ekel P.; D´Angelo M.F.S.V.; Libório M.P.
Title: Multicriteria Group Decision-Making System (MGDM-Sy) Based on Heterogeneous Preference Elicitation Formats
Abstract: This study presents MGDM-Sy, a multicriteria group decision-making system that supports heterogeneous preference elicitation within a unified computational environment. The system allows evaluators participating in the same decision problem to express their preferences using different preference elicitation formats, including ordering of alternatives, direct scoring, and pairwise comparison. Heterogeneous preference representations are automatically transformed into a common score representation suitable for aggregation. For pairwise comparisons, MGDM-Sy incorporates a consistency-improvement mechanism that assists decision-makers in identifying and correcting inconsistent judgments while preserving the original assessments as much as possible. The system also performs consensus analysis at both the individual and group levels and generates decision-support reports. In addition, MGDM-Sy incorporates two methodological contributions: the Card Sorting method, which combines ordering and pairwise comparison while allowing the assignment of zero importance to alternatives, and the Consensus Degree-Enhancement tool, which improves group consensus by filtering assessments according to their individual consensus degree. The system is illustrated through two multicriteria group decision-making applications: (i) the prioritization of regions for agrivoltaic system deployment and (ii) the weighting of the criteria composing the Cost of Doing Business Index. The results demonstrate the applicability of the proposed framework and show that the Consensus Degree-Enhancement tool increases the group consensus degree while preserving representative assessments that would otherwise be unnecessarily excluded. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Bughin J.; Cincera M.
Title: Seeing through the (random) forest: firm-level drivers of remote work
Abstract: This study explains why firms sustain different levels of working from home (WFH) as remote and hybrid work become enduring features of business organization. We develop and test a firm-level microeconomic framework integrating managerial beliefs about workforce effectiveness, productivity trade-offs across work locations, digital investment, organizational constraints, and competitive conditions. Using survey data from 3,100 firms across countries and industries and machine-learning methods, we find that WFH decisions are shaped primarily by prior work arrangements, technology capabilities, leadership, market context, and innovation. Managerial perceptions of employee preferences matter, but mainly as signals that influence productivity beliefs and complementary investment. Belief updating, capability accumulation, and adjustment frictions jointly explain persistent yet heterogeneous WFH practices. The findings position remote work as a strategic, capability-contingent organizational choice and identify the conditions under which firms can sustain productive hybrid models. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Authors: Cahyadi H.; Putra Y.; Tan J.D.; Lee K.Y.; Ardi A.
Title: The impact of governance and financial factors on predicting financial distress: evidence from Indonesian family retail firms
Abstract: As the largest economy in Southeast Asia, Indonesia is strongly driven by family-owned enterprises, particularly in the retail sector. This study aims to investigate the governance and financial aspects of publicly listed Indonesian family retail firms to identify strategies for mitigating financial distress during potential future crises. This study examined how various governance factors—specifically managerial ownership, gender diversity, and board size—and key financial ratios, including profitability, liquidity, sales growth, debt-to-equity ratio, and debt-to-assets ratio, affect financial distress in family retail businesses listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during the 2019–2022 period. Using panel data regression analysis with Eviews 12 software, we found that the debt-to-assets ratio increased the likelihood of financial distress significantly. In contrast, other variables, including gender diversity, board size, debt-to-equity ratio, and asset turnover, did not exhibit a significant effect on financial distress; however, gender diversity exacerbated it. This discovery raises important questions regarding governance and operational frameworks within family-owned firms. Additionally, our moderated regression analysis revealed that firm size significantly influenced the relationship between gender diversity and financial distress, underscoring its role as a crucial factor for board diversity. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of financial distress determinants, particularly within family retail firms, which can contribute to managerial practices and policy frameworks. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Hein-Pensel F.
Title: Organizational identity meets digital transformation: understanding the interplay between transformation and identity in Industry 5.0
Abstract: Purpose – This study explores the relationship between digital transformation and organizational identity, arguing that understanding this relationship is essential for organizations actively seeking to effectively navigate and adapt to the complex changes proposed by Industry 5.0 to reshape modern business and organizational dynamics. Design/methodology/approach – A systematic literature review was conducted to examine the bidirectional relationship between digital transformation and organizational identity. Findings – The analysis reveals that digital transformation and organizational identity continuously influence each other and identity shifts can both drive and be driven by technological change. Moreover, Industry 5.0 emphasizes human-centric and sustainable principles, requiring organizations to adapt their core sense of “who they are” to remain resilient and purpose-driven. Originality/value – This study offers novel insights into the role of organizational identity in the digital transformation process. By examining the role of identity theory in digital transformation and applying an entity-relationship model to map the dynamic interplay, this study extends the discussion beyond the technology-centric lens of Industry 4.0 into the human- and sustainability-focused paradigm of Industry 5.0. Therefore, the contributions of this study are twofold. It offers suggestions for identity realignment strategies and provides an agenda for five future research avenues: Identity dynamics, Employee perception and stakeholder, Structures and cultures, Impact of technology and Measurement. Each offers unique opportunities to deepen the understanding of DT and OI. © 2025 Franziska Hein-Pensel

Authors: Saha R.; Lundh M.; MacKinnon S.N.
Title: Evaluating stakeholders’ interactions for future autonomous European inland waterway transport
Abstract: The European Inland Waterway Transport (E-IWT) industry is transitioning towards a new reality governed by higher levels of autonomous systems. While the E-IWT system is preparing for future changes in technical, legal and business frameworks, it is important to examine the system from a socio-technical perspective. Using a Socio-Technical System (STS) framework, the IWT system was segmented into four subsystems: Technical, Personnel, Work Design, and the Environment. Twenty-nine (29) actors covering 19 nodes within the 4 subsystems were interviewed using a pre-questionnaire survey, which was analysed employing a thematic analysis. Two themes emerged as key findings detailing the subsystems in 3 different scenarios: 1. Work as Done- (a) current conventional operation; 2. Work as Imagined- (b) manned and (c) unmanned remote-control operations. For all 3 scenarios, the results identified task, organisation, data and information for 4 subsystems, and existing or foreseeable gaps to the emergence towards higher Levels of Automation (LOA) through those scenarios. Findings forecast a shift in roles and responsibilities from the vessel to the shoreside, likely including a ‘shift in hub’ from vessel-centric operations to Remote Operation Centres (ROCs), requiring real-time communications, extended redundancies, goal-based regulatory changes, and ROC design requirements. The result further highlights misalignment among different subsystems and the necessity of integrated socio-technical approaches, including stakeholder collaboration, regulatory alignment, and system standardisation, to support the transition towards higher LOA in E-IWT. © The Author(s) 2026.
