Authors: Rurumo J.M.; Okello D.; Ndambi A.
Title: The triple-layered business model canvas as a tool for sustainable BSF farming: A case of smallholder farmers in Kenya
Abstract: Smallholder farmers play an important role in providing food to the world, but they are at risk due to issues like climate change, soil erosion, and high feed costs. The livestock industry, especially poultry, pig, and fish farming, is seriously disadvantaged by Kenya's unsustainable dependence on traditional protein sources, such as fishmeal and soybeans. This paper explores how Black Soldier Fly larvae technology (Hermetia illucens) may reduce these limitations and reinstate opportunities by providing sustainable animal feed and organic fertiliser products, while encouraging circular economy ideologies. The study intensively used focus group discussions (FGDs) in five counties of Kenya (Nakuru, Baringo, Kisumu, Kakamega and Busia), in which 75 stakeholders of the BSF value chain were sampled. Value chain mapping and thematic analysis were applied to understand the roles of actors, the connections, and the dynamics of the system. The sustainability of the technology was evaluated using a Triple-Layered Business Model Canvas (TLBMC) approach in terms of economic, environmental, and social aspects. The results indicated that, in addition to enhancing livestock productivity through high-quality feed, BSF technology also improves soil health through the application of frass. The model generates local jobs, supports waste management, and upholds community well-being. The study ends by suggesting the creation of inclusive business models that will include smallholder farmers as suppliers, processors, and distributors in the BSF value chain. Then, the use of extension services, improved regulatory support, and establishment of financial incentives will help unleash the full potential of BSF technology in Kenya and beyond. Authors: Duzgun E.; Trinh A.T.Y.
Title: Supply Chain Governance and Labour Exploitation Risks: Sustainability Certification, Responsible Labour Practices and Buyer Pressure in Vietnam's Coffee Industry
Abstract: This study examines how external and internal supply chain governance mechanisms shape firms' responses to labour exploitation risks in Vietnam's coffee supply chains. Using survey data from 405 individuals involved in the sector and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM), the study finds that sustainability certification is negatively associated with responsible labour practices but has no significant direct association with labour exploitation risk or worker well-being. In contrast, global buyer pressure positively strengthens responsible labour practices, which subsequently improve worker well-being. Responsible labour practices and worker well-being are also positively associated with reported exploitation-related indicators. Rather than indicating higher exploitation prevalence, this finding suggests that stronger internal governance may improve the visibility and detection of previously hidden vulnerabilities. The results further show that sustainability certification can influence labour outcomes indirectly through responsible labour practices and worker well-being, indicating that certification alone is insufficient to generate substantive social improvements. The study therefore challenges compliance-centred approaches to supply chain governance and highlights the importance of organisational capabilities and buyer–supplier relationships in translating external sustainability requirements into effective labour protections. The findings contribute to research on responsible business and sustainable supply chain governance in emerging markets and provide implications for ethical recruitment, worker protection, responsible sourcing and Sustainable Development Goal 8. © 2026 ERP Environment and John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

Authors: Paudel P.R.; Wang P.
Title: Crowded home: Competitive positioning, internationalization, and firm performance
Abstract: Prior literature has long established that firm performance depends on competitive positioning. While plausible, most studies on competitive positioning conceptualize that firms compete within a single, bounded marketspace (e.g., a country or industry). This approach, however, downplays firms' heterogeneous market expansion, which can largely reshape the returns to competitive positioning. To underscore the important role of market expansion, we specifically examine how firms' international expansion moderates the relationship between competitive similarity and performance. Analyzing a large sample of US firms from 1997 to 2017, we find support for our core claim: The adverse impact of competitive similarity on firm performance is alleviated when a firm has a greater level of international presence. We further observe that the negative impact is mitigated (albeit more marginally) when a firm's competitors are more international. These findings make important contributions to research on competitive positioning and international business. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Yuan J.; Riaz A.; Liu M.
Title: Leveraging IoT for business model innovation in banking: The role of data-driven decision-making, Fintech innovation and artificial intelligence
Abstract: Drawing on Resource Orchestration Theory (ROT), this study examines whether data-driven decision-making (DDS) and adoption of Fintech innovations serves as serial mediation mechanisms linking IoT adoption and business model innovation (BMI). Moreover, it examines whether Artificial Intelligence (AI) capability significantly moderates the relationship between IoT adoption, DDS, and BMI. Using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) on data from 689 bank managers, we found that IoT adoption positive direct relationship with BMI, DDS, and Fintech innovation adoption. Moreover, DDS and Fintech innovation adoption positively affect BMI. DDS and Fintech innovation adoption mediated and serially mediated the relationship between IoT adoption and BMI. Finally, AI capability positively moderates between IoT adoption and BMI, and IoT adoption and DDS. This study advances digital innovation research by explaining how banks transform IoT adoption into business model innovation through data-driven decision-making, Fintech innovation adoption, and AI-enabled resource orchestration. Authors: Dubé J.-P.; Xu A.
Title: Large Language Models and Creative Content Design: a case study of email marketing at Wine Access
Abstract: A sequence of three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) is conducted to support a small online business’ decision of whether and how to implement AI in the creation of email marketing content. Recent developments in frequentist statistical decision theory are used to accommodate small samples available for testing in the small-business setting. The RCTs comprise three test policy cells with email content created by (i) salaried writers (“human”), (ii) a large-language model (“LLM”), and (iii) a “hybrid” combination of a human editing the content created by the LLM, respectively. When a “no email” control policy is included, all three test cells approximately double the gross profits from orders relative to the control cell. The RCTs vary whether the hybrid cell is edited by a salaried writer or the marketing team. The LLM cells vary whether the AI is pre-trained using historic emails or uses a prompt-based generative pre-trained transformer (“GPT”). Decision theory always selects one of the AI cells over the standard human policy on the basis of total annual profit net of related labor and software overhead. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Homer S.T.; Cindy C.; Weissmann M.A.; Paul A.
Title: Turning intent into practice: Operationalising sustainability Co-design in business schools
Abstract: This paper examines how a governance-aware co-design model can turn institutional sustainability intent into scalable, practice-centred learning and assessment in a Southeast Asian Business School. Using a practice-led mixed-methods design, we identify participation drivers and frictions through surveys and focus groups embedded in a short modular intervention. Findings show that time-bounded, hands-on activities, credible lived-experience speakers, blended delivery, and meaningful recognition are decisive for engagement. We synthesise these results into a co-design framework that specifies decision rights for students, staff, and partners; aligns assessment and workload with practice-based tasks; and produces portable artefacts—principles, mapping matrices, and rubrics—that travel across programmes and endure staff turnover. A formative validation step with students and faculty refines the constructs and implementation routines. The study concludes that durable co-design depends less on topic selection than on how authority, recognition, and quality assurance are organised, so engagement becomes routine rather than episodic. Practical implications include embedding engagement indicators and feedback loops into programme review, accreditation, and performance compacts. The contribution is a pragmatic blueprint for institutionalising co-design, so sustainability learning remains legible, auditable, and scalable in resource-constrained contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: K A.; B. Menon R.
Title: Brand recognition and consumer buying behaviour of FMCG in cause-related marketing: social media and brand recall as moderators
Abstract: This research study seeks to explore how social media and Brand recall affect Brand Recognition and Consumer Buying Behavior connected to Cause-Related marketing of fast-moving consumer goods. The theoretical basis of the Theory of Planned Behavior is used to create a conceptual model, and the outlined relationships between its concepts are examined using primary data from India. In Kerala, southern India, data were collected from 411 respondents using convenient sampling across six districts. Researchers built the survey instrument on their own, examined its properties using PLS-SEM, and tested the hypotheses using path analysis. The results demonstrate that (i) Brand Recognition is positively connected to Consumer Attitude, (ii) Consumer Attitude is related positively to Purchase Intention, and (iii) Purchase Intention is connected positively to Consumer Buying Behavior. According to the results, the moderating effect of social media increases the positive relationships between Brand Recognition and Brand Recall, and also between Consumer Attitude and Purchase Intention. It has also been discovered that Brand Recall enhances the positive relationship between Brand Recognition and Consumer Attitude. The study will be useful for Organizations, businesses, and policymakers for effective cause-related marketing practices by ensuring proper Brand Recall and Brand Recognition among customers. All possible efforts have been made to minimize the limitations of this study, including social desirability biases. To our knowledge, the conceptual model was first developed and tested in the context of developing nations, and this study focused on India. Authors: Zhao H.; Lardhi J.S.; Tyagi V.; Al-Adwan A.S.; Ammar O.H.
Title: Reimagining sustainable entrepreneurship: capability integration and business model innovation as catalysts of SDG-driven performance
Abstract: This research examines the relationships between SDG-related capabilities, sustainable business model innovation (SBMI), and multidimensional performance in startups. Using a sample of 284 entrepreneurs from the United States and the United Kingdom, the study employs partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) to test a capability-based approach of SDG literacy, SDG orientation, and SDG integration capability. The results show a differentiated pattern of relationships: SDG integration capability exhibits the strongest positive association with SBMI, while SDG orientation also demonstrates a significant positive relationship with SBMI; in contrast, SDG literacy does not exhibit a significant unique relationship. SBMI, in turn, is positively associated with economic, social impact, and environmental performance, and significant indirect effects of SDG Integration Capability on economic, social impact, and environmental performance are observed through SBMI. Institutional sustainability support does not significantly moderate any of the SDG-capability–SBMI links. Overall, the findings emphasize that operationalizing sustainability through integration capability, rather than through literacy or orientation alone, is more strongly associated with SBMI and multidimensional performance in entrepreneurial ventures. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Zhang Y.; Zhang H.; Wang C.
Title: Strategic leasing-selling mix and emission reduction pathways for durable goods manufacturers under mixed carbon policy constraints
Abstract: Addressing the escalating challenge of global warming, durable goods generate significant carbon emissions across both production and consumption phases. They have thus emerged as a critical focus of carbon regulation. Grounded in consumer utility theory, this paper develops a profit model for a monopolistic manufacturer employing a mixed leasing-selling strategy. The model examines the influence of carbon trading price, initial carbon quota, and carbon tax rate on the firm's production planning and market operations. Key findings are as follows. (1) The mixed carbon policy combining cap-and-trade and carbon tax can motivate manufacturers of lower-quality goods to enhance product durability and transition away from low-end production. (2) The intensity of the mixed carbon policy shapes distinct strategic responses: relatively lower levels of carbon price and tax rate encourage a shift toward leasing, whereas higher levels promote selling. (3) The profitability of the manufacturer is mainly determined by the carbon trading price and the initial quota allocation. (4) A more generous initial quota coupled with a stable carbon price mechanism can substantially enhance the overall emission reduction outcome. (5) The mixed carbon policy reduces consumer surplus, while social welfare improves with higher carbon tax rates. These findings provide new insights into the coordination between business model innovation and emission reduction pathways in the durable goods industry under carbon policy constraints. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Myles P.; Axson E.; Mitchell C.
Title: Data quality, provenance and transparency in real-world data: Aligning quality standards with data governance legal frameworks
Abstract: There have been numerous papers discussing data quality and data protection independently, but there has been little discussion on how data quality relates to data protection and other data governance regulatory frameworks. This paper is a step towards addressing that gap and makes the case for why data quality is relevant for data protection and legal compliance professionals. Real-world data in the context of healthcare refers to data that is routinely collected in the course of delivering healthcare. From a data protection regulatory perspective, Article 5 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) lists data accuracy as one of the principles for data processing. The recently adopted European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act) Article 10 outlines requirements for data and data governance, specifically quality criteria for datasets used to train, test and validate high-risk AI models to address concerns around algorithmic bias due to biases in the training data. The Standards for Data Diversity, Inclusivity and Generalisability (STANDING) Together consensus recommendations for dataset curators on transparency in dataset documentation enable an informed assessment of the suitability of data and examination of biases, for development of AI health technologies. This includes information on data provenance, modifications, sociodemographic composition and bias assessment findings. The Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) database is used to illustrate how these recommendations can be implemented in a practical way using unique identifiers such as digital object identifiers (DOIs), metadata, published data resource profiles with sociodemographic information and data quality assessments using validation and comparability studies. There is considerable alignment between established scientific standards, medical product regulatory and data governance legal requirements on data quality, as well as emerging international consensus which will reduce the compliance burden on curators and users of real-world data. Authors: Ingman K.; Lyly-Yrjänäinen J.; Laine T.; Korhonen T.
Title: Cost awareness as a fundamental prerequisite of advanced manufacturing technology adoption in a supplier–OEM dyad
Abstract: Purpose – The article focuses on the limited cost awareness as a fundamental yet insufficiently understood barrier to advanced manufacturing technology (AMT) adoption and, consequently, enhanced business performance. Design/methodology/approach – The article utilizes a longitudinal, interventionist case study (2015–2021) of an AMT-based supplier and its manufacturer customer in Finland. Findings – The findings of this article show that decisions not to leverage the advantages offered by AMT may be based on inaccurate financial numbers, indicating limited cost awareness. Thus, considerable cost information asymmetry between an AMT supplier and their customer is problematic and hampers legitimizing AMT adoption decisions. Practical implications – Realizing the efficiencies offered by AMTs and their associated services requires a business model transition, which is often justified on economic grounds, particularly through cost savings. However, if cost awareness is inadequate, the business model transition may not be possible and the potential benefits remain unrealized. As a response, the article proposes a framework to analyze and develop the cost awareness of the stakeholders in a customer-supplier dyad. Originality/value – As a unique contribution to the AMT literature, the article argues the importance of utilizing truthful and up-to-date cost information to support the adoption of the AMTs and the benefits they potentially entail. The article brings together literature on value creation, AMT and digital servitization in a novel synthesis, paving the way for critical studies on costs in manufacturing technology adoption. © Kari Ingman, Jouni Lyly-Yrjänäinen, Teemu Laine and Tuomas Korhonen

Authors: Bayraktar M.
Title: From Bosai to Global Resilience: A Systematic Review of Social Capital in Disaster Risk Management Research
Abstract: Social capital is among the most frequently invoked explanations of why some communities withstand disasters better than others, yet the research invoking it is scattered across disaster studies, organizational health, business, and environmental fields that rarely read one another. Japanese bosai culture, in which disaster preparedness is embedded in everyday neighborhood networks, represents the most fully institutionalized case of this resource at work and serves here as the benchmark for reading the wider field. No review has yet mapped this fragmented literature as a whole or asked how far it answers the questions the bosai case raises. This study reviews 217 peer-reviewed articles (1999–2025) retrieved from Scopus and Web of Science, combining bibliometric analysis with a full-text thematic classification. Four clusters emerge: disaster and community resilience (37.8%), business and supply chain risk (33.2%), climate and environmental adaptation (17.5%), and health-related organizational risk (11.5%). Across clusters, bonding ties dominate immediate response while bridging and linking ties govern recovery, and social capital turns insufficient or exclusionary where inequality restricts access to networks. Two questions remain only partially answered: how disasters reshape networks over time, and how social capital interacts with ecosystem resilience, both constrained by the field's reliance on cross-sectional single-case designs. The review treats social capital as a phase-dependent and context-dependent resource rather than an unconditional good, and derives from this position a research agenda spanning five named gaps. © 2026 John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

Authors: Salamin X.; Audrin B.; Chochard Y.; Hofmann S.
Title: On their way to sustainable careers? Exploring the role of career competencies in graduates of an entrepreneurship education program
Abstract: Entrepreneurship education (EE) has gained in popularity over the past decades within higher education institutions, as it is regarded as a promising way to prepare future professionals to evolve in increasingly uncertain and complex business environments. Despite the rise in research examining EE, one aspect that remains under-researched pertains to the outcomes of EE, with studies predominantly emphasizing narrow entrepreneurship outcomes such as venture creation or entrepreneurial intentions. This strongly contrasts with the fact that the majority of EE graduates do not start new ventures and rather enter established organizations. Studies focusing on EE graduates in the workplace are strongly missing, as well as research investigating how EE programs contribute to their graduates' careers. Precisely, this study adopts a “career perspective” on EE, mobilizing the theoretical frameworks of sustainable careers and career competencies. It adopts a qualitative case study design, taking graduates from a Swiss EE program who entered in the labor market, as the case context. The objective of this study is to investigate how these EE graduates perceive their career competencies developed through EE as contributing to their sustainable career development. Findings highlight the perceived contribution of graduates' career competencies to the three indicators of sustainable careers. Results also unveil a form of duality in the role of the program when it comes to the development of career competencies for graduates’ sustainable career development in Switzerland. This study contributes to research on EE and on careers by providing empirical evidence on career development of EE graduates through contemporary career concepts. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Pal A.; Gupta K.; Gaur D.; Tiwari C.K.; Bhat M.A.
Title: Enabling entrepreneurial breakthroughs: the synergistic role of social capital, dynamic capabilities and innovative thinking
Abstract: Given the unique challenges facing entrepreneurs and firms in Oman stemming from resource constraints and changing institutional frameworks, this study aims to explain how social capital can help improve entrepreneurial business performance, with the contribution of dynamic abilities, innovative skills and government support. The research model used in the present work builds on established theories, including the Resource Based View and DCT, to explain how entrepreneurs harness incorporeal assets such as social networks, adaptability, and innovation to obtain a competitive advantage. The data has been collected from 347 entrepreneurs in Oman and is analysed using PLS-SEM. The findings reveal that Social Capital is the basic enabler; it provides networks, trust, and shared understanding that allow entrepreneurs access to resources and knowledge. Dynamic capabilities transform those resources into actionable strategies, which are adaptable and resilient. The insights from the current study have important takeaways for entrepreneurs. Entrepreneurs should actively cultivate and maintain robust networks to enhance their access to resources and knowledge. Emphasizing the relational and cognitive social capital can foster trust and shared vision, which are vital for collaboration and innovation. Policy makers should aim to create policies that increase social capital and dynamic capabilities in the entrepreneurial ecosystem. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Yang Y.; Xie S.; li Y.
Title: Temperature shocks and corporate innovation: evidence from China
Abstract: Extreme weather events have increased significantly in recent years, exerting a profound impact on economic and social development. This paper analyses the relationship between temperature shocks and the innovative performance of companies, as measured by patent data. The results show that high-temperature shocks significantly hinder corporate innovation, and this effect is lagged. Specifically, heterogeneity analysis shows that this negative association is particularly salient in firms with low institutional ownership or profitability. Besides, regional variations in climate conditions serve to moderate the impact of temperature shocks on corporate innovation. It has been observed that firms located in cooler areas exhibit heightened sensitivity to such shocks. The findings of the mechanism analysis indicate that temperature shocks hinder innovation by negatively impacting firms’ human capital and innovation efficiency. Moreover, in addition to impacting the quantity of innovation, temperature shocks also exert a significant impact on the structure and quality of corporate innovation. This research enhances our understanding of the impact of climate change on business operations and highlights the urgency of building climate resilience. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Wu D.C.; Zhang P.; Wu J.; Li G.; Hu M.
Title: Multi-agent collaboration strategies for tourism demand forecasting
Abstract: With the advancement of LLM-based agents, multi-agent collaboration has attracted growing interdisciplinary attention. However, its effectiveness in business planning and decision-making remains underexplored. Therefore, this study proposes different multi-agent collaboration strategies and examines their effectiveness in such business tasks as tourism demand forecasting. The results based on Hong Kong daily inbound tourist data show that there is variability in agent forecasting performance guided by different strategies. The parallel collaboration significantly outperforms both non-collaboration and chain collaboration. Meanwhile, the performance of chain collaboration depends on agent number, independent forecasting ability, and agent order. Furthermore, heterogeneous multi-LLM collaboration consistently exceeds homogeneous multi-role collaboration. This study offers valuable insights and evidence for the design of multi-agent collaboration strategies in business scenarios. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Li M.; Yan L.; Song L.
Title: Advancing Sustainable Development in management education through online learning: Evidence from a Chinese business school
Abstract: Integrating sustainability into management education has become a central institutional priority for higher education and a recognised pillar of the United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Yet evidence on whether and how online pedagogies can foster transformative sustainability learning in undergraduate management programmes remains scarce, particularly across emerging economies where digital instruction expanded rapidly after the pandemic. Drawing on transformative learning theory and education for sustainable Development, this study examines an online course in social and environmental management delivered over 13 weeks at a Chinese business school between January and May 2022, integrating a qualitative case study with action research across five triangulated data sources from 53 undergraduates and applying thematic coding in ATLAS.ti version 8.4. Findings show that a structured pedagogical model blending flipped learning, group projects, and reflective dialogue produced measurable shifts across the three transformative dimensions, with most of the 53 students reporting an expanded understanding spanning environmental, social, and wellbeing aspects and a clear reorientation of career intentions toward ethically responsible employers. The study contributes a pedagogical framework that connects online learning design to transformative learning processes and sustainability competencies, offering management educators a transferable model for cultivating responsible future leaders. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Truden C.; Gansterer M.
Title: Assessing second-price auctions for parcel exchanges in last-mile logistics
Abstract: The rapid growth of e-commerce has led to multiple carriers operating in the same regions, creating opportunities for collaboration. However, logistics companies typically operate independently, leading to inefficiencies. Horizontal cooperation, where carriers share resources and infrastructure, can improve efficiency and reduce costs. This study explores the requirements for a parcel exchange framework through a game-theoretic lens. We focus on auction-based mechanisms to facilitate horizontal cooperation, optimize exchanges, and minimize delivery costs and emissions. Our approach prioritizes ensuring that carriers report accurate marginal delivery costs while maintaining business privacy. First, we define the key properties of an exchange mechanism for redistributing parcels among carriers. Our analysis reveals a conflict between incentive compatibility and budget balance when non-free disposal is enforced. Among the mechanisms considered, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves (VCG) mechanism is the most suitable, though it tends to overpay carriers. The rationale for using VCG is that we consider incentive compatibility and allocation of all parcels more important than budget balance to ensure long-term participation of carriers and delivery fulfillment. In a computational study, we analyze a VCG-based parcel exchange under realistic settings. The experiment considers several parcel carriers within a region with heterogeneous market shares. In the simulated auctions, carriers compute marginal costs for the parcels, and the winner determination problem is solved via a linear program. A random parcel assignment serves as proxy for noncooperative behavior. The results demonstrate that second-price premium reward payments are typically moderate and that second-price compensation for allocated parcels remains superior to noncooperative last-mile parcel logistics. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Li M.; Lin B.
Title: The path towards renewable energy: business transformation processes and inefficient investment
Abstract: The pressing demand for decarbonization within the context of economic development has generated substantial opportunities for the rapid growth of renewable energy. Consequently, further research is essential to promote the advancement of the renewable energy sector, with a crucial emphasis on understanding the barriers firms face when entering this field. This study investigates the aforementioned issue by examining the relationship between business expansion and inefficient investment among China's listed renewable energy companies. First, we compared phased investment (PI-type) and merger-and-acquisition (M&A-type) renewable energy enterprises. The preliminary results revealed the presence of entry barriers: the inefficient investment of PI-type enterprises exhibited an inverted U-shaped relationship with the expansion of their renewable energy business, whereas there was no significant relationship for M&A-type enterprises. Furthermore, we examined the underlying causal relationships by accounting for industry trends and constructing instrumental variables. Additionally, we conduct a moderation effect analysis on the nonlinear relationship based on traditional theories of enterprise business expansion and market competition. By comparing PI-type with M&A-type enterprises, we provide new empirical evidence supporting traditional theoretical frameworks. Finally, considering the unique characteristics of the renewable energy industry, we examine how three types of government roles mitigate entry barriers. These conclusions serve as a reference for governments to formulate policies for renewable energy development and help enterprises understand the trade-offs in transitioning into emerging industries. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Yoon S.-H.; Jang H.; Yang S.-B.; Park S.
Title: Designing a generative artificial intelligence-based hotel review management assistant: a design science approach
Abstract: The increasing reliance on online platforms has substantially reshaped consumer–business interactions, particularly in the travel and tourism sector. Online consumer reviews now serve as key decision-making tools for travelers and vital channels for firms to manage digital customer relationships. However, responding to large volumes of reviews, especially negative ones, poses significant operational and emotional challenges, particularly for resource-constrained tourism businesses. To address these issues, this study develops HormAS, a human-supervised GAI-based review response support artifact, using a design science research methodology. The artifact analyzes customer sentiment, emotion, and intention to generate contextually appropriate and empathetic responses. By shifting the focus from review analysis to response generation, this study contributes both theoretically and practically to the fields of digital marketing, tourism management, and information systems. Under controlled evaluation conditions, the proposed artifact provides preliminary evidence of improved response efficiency and reduced self-reported stress, thereby offering a foundation for future research on scalable, human-supervised systems for managing online review responses in tourism. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Rześny-Cieplińska J.
Title: Integrating urban freight into the 15-minute city: Evidence from Poland
Abstract: The 15mC concept focuses on residents' proximity to basic services but often overlooks the logistical flows needed to sustain them. This paper examines integrating freight distribution into proximity-based urban planning to align with sustainable development goals. While density and mixed land use reduce passenger travel distances, they often paradoxically increase the complexity and frequency of goods movements.This study implements a mixed-method research design: (1) a systematic literature review of international green logistics models, (2) a comparative analysis of European best practices (Paris, Barcelona, Utrecht), and (3) primary empirical research conducted in Poland. The primary research includes semi-structured interviews with municipal planners and a diagnostic survey of last-mile operators and local business owners.The results identify a planning gap in Polish metropolitan areas, where freight is frequently treated as a private commercial issue rather than a public utility. The findings suggest that successful integration requires a tiered infrastructure of decentralized micro-hubs, flexible loading zones, and the promotion of cargo-bike logistics. The paper concludes with a proposed conceptual framework for medium-sized European cities to harmonize freight efficiency with walkable urban environments by linking strategic spatial planning with evidence-based logistics governance recommendations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Viljoen A.; Hein A.; Krcmar H.
Title: Low-code development platform ecosystems
Abstract: Low-code development platforms (LCDPs) such as Mendix, OutSystems, and Microsoft Power Platform are reshaping software development. These platforms enable non-technical users to develop applications by reusing and configuring out-of-the-box components in visual, user-friendly environments. While LCDPs are typically portrayed as new standalone development tools, they also exhibit many characteristics of digital platform ecosystems. For example, similar to traditional app stores, they also offer marketplaces where external developers and business users can contribute what they have developed. Yet, despite these conceptual similarities, the “platform” dimension of LCDPs has received little attention. Accordingly, this Fundamentals paper conceptualizes LCDPs as a distinct type of digital platform ecosystem. We build on research in digital platform ecosystems, boundary resources, packaged software reuse, and platform governance, and explain how LCDPs align with and differ from conventional platforms. Specifically, we show how LCDPs combine infrastructure and reuse, embed design constraints directly into components, and orchestrate ecosystem participation through a logic of “curated enablement” rather than open contribution. We conclude by outlining a research agenda that highlights LCDPs not as marginal tools for end-user development, but as rich, theory-relevant settings for further exploration. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Albaham M.A.; Alsanafi A.A.
Title: Enterprise resource planning role in smart government transformation: cloud computing as a mediator in the Yemeni telecommunications public sector corporations
Abstract: Smart government uses smartphones to provide services to beneficiaries. Organizations face huge obstacles in their attempts to create an efficient methodology for smart government transformation because of the need for successful strategies. Enterprise resource planning and cloud computing are essential techniques for organizations to combat the rapid developments established by smart technologies. An efficient technology to support business requirements is essential, and failure frequently occurs because of the lack of an appropriate cloud computing service model. This research investigates the role of enterprise resource planning and cloud computing in smart government transformation and the role of cloud computing in mediating the relationship between enterprise resource planning and smart government transformation. The research used a descriptive-analytical approach, a questionnaire to collect data, and smart partial least squares for analysis. The research population included 177 employees using enterprise resource planning, applications, cloud computing service providers, and technical support specialists in Yemeni Telecommunications Public Sector Corporations. Because of the limited size of the research population, a careful enumeration method was employed for each individual, resulting in 177 individuals. The findings reveal a significant role for enterprise resource planning and cloud computing in smart government transformation and a crucial role for cloud computing in mediating the relationship between enterprise resource planning and smart government transformation. The findings of this research offer significant directions within the theoretical framework that supports this topic by combining enterprise resource planning, cloud computing, and smart government transformation. These results can help Yemeni Telecommunications Public Sector Corporations establish an approach for the transformation of smart government. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Kriz A.; Kriz A.; Goodman M.; Hessell T.; Barnes L.; Molloy C.
Title: Leader knowledge transformation and competence development: becoming-to-know and sensemaking through action learning
Abstract: Purpose – The purpose of this paper is to explain how action learning and sensemaking can be utilised effectively as tools for knowledge transformation. The motivation for this study was to stimulate growth in smaller owner-managed/family businesses through use of action learning. However, as our participatory action research process unfolded, the overarching research problem was clarified as how does action learning enable smaller owner-managed/family business leaders to transform their knowledge and competence? Jakubik’s knowledge management becoming-to-know framework and Sandberg and Tsoukas’ representational and detached-deliberate sensemaking provided the focal theories for our study. Design/methodology/approach – The authors applied participatory action research with action learning as the intervention for leaders of six smaller owner-managed/family businesses. The intervention consisted of eight half-day sessions over a fourteen-month period, preceded by in-depth leader interviews and company case analyses. Process-as-withness, process-as-narrative and contextualized explanation are used to present the participatory action research analysis, results and discussion. Findings – The authors highlight the underutilized value of action learning as a detached-deliberate sensemaking process for unsticking leader assumptions and transforming knowledge and competence. Participatory action research as a form of representational sensemaking enabled the development of a framework that synthesizes how action learning facilitates sensegiving, sensetaking, sensebreaking and ultimately meaning making in a leader becoming-to-know process. This study responds to Jakubik’s request for a greater use and understanding of action-oriented and experiential approaches to understand how knowledge evolves. Originality/value – Action learning is not new but thus far researchers have not fully explained how this peer-supported process theoretically and practically facilitates effective individual and organizational change. In this paper, the authors explain the action learning processes involved in unsticking and sensebreaking leaders’ affective, cognitive and/or sensory assumptions and meaning making processes to transform knowledge and competence development. © 2026 Anton Kriz, Alexandra (Ali) Kriz, Mike Goodman, Timothy Hessell, Lisa Barnes and Courtney Molloy.

Authors: Smirnova Y.; Saka T.N.; Hormiga E.
Title: Student distrust of AI in entrepreneurship education contexts: development and validation of an empirical scale
Abstract: Purpose – As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more embedded into higher education, it is essential to understand why some students remain sceptical. This study aims to develop and validate a scale that measures university students' distrust of AI within the context of entrepreneurship education. Design/methodology/approach – A three-phase mixed-method research design was used, combining qualitative item development with quantitative psychometric validation. Data was collected from 662 business students in Catalonia using a quota-based sampling strategy. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses were conducted to assess the scale's dimensional structure, reliability and validity. Findings – The results support a robust three-factor model of AI distrust comprising: (1) data protection distrust – contextual concerns about data use, (2) functional distrust – cognitive doubts about educational effectiveness and (3) distrust of AI replacing humans – emotional resistance to losing human interaction in learning. The final 9-item scale demonstrated strong internal consistency, convergent and discriminant validity and model fit across independent samples. Research limitations/implications – Although the study is regionally focused, the findings provide a foundation for future cross-cultural validation and longitudinal research to explore how student attitudes toward AI evolve over time. Cultural and technological variables should be considered when applying the scale beyond the original context. Practical implications – The scale can serve as a practical diagnostic tool for educators, curriculum designers, and developers to identify and address student distrust toward AI to ensure more inclusive AI adoption in entrepreneurship education. Originality/value – This is the first validated scale specifically designed to measure student distrust of AI in entrepreneurship education, offering both theoretical and practical value to researchers and practitioners. © Yelena Smirnova, Tugce Nuray Saka and Esther Hormiga

Authors: Wang A.; Tang M.; Cui G.; Peng L.
Title: Singing praises vs. venting frustration: Multi-dimensional satisfaction gaps as drivers of high-quality hotel reviews
Abstract: High-quality reviews reveal consumer satisfaction with product attributes and greatly affect the decisions of others. However, without incorporating consumer expectations, the motivations to share high-quality remain poorly understood. Drawing on expectation confirmation theory and motivation–hygiene theory, this study constructs positive and negative satisfaction gaps between expectations and evaluations and examines how these gaps affect the sharing of high-quality reviews. We adopt NLP and hierarchical clustering to identify satisfaction dimensions and generate sentiment scores and assess review quality using LLM. An analysis of 10,492 customer reviews from TripAdvisor shows that high-quality reviews are driven more by satisfaction than by dissatisfaction. Positive and negative satisfaction gaps differ in the dimensions involved and their effect sizes. The findings have meaningful practical implications for businesses to improve product performance and customer satisfaction and for review and e-commerce platforms to recommend high-impact reviews. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Le N.; Thai T.D.; Nguyen H.T.H.; Tran M.T.X.; Nguyen H.T.L.
Title: Bridging the perception–behavior gap through digitalization in the OCOP market: the role of QR code–enabled blockchain systems and consumers’ literacy
Abstract: The development of QR code–enabled blockchain (QRB) technology creates new opportunities for OCOP (One Commune One Product) products. This study examines how consumers' experiences with a QRB system impact their perceptions and purchase decisions. A comparative empirical study was conducted using a quota–sampled survey of two independent groups: Study 1 (400 inexperienced consumers) and Study 2 (400 consumers exposed to QRB). The results indicate that consumers exposed to QRB would perceive transparency and traceability. These stimuli could enhance perceived trustworthiness and novelty, reduce greenwashing, and promote consumers' purchase decisions. Furthermore, a key contribution of this study is the moderating role of consumers’ QR code–enabled blockchain literacy in bridging the perception–behavior gap based on the New Literacies Theory. Based on these findings, businesses could encourage consumers to experience QRB to enhance their purchase decisions. Finally, this study also proposes future research directions by exploring additional psychological factors. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Al-Hattami H.M.; Al-Sinawi S.
Title: Ethical reasoning and responsible use of ChatGPT in higher education: Integrating technology acceptance and moral cognition
Abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT into higher education has raised important questions about how students evaluate the ethical implications of AI-assisted academic practices and whether those evaluations are linked to intentions to use these tools responsibly. While previous research has largely focused on technology adoption and acceptance, it has paid less attention to the relationship between ethical reasoning and intentions to use these tools responsibly. This study develops and tests an integrated framework that combines the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and moral cognition theory to examine how technology perceptions and academic and cognitive factors relate to students’ ethical reasoning and intentions to use ChatGPT responsibly. The study used a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design among business and management students in Oman and analysed the data using structural equation modelling. The findings indicate that perceived ease of use, academic pressure, and moral disengagement are positively associated with ethical reasoning, whereas perceived usefulness is not significantly associated with ethical reasoning. Ethical reasoning is positively associated with behavioural intention to use ChatGPT responsibly. In contrast, ChatGPT usage does not significantly moderate the relationship between academic pressure and ethical reasoning. These findings suggest that students’ responsible-use intentions are associated with their ethical evaluations of ChatGPT-assisted academic practices, while conventional technology acceptance perceptions and usage frequency alone offer a more limited explanation of ethical reasoning. The study contributes to emerging research on responsible generative AI use by extending TAM beyond conventional adoption outcomes and integrating it with a moral cognition perspective. It highlights the relationship between ethical reasoning and responsible-use intentions while distinguishing ethical evaluation from technology acceptance and usage frequency. The findings also provide context-specific evidence from Omani higher education, while recognising the limitations of the cross-sectional design, self-reported measures, and a context-specific sample. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Xiao J.; Yang H.; Wu X.; Wang K.; Jiang C.; Hou M.
Title: How does China's unilateral visa-free policy affect its international aviation market? empirical evidence on passenger volume, flight frequency, and airfare
Abstract: China introduced a unilateral visa-free policy in late 2023 as part of its broader effort to restore international mobility and support post-pandemic economic reopening. The policy grants ordinary passport holders from selected countries visa-free entry to China for short stays, thereby reducing travel frictions and potentially stimulating inbound tourism and business travel. Against this background, this study examines how China's unilateral visa-free policy has shaped the recovery and structural evolution of its international aviation market. Using route-level data from January 2023 to March 2025, we apply a staggered difference-in-differences (DID) framework to identify policy-induced changes in passenger volume, flight frequency, and airfare. The empirical results show that the policy substantially increases international passenger volume and flight frequencies. Airfares rise in the short term following the policy change, but this increase fades over time. Heterogeneity analyses further uncover substantial variation across regional markets and routes departing from Chinese airports with different levels of slot constraints. Specifically, on European routes, capacity expansion is driven primarily by the deployment of larger aircraft, whereas on Asian routes it is achieved mainly through increased flight frequency. Moreover, estimated airfare effects are positive on routes serving more slot-constrained airports and negative on routes serving less constrained airports, consistent with differences in the flexibility of capacity adjustment. These findings offer nuanced insights into the joint responses of passenger traffic, airline capacity, and airfares to visa facilitation, providing actionable guidance for airline capacity optimization and strategic aviation policy design. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Haqqani K.; Aleem M.; Mahmood S.; Alhussan A.A.; Khafaga D.S.; Eid M.M.; El-kenawy E.-S.M.
Title: Green intellectual capital and organizational learning: pathways to sustainable innovation and firm performance in Pakistani SMEs
Abstract: Purpose – This study investigates the impact of green intellectual capital (GIC) on green innovation (GI) and firm performance (FP) in Pakistani manufacturing small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). The study aims to analyze the mediating role of organizational learning capability (OLC) between GIC and GI and evaluate the direct and indirect effects of GIC and GI on FP. Design/methodology/approach – A quantitative research approach was employed, using partial least squares structural equation modeling to test the proposed relationships. The data were collected from 452 executives across Pakistani manufacturing SMEs in sectors including textile and apparel, food processing, and chemical manufacturing. A structured, self-administered survey was conducted over a three-month period (February to April 2025). Findings – The results demonstrate that GIC significantly influences GI and FP, with OLC mediating the relationship between GIC and GI. GI also positively impacts FP, both directly and indirectly through GIC and OLC. Practical implications – This study contributes to the resource-based and dynamic capabilities literature by highlighting the role of intangible green resources in driving sustainable innovation and enhancing firm performance. For SMEs, investing in intangible green assets and integrating organizational learning capabilities are crucial for fostering innovation and achieving sustainability. Policymakers and business leaders can leverage these insights to support green innovation and promote long-term sustainable growth. Originality/value – This study expands on the RBT and dynamic capabilities theory by examining the role of GIC and OLC in driving GI and sustainable firm performance within Pakistani SMEs, offering a unique contribution to the literature on sustainability in emerging economies. © 2026 Kanwal Haqqani, Muhammad Aleem, Shahid Mahmood, Amel Ali Alhussan, Doaa Sami Khafaga, Marwa M. Authors: Sahhar Y.; van Fenema P.C.; van Strien J.
Title: Taking the pulse of service ecosystems: exploring viability through valences and forms of becoming
Abstract: Purpose – Service ecosystems are arenas for value co-creation, yet how and why they become (un)viable over time remains underspecified. This study explores how service ecosystem viability unfolds through the interplay of valence (positive-negative) and forms of becoming (building-dwelling). Design/methodology/approach – Drawing on a rich palette of qualitative data from a single-case study of a two-year open-innovation initiative in the Netherlands in a tightly regulated, high-tech public–business context, we scrutinize how intra- and inter-organizational dynamics evolve within and contribute to the viability of service ecosystems. Findings – The findings reveal that intra-ecosystem interactions and performative landscape factors – including institutional arrangements, rules of engagement, legislation and inter-ecosystem trade-offs – episodically shape the viability of service ecosystems. Critically, actors’ relational embeddedness and awareness strongly influence the viability of the service ecosystem. Originality/value – Theoretically, the study advances service research by offering a process-sensitive account of viability as a dynamic interplay of bright-dark valences and building-dwelling becoming. We propose an integrative framework with theoretical and empirical cues for tracing service ecosystem viability episodically. Managerially, the study offers pathways and warns of pitfalls in “wayfinding, ” fostering organizations’ capability to navigate resiliently in service ecosystems. 2026 © Yasin Sahhar, Paul C. van Fenema and Jeroen van Strien

Authors: Xu H.; Wu H.; Zheng W.; Chan K.C.; Fang Q.
Title: Business groups and affiliated firms’ digital transformation
Abstract: Considering the practical challenges of digital transformation (DT), this study examines whether business groups facilitate affiliate firms’ DT through internal markets. Using a sample of Chinese firms, we find that group-affiliated firms exhibit higher levels of DT than comparable unaffiliated firms. The effect operates primarily through internal intangible markets—labor, technology and entrepreneurship—rather than internal capital markets. Central government-controlled business groups promote DT more effectively, whereas greater intra-group cultural diversity can impede DT. This impact is stronger under high product market competition, low economic policy uncertainty, low regional digitalization, low industrial structure upgrading and strong government support, and in provinces where DT is emphasized. Moreover, an affiliate’s total factor productivity and Tobin’s Q both increase after its DT is promoted by a business group. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Sarkar G.; Putrevu V.S.C.; Shukla S.K.
Title: Understanding Jamtara cybercriminals: poverty, opportunity, and the rise of organized criminal networks
Abstract: Despite having limited formal education, individuals from India’s Jamtara and New Jamtara regions, as well as several economically disadvantaged districts, have become adept at orchestrating sophisticated cybercrimes by exploiting societal trust and systemic vulnerabilities. Beyond targeting domestic victims, these criminal activities have evolved into transnational operations, affecting individuals worldwide. Cybercrimes have been normalized within their local communities, with criminal enterprises increasingly structured as well-organized, family-run businesses, perpetuating a cycle of intergenerational involvement. To investigate the socio-economic and human factors underpinning this evolution and persistence of the Jamtara cybercrime networks over the past decade, this study employs a rigorous qualitative methodology. First, a systematic narrative review is conducted, integrating document analysis of credible media sources to identify recurring patterns, operational strategies, and network dynamics. To further enhance validity and depth, methodological triangulation is achieved through semi-structured interviews with four key offenders from Jamtara, providing firsthand insights into their practices and motivations. The findings reveal a chronological evolution of the Jamtara networks, highlighting behavioral drivers such as advanced social engineering capabilities, sophisticated concealment of traceability, strong social and moral support systems, organized division of labor, and rapid financial gains. Additional enablers include informal “crash courses” in cybercrime, the commodification of illicit services known as “cybercrime-as-a-service,” and systemic factors such as policing deficiencies, political corruption, weak cyber legislation, and socio-economic pressures, including poverty and unemployment, that render cybercrime an attractive career path for young people. The results underscore the pressing need for substantial systemic reforms to address the root causes of cybercrime in these regions. A holistic approach that integrates strengthened law enforcement, social reforms, and robust anti-corruption measures is essential to dismantle the socio-economic conditions that enable the proliferation of the Jamtara cybercriminal network. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Knels V.; Guenther E.; Guenther T.
Title: Integration matters: the relationships between environmental management control systems and environmental and financial performance
Abstract: Purpose – This study investigates the integration of environmental management control systems (EMCSs) into core business activities and its implication for environmental performance (EP) and financial performance (FP). Prior research highlights the potential benefits of EMCSs but often overlooks integration dimensions and their role in organizational change. This study aims to address these gaps by differentiating the technical and management dimensions of integration in a cross-sectional context. Design/methodology/approach – This study employs a dyadic survey of 112 large German firms to empirically assess the influence of different dimensions on the relationship between EMCSs and performance. Using partial least squares structural equation modeling, we test whether management and technical integration moderate the effectiveness of EMCSs in improving EP and FP. Findings – The results indicate that integrated EMCSs are associated with improvements in both EP and FP, though the impact varies based on the type of integration. Management integration strengthens the positive link between EMCSs and EP, whereas the positive relationship between EMCSs and FP is contingent upon high levels of technical integration. These findings indicate the conditions under which a win–win scenario for EP and FP may emerge. Originality/value – This study distinguishes technical and management integration as contingencies in the EMCS–performance relationship and interprets them as deliberate change activities that enable organizational change. The findings suggest that integration can support both performance improvement and organizational transformation tendencies, refining contingency theory and offering managers guidance on embedding sustainability while balancing environmental and financial goals. © 2025 Valeria Knels, Edeltraud Guenther and Thomas Guenther

Authors: Homer S.T.
Title: From fragmentation to integration: Rethinking the measurement of responsible management education
Abstract: Responsible Management Education (RME) has become a central agenda within business schools, as institutions seek to prepare graduates capable of addressing complex sustainability and societal challenges. Despite its growing prominence, approaches to evaluating RME remain fragmented, with studies measuring diverse educational, institutional and societal outcomes using inconsistent conceptualisations and indicators. This study systematically reviews the contemporary literature to examine how RME is currently measured and develop a more coherent conceptual framework for evaluation. Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic literature review of 62 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2016 and 2026 using the Scopus database—an AI-assisted, human-in-the-loop thematic synthesis identified and consolidated 328 measurement-related concepts. The synthesis identified five complementary measurement domains: implementation, learning, behaviour, performance and impact, alongside five stakeholder groups: students, educators, institutions, industry and society. Building on these findings, the study proposes the Integrated Responsible Management Education Measurement Framework (IRMEF) as a multidimensional conceptual evaluation architecture that organises these domains and stakeholder perspectives. Rather than representing an empirically validated measurement model, the IRMEF provides a common conceptual vocabulary for organising existing approaches and guiding future evaluation and empirical validation. It provides a foundation for greater theoretical coherence and methodological consistency while supporting business schools, accreditation bodies, and policymakers seeking more balanced, multidimensional, and contextually appropriate approaches to RME evaluation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Ante L.
Title: Micro-processes of paradoxical learning: how entrepreneurs reconcile financial and ESG tensions
Abstract: This study explores the micro-processes through which entrepreneurs learn to reconcile the inherent paradoxical tensions between financial viability and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) goals. Drawing on organizational paradox theory and entrepreneurial learning, we conducted in-depth interviews with entrepreneurs leading ventures that explicitly integrate financial and ESG objectives. Relying on a Gioia methodology for inductive analysis, we developed a process model of paradoxical learning that reveals four interconnected micro-processes: (1) cognitive reframing, (2) emotional regulation, (3) behavioral experimentation, and (4) social sensemaking. Our findings demonstrate that entrepreneurs move through three distinct phases of paradoxical learning: (a) tension recognition, (b) paradox acceptance, and (c) integration capability development. We find that digital technologies, digital business models, and digitally mediated feedback loops shape these learning processes in distinctive ways, accelerating experimentation cycles, enabling distributed sensemaking across digital ecosystems, and providing data-driven tools for developing integration capabilities. The findings contribute to entrepreneurial learning theory by revealing the dynamic capabilities required for managing persistent contradictions, extending organizational paradox theory to the entrepreneurial context, and offering practical insights for entrepreneurs seeking to foster integrated value creation. The study reveals that successful ESG integration requires not just strategic thinking but fundamental shifts in how entrepreneurs perceive, experience, and resolve competing demands, with digital ventures facing unique tensions and opportunities that shape the nature and trajectory of paradoxical learning. Authors: Martinez L.; Arenas J.B.; Vettori B.; Tellioglu H.; Keserü I.
Title: Who shapes the streets? A stakeholder analysis of street redesign processes in European cities
Abstract: Street redesign projects are used to support urban regeneration and advance sustainable mobility by modernising road infrastructure, reallocating public space, and facilitating the use of non-motorised transport modes. Such projects often face conflicting positions among diverse actors due to differing interests and degrees of influence in decision-making. Yet, there remains a limited understanding of who these stakeholders are and how they shape street redesign processes. This paper addresses this gap through qualitative case study research conducted in five cases across four cities: Brussels, Istanbul, Stockholm, and Vienna. The study combines media content analysis with semi-structured interviews with local actors to identify and categorise stakeholders involved in ongoing street redesign projects that affect urban mobility. This mixed qualitative approach allows for an examination of how stakeholders are represented in public discourse and how they perceive their roles within planning and implementation processes. Five stakeholder groups were identified across cases: public authorities, public organisations, local businesses, civic organisations, and inhabitants and visitors. The findings reveal that stakeholder interests are at times conflictual, yet they also share overlapping goals and concerns. Moreover, public authorities dominate formal decision-making, while other stakeholders influence outcomes through visibility, participation, and advocacy. The analysis demonstrates that influence is exercised not only through institutional authority but also through representation, legitimacy, and communication. The paper contributes theoretically by extending understandings of collaborative urban and transport planning within street redesign processes, and practically by offering relevant insights for policymakers and practitioners. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Chen Y.-Y.; Ahlstrom D.
Title: Knowledge governance in internationalized business groups: Ownership ties, structural holes, and headquarters innovation in Taiwan
Abstract: How do internationalized business groups (BGs) use ownership-based governance to support headquarters (HQ) innovation? Drawing on internalization theory and network brokerage arguments, this study treats equity ties as a formal ownership network and examines how its structure shapes HQ technological innovation. We conceptualize structural hole spanning in this ownership network as ownership-network brokerage potential rather than as direct evidence of realized knowledge exchange among affiliates. Using 240 Taiwan-based high-tech BGs during 2008–2012 (24,385 affiliate-year observations), we find that greater structural hole spanning within the BG ownership network is associated with higher HQ patent output. We further show that BG internationalization, measured by foreign assets held, positively conditions this relationship, although the moderation evidence is interpreted cautiously. The findings are consistent with the view that cross-border operations increase knowledge heterogeneity, while ownership-based governance helps protect, transfer, and recombine dispersed knowledge for HQ innovation. This study contributes to international business research on BGs, ownership networks, and innovation by clarifying how internationalized BGs differ from MNEs yet confront cross-border knowledge-governance problems, when ownership-based networks create innovation value, and how internationalization operates as a knowledge-governance contingency rather than as a purely additive driver of innovation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Jin X.; Mou S.
Title: Justifying membership fees through quality and pricing in a competitive supply chain
Abstract: While membership-based retail has experienced substantial growth, how membership stores can justify membership fees through product quality remains underexplored from a supply chain perspective. This study examines a supply chain consisting of a manufacturer, a membership store, and a traditional retailer, where consumers differ in their perceived value of exclusive membership services and may exhibit the sunk cost effect generated by the prepaid membership fees. We investigate how this behavioural mechanism affects retail pricing and the manufacturer's quality investment. The results show that the sunk cost effect not only reshapes the membership store's pricing strategy but also affects the manufacturer's quality investment decision, thereby enabling the membership store to justify its membership fee. The equilibrium outcomes are jointly determined by the membership store's competitive advantage and the perceived membership fee. Based on these two dimensions, we derive a strategic decision matrix comprising four equilibrium regimes. We use several business cases to help understand how membership stores can adjust their quality and pricing decisions according to their specific characteristics to justify membership fees. This study thus translates analytical results into a managerial framework and provides managerial insights for membership stores’ strategic decision-making. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Machingura T.; Mbewe J.K.; Adetunji O.; Maware C.
Title: An assessment of the impact of lean framework design and lean enablers on business operational performance
Abstract: Purpose – The research explores the relationships between the effectiveness of lean framework design, lean implementation enablement and business operational success, thereby establishing a broader ground for successful lean implementation. Design/methodology/approach – A questionnaire was used to collect data across various industries in South Africa. A total of 198 valid responses were obtained and analyzed using SMART-PLS 4. Findings – A strong relationship was found between effective lean framework design, lean implementation enablement and business operational success. Also, lean implementation enablement mediates the relationship between lean framework design effectiveness and business operational success. This result indicates that paying proper attention to a lean enabling environment increases the likelihood of improving operational performance through the adoption of lean frameworks. Originality/value – Researchers have attempted to understand how the presence of enablers affects the success of lean, and the role of lean frameworks in the success of lean implementation. No study has considered contextualized framework design and the mediatory influence of lean enablers on the effectiveness of lean frameworks, and their interactive influence on the success of lean implementation. By grounding this investigation in contingency theory and socio-technical systems theory, this study addresses this gap. It illuminates how organizations can strategically integrate framework design with lean enablers to achieve superior operational performance. © 2026 Tinotenda Machingura, Josephine Koketso Mbewe, Olufemi Adetunji and Catherine Maware

Authors: Vörösmarty G.
Title: Doing it right—Which factors drive ethical procurement?
Abstract: Recent developments have introduced significant challenges to ensuring supply continuity for purchasing professionals. However, limited research exists on how these individuals perceive the ethical dimensions of these emerging challenges. This study conducts a review of the procurement and supply chain literature to identify key factors influencing ethical behaviour comprehensively. To refine and prioritize these factors, a multi-stage Delphi analysis was conducted with a panel of 30 procurement experts. The findings offer a structured overview of the factors based on their perceived importance and the level of expert consensus. The results suggest that while business ethics have been studied within procurement and supply chain contexts, evolving conditions present new ethical considerations that merit further investigation. The set of 21 identified factors, of which 11 are based on the literature and 10 were identified during the study, provides a more holistic perspective on the determinants shaping ethical behaviour within procurement practices. Challenges in supply management that demand swift responses indicate that informal components of ethical culture are particularly influential: notably, the personal values of individuals play a significant role; however, greater attention should be paid to leadership influence, the strategic importance attributed to procurement, and differences of procurement situations. From a theoretical perspective, the results underscore the need to expand existing ethical frameworks to better address the complexities of supply chains. The practical implication is that, in the case of supply chain disruptions, efforts should be made to strengthen informal control instruments related to corporate transparency. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Shalev L.; Heim I.; Kalyuzhnova Y.; Laker B.
Title: Non-market strategies and environmental management: Framework for effective sustainable transformation
Abstract: As environmental concerns intensify, businesses are increasingly adopting non-market strategies (NMS) to navigate regulatory pressures and improve environmental performance (EP). However, there has been no systematic effort to synthesise existing studies on the environmental benefits of NMS and to provide an integrated conceptual understanding of the field. As a result, there remains limited understanding of how these strategies influence firms’ EP and the boundary conditions under which they are effective. To address this gap, this study conducts a systematic review of 151 peer-reviewed articles and develops a comprehensive integrative framework linking NMS to firm-level EP. The framework highlights the effectiveness of combined NMS in comparison to single strategies, emphasising the role of dual legitimacy activation. This synthesis provides a foundation for more nuanced future research and offers practical guidance on aligning political engagement, governance capacity, and innovation investment to enhance sustained EP across varying institutional contexts. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Ernez M.; Said F.B.; de Bruyn C.; Meyer N.
Title: Sustainable entrepreneurship and green innovation in emerging economies: a bibliometric mapping of two decades of research
Abstract: Emerging economies are under significant sustainability pressures while also possessing great potential for innovation-driven entrepreneurship. However, the existing research on how these dynamics interact is fragmented and uneven. This study aims to map and synthesize the intellectual and conceptual frameworks of research on innovation and sustainable entrepreneurship in emerging economies. Conducting a bibliometric analysis of 504 documents indexed in Scopus and Web of Science from 2001 to 2024. Findings suggest that this field, while still relatively young, is growing rapidly. However, we observed that authorship is quite dispersed and that international collaboration is limited. The key themes in this area focus on green innovation and green entrepreneurial orientation (GEO). It was found that GEO significantly contributes to sustainability outcomes, with various mediating factors influencing these outcomes, including green intellectual capital, knowledge management, organizational support, and innovative sustainable business models. Notably, these relationships are further shaped by environmental awareness and green technological dynamism. Additionally, we identified disruptive innovation and ecosystem-level conditions as emerging, yet critically important avenues for future research. The policy implications suggest that strengthening innovation ecosystems in emerging economies requires expanding access to finance, building digital infrastructure and capabilities, and creating context-sensitive regulations that encourage green innovation and entrepreneurial experimentation. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Dadhich M.; Bhaumik A.; Hiran K.K.; Janarthanan M.
Title: Demystifying the enablers of business management students’ path towards sustainable entrepreneurship education: dual-edge SEM–ANN analysis
Abstract: This study quantifies the factors influencing business management students’ attitudes toward sustainable entrepreneurship education using the Theory of Planned Behavior framework. It investigates the impact of Cognitive Elements, Affective Elements, Behavioral Elements, and the Entrepreneurial Environment on entrepreneurial intention. The research utilizes 580 management students, enabling a comprehensive analysis of both the linear relationships posited by SEM and the nonlinear patterns captured by ANN. This methodological fusion offers a nuanced understanding of the complex interactions among the variables under study. The findings confirm significant relationships as hypothesized: Cognitive Elements, Affective Elements, Behavioral Elements, and the Entrepreneurial Environment significantly influence entrepreneurial intention among business management students. The study underscores integrating these factors into educational frameworks to enhance students’ attitudes toward sustainable entrepreneurship. This study contributes novelty by integrating advanced SEM–ANN analysis with the Theory of Planned Behavior and underscores the practical implications for educators and policymakers in fostering a new generation of business leaders committed to sustainable business practices and societal impact. © The Author(s) 2026.
