Authors: Gramberg T.; Burgel A.; Eggert A.; Bauernhansl T.
Title: Building resilient product portfolios in B2B manufacturing: A multi-criteria decision-making framework for managing disruptive factors
Abstract: This study develops a methodologically grounded decision-support framework for product portfolio management (PPM) in manufacturing business-to-business (B2B) firms, aimed at systematically addressing the growing challenges posed by disruptive change, particularly those arising from digital and sustainable transformations. A preliminary study and systematic literature review reveal that current evaluation approaches fall short in addressing these emerging challenges. To address this gap, the proposed PPM-specific framework integrates established multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) methods: the analytic hierarchy process (AHP), the decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory (DEMATEL), and the weighted sum model (WSM). In addition to the three established PPM target dimensions – value maximization, strategic fit, and balance – the proposed methodology introduces a fourth dimension: resilience to disruptive factors. This expanded framework enables a structured derivation and weighting of evaluation criteria, identification of interdependencies within the product portfolio, and a systematic assessment of the strategic value contribution of individual portfolio elements. A case study with a global automation technology provider and evaluation workshops with three additional globally operating B2B industrial firms demonstrate the framework's practical relevance. The results indicate enhanced transparency, more objective decision-making, and systematic portfolio governance. This research contributes a formal and transparent decision support tool that facilitates strategically robust portfolio design in times of disruptive transformation, thereby addressing critical gaps in existing literature. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Ma Y.; Wang W.; Cheng Y.
Title: Forecasting Crude Oil Futures Prices: A Stacking Model With Mixed-Frequency Predictors, Machine Learning, and Forecast Combination
Abstract: Low- and high-frequency data are widely used in crude oil futures price forecasting, and machine learning techniques exhibit strong performance. To enhance predictive accuracy, this study presents a stacking model that integrates mixed-frequency predictors, machine learning models, and forecast combination methods. Specifically, 18 low-frequency and 20 high-frequency predictors are selected, and 15 distinct machine learning models are applied for prediction. The forecasts of the top 10 individual models are screened based on out-of-sample performance over the past decade, then synthesized using the discounted mean squared prediction error combination method. Against 26 competing benchmarks, empirical results show that the proposed model consistently outperforms all benchmarks, underscoring the advantages of mixed-frequency data, machine learning, and combination methods. It further explores the model's dynamic forecast selection to clarify operational logic. In addition, we confirm its robustness across the business cycle and provide preliminary, small-sample evidence from the COVID-19 pandemic. © 2026 Wiley Periodicals LLC.

Authors: Udin U.; Nikzad M.; Chanthes S.; Sriboonlue P.
Title: Agile leadership and job satisfaction: Mediating role of job redesign within the framework of dynamic capability theory
Abstract: In today’s dynamic and highly competitive business environment, organizations face constant pressure to adapt quickly to changing market conditions, technological advancements, and evolving customer expectations. Agile leadership has emerged as a critical capability for driving organizational flexibility and enhancing employee outcomes. Despite growing interest in this leadership style, the mechanisms through which agile leadership influences job satisfaction remain underexplored. Grounded in Dynamic Capability Theory (DCT), this study investigates both the direct effect of agile leadership on job satisfaction and the mediating role of job redesign. A cross-sectional survey was administered to 167 employees of First MicroFinance Bank, Afghanistan, using validated measurement scales for agile leadership, job redesign, and job satisfaction. Data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with SmartPLS (version 3.3.0) to test the hypothesized relationships. The results reveal that agile leadership significantly enhances job satisfaction, demonstrating both a direct positive effect and an indirect positive effect through job redesign. Job redesign also emerged as a strong predictor of job satisfaction, highlighting its strategic importance for aligning work structures with employee needs and organizational goals. Mediation analysis confirmed that job redesign partially mediates the relationship between agile leadership and job satisfaction. These findings provide important theoretical insights into the dynamic capability perspective and offer practical implications for managers seeking to strengthen employee well-being and organizational outcomes through agile leadership and thoughtful job redesign strategies. © 2026 Conscientia Beam. Authors: Hadjielias E.; Christofi M.; Benedetti C.
Title: Between Financial and Socioemotional Wealth: Navigating Knotted Tensions in Family Business Innovation
Abstract: Current research on family business innovation tends to isolate individual tensions for analysis, while in reality, these tensions often arise in complex entanglements. To fill this research void, we focus on understanding how multiple tensions occur in the innovation process, how these tensions are entangled, and how they are managed. We turn to the financial wealth–socioemotional wealth [FW-SEW] trade-off, which is a useful lens for understanding how family managers address tensions in a family business. We draw on a semi-grounded multiple case study research that includes 51 in-depth interviews across six private Cypriot family businesses. To assist in interpretation and analysis and enhance the robustness of our findings, we triangulate our data with 53 observations and 288 documents across the cases. We identify three knotted innovation tensions sensed by family managers based on the FW-SEW trade-off: inclusive innovation, stewardship-focused innovation, and family routine innovation tensions. Our findings also reveal three corresponding strategies for managing knotted innovation tensions—controlled inclusivity, family-driven responsible innovation, and fostering family-business harmony—each aimed at balancing FW and SEW priorities. Our study re-conceptualizes innovation tension management in the family business as entanglements of multiple tensions that must be properly sensed and managed. © 2025 The Author(s). Authors: Wang M.; Wang N.; Gansterer M.
Title: Upgradable remanufacturing in the presence of green consumers: strategic analysis from a supply chain perspective
Abstract: Increasing consumer environmental consciousness drives many manufacturers to sell remanufactured products. Particularly, some offer upgraded remanufactured products equipped with critical components that match the quality of new ones. However, remanufacturing affects demand for new products, the supplier's wholesale pricing, and consequently, the manufacturer's profits. This study examines the manufacturer's remanufacturing strategy in the presence of green consumers by developing a model involving one supplier and one manufacturer. It encompasses no-remanufacturing, basic-remanufacturing, upgraded-remanufacturing, and hybrid-remanufacturing models. We find that when consumers place a high valuation on remanufactured products, the hybrid-remanufacturing model is optimal if the proportion of green consumers is medium, while the upgraded-remanufacturing model is optimal if the proportion of green consumers is high. If the proportion of green consumers is larger than a threshold and consumer valuation of remanufactured products is low, the basic-remanufacturing model is optimal. Interestingly, we also identify scenarios where the manufacturer benefits from not developing any remanufacturing business. When the production cost of critical components is low, the manufacturer's sale of upgraded remanufactured products leads to a win–win outcome. If the proportion of green consumers is large, remanufacturing enhances social welfare, but it may also decrease environmental performance. © 2025 International Federation of Operational Research Societies.

Authors: Quinn L.; Otero J.; Vinardell S.; Valderrama C.
Title: Toward a sustainable and resilient EU energy transition: Prospective life cycle assessment of material stocks and supply-chain alternatives
Abstract: The rapid expansion of clean-energy technologies is central to global decarbonization but intensifies reliance on critical raw materials, raising environmental and supply chain concerns that intensify toward mid-century. This study applies a prospective life cycle assessment (2000-2050) with temporal modeling of installed-capacity stocks and comprehensive uncertainty analysis, quantifying environmental burdens across six key technologies: solar photovoltaics, onshore and offshore wind, and three battery chemistries. The assessment compares business as usual (BAU) and regional supply chains aligned with the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA). This study captures the temporal evolution of installed-capacity stocks, supply chain variability, and the environmental trade-offs associated with alternative sourcing strategies. Results show mineral depletion reaching 1.99 × 109 kg Cu-eq in 2050, with NMC622 alone contributing over 70%, whereas solar PV and wind account for less than 2% owing to their lower material intensity. Within NMC622, nickel (43%) and copper (37%) dominate the depletion profile, followed by graphite and aluminum. Carcinogenic toxicity reaches 5.06 × 109 kg 1,4-DCB-eq, and embodied climate-change burdens reach 2.55 × 109 kg CO2-eq. China accounts for approximately half of the cradle-to-gate climate-change impact under BAU, dropping below 0.1% under diversified sourcing. Alternative sourcing reduces material depletion by approximately 3%, redistributing environmental pressures to EU and allied regions. Overall environmental burdens remain largely unchanged, indicating that supply diversification alone is insufficient. A resilient and sustainable energy transition will therefore require coordinated advances across multiple fronts, including low-impact battery chemistries, cleaner refining, and high-efficiency material recovery. Authors: De Stefano R.M.; Alonso-Martinez D.
Title: Regenerative business models in B Corps: seven multi-level criteria for identification, drivers of transition, and a maturity trajectory
Abstract: The body of literature on regenerative business models is growing rapidly. Nevertheless, three significant gaps remain unresolved: no operational criteria distinguish regenerative enterprises from sustainable firms; the drivers enabling transition toward regeneration remain poorly understood; and only a few frameworks explain how regenerative practices develop within organizations. Together, these gaps hinder coherent understanding of regenerative enterprises. This research aims to address these gaps through an exploratory qualitative study based on multiple case studies of Italian B Corps. Following a multi-stage selection process, seven B Corps with regenerative characteristics were selected for in-depth analysis. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using an abductive approach and the Gioia methodology. The findings reveal that visionary leadership, organizational culture, and authentic purpose are the most significant drivers of regenerative transition, whereas regulatory and market pressures play a comparatively marginal role. This result diverges from the prevailing assumptions in the circular economy literature. The contribution of the paper is fourfold. First, it adapts the analytical logic of the Multi-Level Perspective (MLP) to the regeneration domain, providing an integrative framework that links individual, organizational, and institutional dimensions. Second, it develops and validates seven multi-level operational criteria distinguishing regenerative enterprises from advanced sustainability-oriented firms. Third, it identifies and organizes the main drivers of regenerative transition within a multilevel framework. Fourth, it introduces regenerative maturity as an emerging evolutionary path inferred from cross-case patterns among pioneering regenerative firms. Finally, the paper outlines several operational guidelines for managers and policymakers seeking to promote systemic regenerative transitions. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Gadola S.; Trabucchi D.; Buganza T.
Title: Enhancing collaboration and knowledge sharing through intra-organizational platforms: a design science research study
Abstract: Platforms have revolutionized value creation by enabling efficient matchmaking between customer groups. While traditionally associated with external value exchange, platform thinking represents the mechanism that, through matchmaking, supports established firms to innovate by orchestrating available resources. While platforms are known in the literature for creating value by efficiently connecting external customer groups, their potential to support efficient collaboration among internal units in established organizations remains underexplored. How to adopt platform thinking to promote intra-organizational collaboration is also a problem faced by the manager of Confcooperative Lombardia, a business association supporting cooperatives in value creation, seeking to improve internal collaboration. By adopting a Design Science Research, which included physical and digital workshops involving the entire organization, this study developed an artifact that illustrates how platforms can serve as a framework for redesigning collaboration and knowledge sharing between internal units. Matchmaking becomes a ritual that employees can flexibly adopt to ask for support and share best practices. This research reframes platforms as tools for guiding collaboration within organizations, extending beyond their digital functionality. Since the platform operates as an intra-organizational process rather than a digital system, its functioning depends on empowering individuals, who collectively act as the algorithm that drives matchmaking and knowledge exchange. Employees are guided by agile and platform thinking as cultural frameworks that sustain collaboration, presenting platforms as processes that can be scaled across the organization. By leveraging this process, organizations can better utilize resources distributed across various units. Managers, in turn, can adopt platform thinking into organizational culture to create a scalable process that guides internal collaboration and knowledge sharing. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Cammarano A.; Avallone M.; Caputo M.
Title: Mapping the latent nexus between open innovation and the circular economy: Evidence from application-oriented studies
Abstract: Scholarly interest in the relationship between the circular economy and open innovation is increasing, yet the literature that explicitly discusses both concepts remains limited. A focused review identifies only 81 journal articles that formally address the two themes together, and this stream highlights the lack of cumulative and structured evidence as a major gap. This paper argues that the nexus is underestimated, because a substantial body of application-oriented research incorporates openness mechanisms within circular initiatives, or circular strategies within open innovation settings, without making the connection explicit. A structured database is built from Scopus-indexed journal articles published between 2019 and 2025 and reporting business-oriented applications. Articles primarily framed around either circular economy or open innovation are coded to examine whether constructs from the other domain are present within the described applications. The mapping covers 51 circular economy constructs and 43 open innovation constructs, organized into 13 and 8 macro-categories, respectively. Relationships are assessed through three complementary measures capturing pairwise associations, combined with a frequent pattern analysis to identify recurrent multi-construct configurations. The results reveal a structured nexus that is broader than suggested by the explicit joint literature. Positioned against prior work, the evidence confirms core relationships, extends previously suggested linkages, identifies emerging connections, and shows that some assumed relationships are weak or secondary. The paper contributes a construct-level evidence map and identifies recurring configurational patterns between openness and circularity. It also advances the concept of Open Circular Business Model Innovation as an integrative perspective linking openness mechanisms, circular strategies, and governance configurations, while providing guidance for future research and managerial practice. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Yaraghi N.; Gomes J.F.; Ahokangas P.
Title: Leading the transition: How companies create nature-positive value through integrated capitals and innovation
Abstract: The shift from reducing environmental harm to actively restoring ecosystems is redefining sustainability practice. This study examines how firms transition toward Nature-Positive Business Models (N-PBMs), business models that contribute to biodiversity recovery and ecosystem integrity, drawing on 21 semi-structured interviews with CEOs, sustainability managers, and operational leaders in the energy, ICT, and construction sectors in Northern Ostrobothnia, Finland. Using thematic analysis that combines deductive coding across six capital dimensions (natural, financial, human, intellectual, social, and production) with inductive identification of emergent patterns, we find that nature-positive transformation is driven not by isolated practices but by the coordinated alignment of leadership, financial structures, innovation, stakeholder engagement, and governance. Leadership acts as the key coordinating force, while cross-capital synergies enable firms to integrate ecological and economic objectives. Theoretically, the study positions N-PBMs as systemic configurations of interacting organizational elements rather than a distinct set of practices, offering guidance for firms and policymakers embedding biodiversity goals into strategy. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Kumpas G.
Title: Federal broadband investment and rural business formation: Evidence from rejected applicants
Abstract: Evaluations of the 2009 Recovery Act's $7.2 billion broadband programs (BIP and BTOP) typically compare funded areas to eligible areas that never sought the money, because no public file records who applied and lost. I hand-build that record from archived NTIA application data: a universe of 328 U.S. counties intersected by the proposed service areas of rejected BIP/BTOP infrastructure applications and by no funded project. The roster delivers a diagnostic and an estimate. The diagnostic: in a county-level eligibility universe reconstructed from the criteria used in the literature, 47 percent of the “eligible, unfunded” control counties are rejected applicants. Eligibility-based control groups therefore mix places that never revealed demand for federal investment with places that revealed demand and were denied, in proportions set by each program's rejection rate. The estimate: after a placebo adjustment netting out pre-completion drift, funded counties ended up with about 0.8 percent more business establishments than rejected applicants, on the order of 51,000 additional business locations, while county-aggregate employment shows no detectable effect. That effect holds at 0.77 to 0.94 percent under all three control universes, so the payoff is diagnostic rather than corrective: the paper reveals what the standard control group contains and supplies the applicant-conditional data future evaluations need. Competitive-award programs such as the $42 billion BEAD rollout generate exactly such records. © 2026 The Author

Authors: Shakya S.; Ammons J.D.
Title: Town, gown, and touchdowns: How athletic reclassification shapes local entrepreneurial ecosystems
Abstract: Local business activity can change when a major local institution gains or loses public status. We study one clear example: when colleges move up or down in athletic division. We treat these moves as public status signals and test whether nearby business outcomes change. Using U.S. business records from 2003 to 2023, we compare places near schools that reclassified with similar places near schools that did not. We examine 11 types of reclassification and four predictions about direction, distance, and football effects. We find upward moves tend to increase local sales and employment more than business counts. Higher-profile moves affect areas farther from campus. Football-related moves have larger effects. Downward moves do not create uniform decline. They shift activity across nearby areas. The results show that visibility shocks can shape local economies. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Elf P.; Verfuerth C.; Pasa Gómez C.
Title: Disrupting emerging consumer cultures: The role of ‘avalanche events’ in uprooting and reorganising (un)sustainable consumption practices in Brazil
Abstract: Amidst the environmental breakdown fuelled by unsustainable consumption practices, attempts to introduce the necessary change have been both slow and insufficient. Providing a potential opportunity to revise existing consumption practices, crises caused by significant events can disrupt existing lifestyles and practices, forcing people to reorganise their daily routines. Drawing on mixed-methods data collected in Brazil at two points during the COVID-19 lockdowns, we interrogate how the pandemic functioned as a disruptive ‘avalanche’ event that uprooted existing consumption practices and prompted shifts towards more sustainable consumption. Our findings show an increased awareness of environmental issues and motivations to change existing practices. However, initial shifts in consumer practices following the breaking and (re-)making of consumption practices were absorbed by emerging online systems of provision that stalled a shift towards lasting, sustainable consumption patterns. We examine how individual agency interacts with new online consumption opportunities, reflecting on the extent to which disruptive events can reshape consumption patterns. Finally, we highlight the need for active structural support from societal actors—such as businesses and legislators—to create the enabling systems required to translate motivation into lasting change. © The Author(s) 2026. Authors: Hossain M.A.; Li S.X.; Malek M.A.
Title: Risk preference, investment decision, and household welfare: Evidence from a microcredit experiment in Bangladesh
Abstract: Recent microcredit field experiments document low microcredit uptake and heterogeneous treatment effects. We posit the risk preference of households as a possible explanation. In a randomized field experiment in Bangladesh, we find that, in response to a microcredit intervention, household risk preference is significantly associated with microcredit uptake and its outcomes. Households with a more risk-seeking attitude are more likely to take microcredit, rent more land under fixed-rental contracts than share-cropping, adopt more technology, and expand businesses; these responses are accompanied by higher total income. In contrast, risk-averse households did not show such gains. Our results suggest that risk preference is an important dimension of heterogeneity in microcredit uptake and responses to the intervention. Authors: He M.; Ragmoun W.; Sibghatullah A.; Khudoykulov K.
Title: The role of AI capability and green supply chain practices in driving innovation: Moderated mediation of knowledge sharing and organizational learning orientation in Chinese enterprises
Abstract: This research determines direct impacts of artificial intelligence capability (AIC), green supply chain practices (GSCP), and enterprise management support (EMS) on innovation performance (IP). However, examining mediating role of knowledge sharing (KS) and moderated mediating impact of organizational learning orientation (OLO) within Chinese business context. Quantitative research design was employed by using survey data collected from 580 respondents showing diverse range of enterprises across China. Established and validated measurement scales were adopted for operationalizing the constructs of study. Proposed conceptual framework was analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) through Smart PLS. The analysis of study was carried out in two stages: assessment of measurement model for establishing reliability and validity, followed by evaluation of structural model to test direct, indirect and moderated mediation relationships. Outcome of study show that AIC, GSCP, and EMS show significant positive effects on both KS and IP. Additionally, KS serves as significant partial mediator in relationships among these organizational capabilities and innovation outcomes. This indicate that knowledge exchange shows significant mechanism through which enterprises convert strategic resources into enhanced innovation performance. Moreover, additional direct pathways also contribute towards innovation success. The outcomes further indicate that OLO positively influence KS and significantly strengthens indirect effects of AIC, GSCP and EMS on IP through KS. Specifically mediating effects of KS becomes more pronounced in organizations characterized by higher levels of learning orientation, by highlighting crucial role of organizational learning in amplifying innovation benefits derived from technological, managerial and sustainability-oriented capabilities. This research also contributes towards literature by integrating digital capability, sustainable supply chain management, knowledge management, and organizational learning perspectives into comprehensive framework for explaining enterprise innovation. Findings of study offers significant insights for managers and policy makers to underscore the need for investing in artificial intelligence capabilities, environmentally sustainable supply chain practices, supportive management structures, and learning-oriented organizational cultures. Authors: Lin T.-C.; Lin B.M.T.
Title: Scheduling optimization of optical lens polishing
Abstract: Optical systems have achieved notable progress in focusing and imaging technologies; however, manual grinding remains indispensable, resulting in elevated costs, extended timelines, and inefficiencies. These difficulties are compounded by operational constraints, uneven machine utilization, and risks of order delays and escalating expenses, which threaten customer trust and business stability. Fine grinding, a vital stage in lens manufacturing, includes trial processing testing, and mass production, with setup time identified as a major determinant of production efficiency. This study integrates setup times into scheduling decisions to enhance monthly order fulfillment. The objectives are to reduce tardiness costs and optimize both machine utilization and overall efficiency. Three approaches are examined: manual scheduling, dispatching rules, and an integer programming model. Results demonstrate that the mathematical model achieves dominant efficiency when order volumes match capacity and reduces tardiness penalties to one-fourth of those under manual scheduling when capacity is exceeded, underscoring its practical relevance for lens manufacturers. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Gidage M.; Bhide S.
Title: Corporate Reputation as the Nexus: Linking Moral and Social Responsibility, Green Practices, and Organizational Performance
Abstract: This study explores the intervening role of corporate reputation within the nexus of moral and social responsibility, green practices at work, and organizational performance. It aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of how organizations can utilize moral and social responsibility and green practices at work to enhance their competitive advantage while fulfilling their social obligations. Employing a quantitative approach, the research utilizes survey data from organizations in India and applies path analysis to test the hypothesized relationships. The findings confirm that moral and social responsibility, and green practices at work, positively influence organizational performance. This study offers new insights into how green practices at work and social and moral responsibility are not only ethical imperatives but also strategic assets that enhance both reputation and performance, particularly in emerging markets like India. The results underscore the importance of integrating moral and social responsibility, as well as green practices at work, into organizational strategies to boost performance and reputation. Business leaders and policymakers in emerging markets can use these insights to foster a culture of ethical behavior and sustainability, driving long-term success. By emphasizing moral and social responsibility, this research highlights the broader societal impact of ethical practices. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Limited 2024.

Authors: Lee E.; Wang Y.; Zhao H.
Title: Who will generate buzz for you? Predicting review writers for local businesses and online sellers
Abstract: Despite extensive research on electronic word of mouth, few studies predict which existing buyers will write reviews, although reviews are critical for businesses seeking online buzz. A key challenge is identifying features that link a potential reviewer to a specific product. Drawing on two ostensibly opposing social mechanisms—homophily and differentiation—we derive two review-style-matching measures that capture a consumer's tendency to bond with existing reviewers or stand out from them. Rating style matching reflects similarity between a user and a product's existing reviewers in rating tendencies, while topic matching captures similarity in the topics they discuss. We also construct measures of users’ review experience, which interact with review style matching in shaping review decisions. Predictive analytics using data from two platforms show that the proposed theory-driven features substantially improve performance relative to baseline user-level characteristics. On average, AUC increases by about 32% when the proposed features are incorporated. More importantly, the results reveal that review decisions are multi-dimensional: users can exhibit homophily in rating styles while simultaneously pursuing differentiation in topic coverage, and vice versa. Rather than a binary choice, homophily and differentiation emerge as concurrent dimension-specific tendencies. We further identify experience-based conditions under which different social strategies arise, showing that both the depth and breadth of review experience shape review decisions. These patterns extend social theories of online participation by showing that similarity-seeking and distinctiveness-seeking are not mutually exclusive but operate jointly across behavioral dimensions, and they enable more targeted identification of existing consumers as potential review writers. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Kashif A.; Maseda A.; Iturralde T.
Title: Harnessing social capital in family firms: unlocking new insights and future directions
Abstract: Social capital (SC) is deeply embedded in the dynamics of family firms—the world’s most prevalent business form—shaping interactions within the family, across the organization, and with external stakeholders. Despite growing scholarly interest, research on SC in family firms remains fragmented, often examining its dimensions in isolation or within narrowly defined contexts. This study offers a comprehensive and integrative perspective on SC as a multidimensional and ambivalent resource in family firms, highlighting both its strategic benefits and its potential constraints. Drawing on a bibliometric–systematic literature review of 222 articles published in leading journals, we identify four thematic domains: (1) social and business networks, (2) governance and succession, (3) innovation and knowledge management, and (4) family SC. Across these domains, SC operates through the interplay of structural, relational, and cognitive dimensions, as well as through bonding and bridging mechanisms that connect internal cohesion with external openness. The review reveals key theoretical tensions, including the tradition–innovation paradox and the “dark sides” of SC, such as overembeddedness, groupthink, and strategic rigidity. Building on these insights, we develop a structured research agenda with short-, medium-, and long-term priorities. These priorities emphasize the need for dynamic and multilevel models of SC, deeper theoretical integration with socioemotional wealth and dynamic capabilities, and comparative research across cultural and institutional contexts. By consolidating dispersed knowledge and theorizing from emergent patterns in the literature, this review advances theory and offers practical guidance for leveraging SC in family firms. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Gharbi M.; Jarboui A.
Title: Digitalization and Sustainable Business Practices: The Role of Carbon Footprint in European Firms
Abstract: Purpose: This study examines how digital transformation moderates the relationship between Sustainable Business Practices and digital transformation. Specifically, it aims to clarify whether and how Carbon Footprint strengthens or weakens the impact of digital transformation on Sustainable Business Practices. Design/Methodology/Approach: Using panel data from 250 UK-listed companies over the period 2012–2022, we apply multiple regression analyses to test both the direct effects of digital transformation on Sustainable Business Practices and the moderating role of digital transformation. Findings: The results indicate that digitalization has a positive and statistically significant impact on the implementation of sustainable business practices among European firms. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the carbon footprint acts as a significant moderating variable, strengthening the relationship between digitalization and sustainability. Specifically, firms with lower carbon footprints tend to derive greater sustainability benefits from digitalization compared to high-emission firms. Originality/Value: This research addresses a critical gap in European sustainability studies by contextualizing digitalization within carbon-intensive sectors. The integration of carbon footprint as a moderator reflects the growing importance of emission accountability under EU regulations such as the CSRD and the European Green Deal. © 2025 Wiley Periodicals LLC.

Authors: Gantino R.; Widodo A.M.; Ruswanti E.; Cahyadi L.; Prastyani D.
Title: Determinants of Corporate Value in Several Industrial Sectors in Indonesia
Abstract: The value of companies engaged in various fields is influenced by many factors, therefore this study aims to determine the influence of profitability, activities, solvency, liquidity, company size, business strategy and intellectual capital on the value of companies listed in the Non Consumer Cyclical, Consumer Cycli-cal, Property & Real Estate, Transportation & Logistics sectors and the Health-care sector listed on the IDX for the 2017-2022 period. This research is an explanatory research with a quantitative approach. Sample selection using pur-posive sampling. The results of this study are that profitability has a significant positive effect on the Non Consumer Cyclical and Consumer Cyclical sectors, but in the Transportation & Logistics sector it has a negative effect while in the other 2 sectors it has a negative effect on the other 2 sectors. Activity had a negative effect on the Consumer Cyclical and Property & Real Estate sectors, while other sectors had a negative impact. Solvency has a significant positive effect only on the Non Consumer Cyclical and Consumer Cyclical sectors, but in the Transportation & Logistics sector the effect is not significant, while in the Property and Real Estate and Healthcare sectors it has a negative effect. The value of the company is not affected by Liquidity in all industrial sectors. The company’s growth had a positive and significant effect on the Property & Logistics sector and the Transportation & Logistics sector, but in the Non-Consumer Cyclical sector it had a negative effect and on the other 2 sectors it had a in-significant effect. Business strategy has a negative effect on the Non Consumer Cyclical and Healthcare sectors, while the other 3 sectors have a negative ef-fect. Authors: Atmaja H.E.; Nur S.A.; Hutajulu D.M.; Ikhwan K.; Lada S.; Aldianti R.D.
Title: Scaling Up Micro Enterprises Key Success Factors and AI-Driven Development Model
Abstract: In the development of MSMEs, there is a gap: micro businesses dominate in terms of quantity, but there has been no significant increase in those that have scaled up to become small or medium-sized businesses. Therefore, this study aims to analyze key factors for increasing the scalability of micro businesses and to examine an artificial intelligence-based micro business development model for upgrading to small and medium-sized businesses. This study employs a mixed-method approach with an explanatory sequential design. The population includes micro-enterprises in four regions with the highest number of SMEs: West Java, Central Java, East Java, and Jakarta, totalling 2,387,288 micro enterprises. A sample of 385 respondents was selected using a sampling technique. Proportionate stratified random sampling was used to ensure a representative sample distribution across each province. Qualitative data were collected through purposive sampling with two groups of micro businesses: those that successfully scaled up and those that did not. The analysis results indicate that sustainable leadership and absorptive capacity significantly influence the scalability of micro businesses, while innovation capacity does not. Furthermore, it was found that AI adoption can strengthen the influence of innovation capacity on the scalability of micro businesses. Additionally, the findings indicate that there are six strategic steps to enhance the scalability of AI-based micro businesses awareness, digital readiness assessment, simple AI pilot project, scaling up digital systems, partnerships and ecosystems, and monitoring and feedback loops. © Authors.

Authors: Monod E.; Korotkova N.; Joyce E.; Pan H.H.; Meythaler A.; Khalil S.; Gibbs J.
Title: Complementary-yet-conflicting: how ERP systems and consumer social media shape cross-functional collaboration
Abstract: Enacting cross-functional collaboration remains a significant challenge in organizations shaped by multiple, often conflicting, institutional logics. Both enterprise and consumer technologies hold the potential to address this challenge. In particular, the increasing use of opaque consumer social media (CSM) in business is expected to support cross-functional collaboration by counteracting the rigidities of hierarchy-reinforcing, visible enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems. Our case study of a manufacturing company shows that CSM only partly reduces conflicts between the logics of different organizational functions when used as an opaque shadow system alongside visible ERP systems. Although CSM offers greater flexibility, its lack of standardization and inability to establish durable cross-functional links limits its effectiveness in fostering collaboration. The study also reveals that the logics of CSM and ERP are “complementary-yet-conflicting,” adding complexity to collaboration across functions shaped by different institutional logics. As a result, the parallel use of ERP and CSM technologies is insufficient for resolving tensions between organizational functions with distinct logics. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Liu F.; Xiao Y.; Jia S.; Wang X.
Title: From knowledge to cognition: Digital-intelligent dual transformation and the quantity-quality transformation of green innovation
Abstract: Advancing the quantity-quality transformation of green innovation (QQT-GI) is pivotal for attaining sustainable green innovation. Grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, this study establishes a “knowledge-cognition” analytical framework to examine how the dual transformation of digitalization and intelligence (DTDI) influences corporate green innovation. Using a large language model to identify corporate DTDI practices, we conduct empirical analyses based on 48,503 time-individual observations from Chinese A-share listed companies from 2010 to 2024. The results show that DTDI acts as a critical engine for shifting corporate green innovation from a quantity-chasing to a quality-oriented paradigm. This transformation facilitates the accumulation and integration of green knowledge, which strengthens corporate perceptions of environmental governance responsibility, green innovation opportunity, and green innovation efficacy, thereby redirecting green innovation objectives. The positive impact of DTDI on green innovation quality (GIQ) is amplified by appointing executives with green experience or higher education, or by improving the local business environment. In contrast, heightened compliance risk weakens this effect. Moreover, implementing DTDI in non-state-owned enterprises or heavily polluting industries proves more effective in fostering the transition from green innovation quantity (GIQu) to GIQ. Further analysis indicates that the integration of green innovation knowledge across entities and the cross-boundary fusion of digital and green innovation knowledge are key sources through which DTDI enhances corporate cognition of green development. These findings highlight potential sustainability challenges posed by the rapid growth of GIQu in the digital-intelligent era, offering a theoretical basis for moving corporate green innovation practices beyond symbolic compliance toward substantive quality enhancement. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Gull S.H.; Lone M.A.; Jan S.; Gull I.
Title: Assessing the nexus between sustainable business practices and trade competitiveness in India: an ARDL bounds testing approach with structural breaks
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between sustainable business practices and trade competitiveness in India over the period 1995–2024 using the Autoregressives Distributed Lag (ARDL) bounds testing approach to examine both long-run and short-run dynamics. In the empirical analysis, renewable energy consumption (REC) is used as a proxy for an important environmental dimension of sustainable business practices, while exports of goods and services as a percentage of GDP (EXGS) are used as a proxy for trade competitiveness, reflecting export performance and trade intensity. Structural breaks in 2004 and 2011, identified through the Bai–Perron test and incorporated into the ARDL model, account for major policy reforms and economic transitions associated with changes in India’s trade performance. The ARDL bounds test provides evidence of a long-run relationship among EXGS, REC, trade openness (TOP), and gross capital formation (GCF). The long-run results indicate that renewable energy consumption, trade openness, and gross capital formation are positively and statistically significantly associated with EXGS, used as a proxy for trade competitiveness, with renewable energy consumption showing the largest estimated positive relationship with export performance. The short-run estimates also reveal positive and statistically significant relationships between changes in the explanatory variables and EXGS, while the highly significant and negative error-correction term confirms the presence of an adjustment mechanism toward the long-run equilibrium. Overall, the findings indicate that renewable energy consumption, representing one environmental dimension of sustainable business practices, together with trade openness and productive investment, is positively associated with India’s export performance and trade competitiveness as proxied by EXGS. The results provide useful evidence for policies that support renewable energy adoption, productive investment, and international market integration in the pursuit of sustainable economic growth. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Authors: Bridi T.H.V.; Pohlmann M.N.; de Almeida C.M.V.B.; Gonçalves R.F.
Title: Decentralized autonomous organization for circular economy: A proof of concept in the e-waste recycling process
Abstract: This paper investigates the potential of Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs), leveraging blockchain technology, to establish the essential features for effective Circular Economy (CE) business models. Key requirements for these models often include network governance, stakeholder empowerment, and enhanced regulatory transparency for both government and civil society. We specifically explore the feasibility of employing a DAO to realize these features within the distinct context of the electronic waste (e-waste) recycling circular flow. To assess technological viability and operational characteristics, we conducted a proof-of concept (PoC). This DAO was codified using smart contracts and deployed in a private instance of Ethereum blockchain network. The transaction costs (Ethereum “gas fee”) involved in public Ethereum blockchain are also evaluated. The results indicate the technical feasibility of several critical features, including: process automation, transparent traceability, democratic decisions about rules, and the implementation of token-based payments and credits. These capabilities show significant potential for attaining the desired characteristics necessary to foster innovative circular business models, despite the limitations inherent to a specific-case PoC. However, the results also shown that transactions costs of the public Ethereum network can turn economically unviable small-scale recycling business models or low value-added waste other than e-waste. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: lee J.; Lee J.; Kim M.-H.; Gim T.-H.T.
Title: Zooming in and out of compact urban centres in a rapidly developed metropolis: a multi-scale investigation through an isobenefit lens in Seoul
Abstract: Compact city policy in rapidly developed metropolitan areas increasingly seeks balanced urban development through compact multi-centred planning. Cities such as Seoul have pursued a more even distribution of liveability opportunities by expanding public transport networks and promoting multiple socio-economic hubs around key transit nodes. Yet, tools for critically evaluating whether these strategies align macro-scale connectivity with micro-scale everyday service accessibility remain limited. Drawing on the concept of isobenefit cities, this study develops and applies Multi-Scale Investigation (MSI) as a spatial diagnostic framework for evaluating the social outcomes of compact multi-centred planning. MSI “zooms in and out” of strategic urban centres by jointly assessing two non-substitutable dimensions: city-wide public transport connectivity and local service accessibility. The framework is applied to three selected policy-designated centres in Seoul, an exemplar of rapid urban growth followed by compact polycentric policy and major transit investment. The analysis reveals differentiated macro–micro configurations across the selected cases. All three centres occupy relatively prominent positions within the wider subway network while local service accessibility often fell below policy expectations. The selected Central Business District node exhibited the clearest scalar imbalance, combining the highest city-wide connectivity with the lowest local accessibility. The selected Quarter Centre node showed a connectivity-constrained configuration, suggesting its limited consolidation as a local hub. In contrast, the selected District Centre node displayed a more coherent macro–micro alignment, achieving the strongest overall MSI profile among the three cases. These findings show how MSI can reveal scalar tensions within policy-designated centres and generate case- specific planning feedback. Rather than offering a universal index, MSI provides a calibrated diagnostic logic for identifying where compact polycentric strategies require centre-specific adjustment to better align with isobenefit conditions. The MSI procedure—centre-hierarchy identification, node selection, and scalar tension diagnosis—can be recalibrated and applied in other transit-intensive metropolitan contexts with comparable planning conditions. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Dougall S.D.; Gillespie J.; Sav A.; Ramirez J.C.; Haswell M.R.; Potter R.; Dollard M.
Title: Unseen, Unmanaged, Unsafe: Farming workplaces and occupational risk from co-located energy systems
Abstract: Policies governing unconventional gas (UG) expansion are reshaping agricultural work, creating hybrid workplaces where farming and energy production are co-located. Host farmers, primary producers legally required to accommodate UG infrastructure, constitute a distinct but largely unrecognised occupational cohort within this interface. This study examines how UG co-location alters the organisation and management of farm work, generating psychosocial, physical, and organisational hazards that fall outside the scope of current governance and research. A scoping review was conducted to reinterpret the social science literature on UG impacts through a work health and safety (WHS) lens. This approach enabled the identification and classification of UG-related impacts as workplace hazards, with findings validated using the FOREC framework. The findings show that host farming workplaces are routinely exposed to unmanaged hazards without the protections, controls, or participatory mechanisms afforded to other occupational groups. These risks arise from governance arrangements and contractual structures that shift responsibility for hazard exposure onto farmers. In response, this study introduces the Psychosocial Safety Climate Policy Scorecard (PSC-PS) as a structured framework for assessing how psychosocial risks are recognised and governed within the host farmer–UG interface. By producing a practitioner-facing WHS evidence base, the study establishes a foundation for targeted intervention and risk-based policy reform, highlighting the need to translate existing knowledge into enforceable protections for host farmers in co-located agricultural–industrial systems. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: González-Serrano M.H.; López-Carril S.; Jiménez-Jiménez P.; Molina-García N.
Title: Enhancing creativity and digital skills in motion: TikTok in higher education
Abstract: In a rapidly evolving digital society, higher education must equip students with essential twenty-first century skills such as creativity and digital literacy. This study explored the educational potential of TikTok through an active learning experience implemented in a “Foundations of Body Expression” course within a sport sciences degree program. A quantitative, quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design, complemented by a qualitative descriptive component based on students’ responses to one open-ended question was used to investigate the perceptions of 156 university students regarding TikTok’s impact on their creativity, digital skills, and overall learning engagement. Quantitative findings showed statistically significant improvements in all variables, with self-perceived creativity displaying the greatest perceived growth. The qualitative analysis identified five thematic areas: (1) learning and creativity, (2) psychological and social benefits, (3) teaching methods and tools, (4) promotion and digital skills, and (5) critical considerations and warnings. Students described TikTok as an engaging, accessible, and motivating tool that promoted creative expression, active participation, and digital skills development. They particularly valued its integration of music, rhythm, and visual effects, which enhanced their ability to communicate and express through movement. Some students also noted potential risks such as distraction or misalignment with academic objectives. Overall, the findings support TikTok’s potential to enrich university teaching when framed within a student-centred, pedagogically sound approach. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Zilz K.; Höttecke D.
Title: Students Rate the Credibility of Climate Change Information
Abstract: Students are increasingly using social media to find out about scientific topics and, as recipients of information, must independently assess the credibility of information. From a theoretical perspective, this evaluation might be based on either or both of two different strategies: plausibility strategies, which assess the truthfulness of scientific information, or trust strategies, which assess the trustworthiness of spokespersons. A high-quality assessment of plausibility requires scientific expertise. An assessment of the trustworthiness of a spokesperson, on the other hand, necessitates knowledge of the social and communicative aspects of the Nature of Science (NOS). In a cross-sectional study using an authentic performance test, N = 91 tenth-grade students with no prior training were presented with case vignettes containing information about the consequences of human-caused climate change. The vignettes were constructed in a way that they potentially allow for the application of either or both strategies. The students were prompted to rank the case vignettes according to their credibility and to justify their rankings. During this process, students had unrestricted access to the internet. It was found that the participants preferred making plausibility judgments compared to trust judgments. However, the results also indicate that the application of trust strategies led relatively more often to adequate assessments of credibility compared to plausibility strategies. At the same time, students’ justifications reveal underlying preconceptions regarding NOS. Based on these findings, learning opportunities should be developed that reinforce trust judgments about spokespersons while building on the students’ pre-instructional ideas about the social aspects of NOS. © The Author(s) 2025.

Authors: Savolainen J.; Skardhamar T.
Title: The growth of knowledge in criminology: toward a more optimistic appraisal of theoretical progress
Abstract: Criminology is often portrayed as theoretically stagnant – a view reinforced by an influential review that interpreted the modest explanatory power of published research as evidence that criminological theory had failed to advance. We argue that this diagnosis rests on the wrong yardstick. Explained variance is neither a necessary nor a sufficient indicator of theoretical progress. Drawing on a post-Popperian conception of scientific growth emphasizing the problem-solving capacity of competing research traditions, we propose evaluating criminological theory according to its ability to resolve empirical puzzles and reduce crime-related harm. We illustrate this approach with two examples. First, evidence from competing theories of desistance has increasingly converged on the view that structural turning points are better understood as facilitators and consequences of change than as exogenous catalysts, shifting attention toward agency, cognitive transformation, and reciprocal processes. Second, routine activities theory emerged in response to the puzzle of rising crime amid postwar prosperity and generated a highly productive research tradition encompassing environmental criminology, hot-spots research, and situational crime prevention. In turn, situational crime prevention translated these theoretical insights into a cumulative body of evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of opportunity-reducing interventions. These episodes suggest that theoretical progress in criminology is best understood in terms of the capacity of competing research traditions to resolve anomalies, generate fruitful lines of inquiry, and produce practical solutions. More broadly, they demonstrate that theoretically pluralistic social sciences are capable of cumulative progress even in the absence of a dominant paradigm. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature B.V. 2026.

Authors: Cretney R.; Bernau S.; Nissen S.; Palmer A.; Black A.; Dearden P.
Title: ‘Stuck in a Time Warp’ or ‘Going Forward With Care’? Traversing the Environmental Politics of Genetic Modification in Aotearoa New Zealand
Abstract: This article offers an environmental politics history of genetic modification (GM) in Aotearoa New Zealand. GM has been on political agendas for half a century. It has again come to the fore with proposals to enable the technology after decades of stringent regulations. To better contextualise the major changes now in motion, this article traverses the evolution of GM politics in Aotearoa. We identify five key eras of GM politics, drawing on a database of social science literature and media and policy documents spanning the 1970s to today. This history is often sidelined in contemporary debates; however, we argue that engaging with past controversies, and the wealth of social science and humanities scholarship that analyses it, is vital if we are to progress democratic and informed debate about GM. This history underscores that GM is a political issue, not just a technical one, requiring concerted attention to the purposes and terms by which GM is utilised. We trace five consistent threads across the complex history of GM, including the dominance of narrow economically-driven and technocratic decision-making, the marginalisation of Māori rights and the importance of public deliberation for navigating the significant questions of justice, rights and responsibility at stake. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Lin P.-S.S.
Title: Navigating nature-based solutions for social-ecological resilience: Citizen science in the dune stewardship–coastal disaster risk reduction Nexus
Abstract: Ecosystem-based Disaster Risk Reduction (Eco-DRR) is a critical Nature-based Solution (NbS) for mitigating risk and enhancing human well-being, whose long-term success hinges on adaptive governance and social-ecological resilience rather than ecological techniques alone. However, it often faces significant governance barriers, shifting focus from purely ecological interventions to complex human–environment interactions for risk governance. This case study of the Caota Sand Dunes in Taiwan employed participant observations and in-depth interviews to understand how citizen science contributes to building social-ecological resilience that supports coastal Eco-DRR. Cultural services act as mediators that enhance public awareness and appreciation of ecosystem-regulating services while fostering a sense of place. This mechanism generates sustained public engagement and citizen agency for long-term social-ecological system resilience. Different citizen science participation types play complementary roles: contributory efforts build environmental literacy, while collaborative efforts deepen understanding of dynamics. This study identified a coalescence typology, where scientific knowledge is merged with citizen-driven local knowledge, co-producing risk knowledge and deepening disaster risk awareness. Citizen science provides a collaborative platform that aligns public perception of environmental risk with the social mechanisms for social-ecological resilience. It supports the stewardship of coastal landscapes and ecosystems while offering opportunities to strengthen community well-being. This process activates polycentric governance and strengthens the connections between people and the dynamic environment under climate uncertainty. To ensure the sustainability of Eco-DRR pathways, future NbS should enhance the role of citizen scientists and integrate their insights into formal policy-planning processes. © 2026 The Author. Authors: Zhang C.; Huang S.; Wu S.; Chen Y.; Lc R.
Title: "We are all in big trouble! *Shock Emoji": Personal Narratives in Expressing Emotions, Opinions, and Data Regarding Climate Change in TikTok Short Videos
Abstract: Climate change is a source of anxiety about the future. Understanding how people express themselves about climate change enables us to address such concerns. To study climate change expression on social media, we analyzed 200 TikTok videos tagged with #climatechange, identifying four categories of content: expression-feelings, views-appeals, news-information, and trend-hijacking. We found that creators use humor to package sharp critiques, avoiding direct confrontation. They replace complex discussions with life stories, such as adopting a vegetarian lifestyle or deleting emails. They borrow from news media to present fragmented information as scientific interpretations, creating a perception of scientific credibility, balancing scientific accuracy with emotionality. Analysis of viewer responses showed they engaged empathetically, reshaping interpretations of videos. These interactions risk reinforcing existing views but help build community on TikTok, which lacks community structure. This study reveals how creators may retell news on science using personal narratives, highlighting how short-form videos enable climate communication. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Authors: da Fonseca D.P.; Thomé K.M.; Limongi R.
Title: Types and dimensions of intermediaries in the customer journey
Abstract: Purpose – This paper aims to examine the role of marketing intermediaries in the customer journey, identify key dimensions and analyze how different intermediaries influence customer experiences across various purchase stages. Design/methodology/approach – A systematic literature review analyzed 36 articles from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. The methodology followed a structured approach using assembling, arrangement and assessment criteria, complemented by coding and categorization processes to identify key dimensions and patterns in the literature review. Findings – The analysis identified ten key dimensions that define marketing intermediaries’ roles and four main types: surrogate consumers, opinion leaders, expert sources and supplier-affiliated intermediaries. The results show that surrogate consumers and supplier-affiliated intermediaries affect all stages of the journey, while opinion leaders and expert sources primarily influence the pre-purchase stage. This study reveals that, despite shared characteristics, the impact of intermediaries varies significantly across contexts and types. Research limitations/implications – This study advances consumer behavior theory by providing a comprehensive framework of marketing intermediary dimensions and their influence on customer journeys. It also strengthens stakeholder theory by systematically analyzing diverse intermediaries in the value-creation process. Practical implications – Organizations can develop more effective marketing strategies by selecting appropriate intermediaries for different journey stages and enhancing service personalization and customer experience management through targeted engagement with intermediaries. Social implications – This research illuminates how marketing intermediaries shape consumers’ decisions and experiences in the digital age. This contributes to a better understanding of social influence on purchase decisions and market dynamics. Originality/value – This systematic investigation of marketing intermediaries in the customer journey provides a novel framework for understanding their defining dimensions and their impact across purchase stages, thereby filling a significant gap in the marketing literature. © 2026 Daiane Pereira da Fonseca, Karim Marini Thomé and Ricardo Limongi.

Authors: Han G.; Li H.
Title: Integrating Values Education into Undergraduate Chemistry Curricula: A Review
Abstract: This study systematically explores integration pathways and assessment methods for values education in undergraduate chemistry curricula to facilitate effective implementation. Following the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) framework, we screened and analyzed 63 peer-reviewed publications from 2016 to 2025 indexed in Web of Science, Scopus, and two targeted chemistry education journals, focusing exclusively on values education in undergraduate chemistry courses. The results reveal that scientific thinking (encompassing scientific inquiry, technical literacy, engineering design, and mathematical thinking) emerges as the most extensively researched domain, followed by ethical and ideal belief education. As a complementary perspective, chemical comprehensive literacy covers eight dimensions, including thinking ability, learning ability, innovative practical ability, and social ethical responsibility, with thinking ability as the focus. However, academic integrity and cultural literacy remain under-studied. In terms of values education integration carriers, experiments serve as the primary carrier, followed by chemistry outline, open-ended questions, calculation, and case-based learning, while innovative tools such as AI-assisted methods remain underutilized. Regarding assessment practices, final investigation assessments dominate, followed by evaluation tools and pre- and postinvestigations. Additionally, most included studies lack a stratified analysis of intervention effects on marginalized student groups. These findings highlight critical gaps in current value education implementation, emphasizing the need for expanded research on neglected domains and validated assessment systems to advance value education in chemistry curricula. © 2026 American Chemical Society and Division of Chemical Education, Inc.

Authors: Gurba V.N.; Kazantsev O.A.
Title: Reduction of ethnic nepotism to amoral familism: Once again on the defects of primordialist thinking; [Редукция этнического непотизма к аморальному фамилизму: еще раз об изъянах примордиалистского мышления]
Abstract: The article attempts to criticize the primordialist (sociobiological) approach to understanding ethnic conflicts. Despite the decline of academic attention towards such methodology in sociological and political ethnicity studies in the second half of the last century, the growing interest in the social sciences in evolutionary biology discoveries, cognitive science and genetics contributes to the renewal of previous discussions. Therefore, the search for additional heuristic resources by sociologists and political scientists to justify their autonomy and independence on the research path, for example, in the study of ethnic conflicts, remains relevant and significant. Next, we will select T. Vanhanen's concept of ethnic nepotism as an example of the primordialist approach and consider its modern applications in the social sciences. Then we will introduce the concept of amoral familism by E. Banfield and discuss its usage in economics and sociology up to the present day, after which we will provide justification for the possibility of a comparative analysis of the two presented theoretical constructs in a general context. As a result, we will show a number of specific examples of interethnic interactions that cannot be interpreted in the spirit of T. Vanhanen's primordialism and generally sociobiological reasoning about social processes and phenomena. Thus, a comparison of the concepts of ethnic nepotism and amoral familism as specific forms of individual's rationalization and collective behavior using empirical (historical) material displays that these and other behavioral models are determined by qualitative factors and sociocultural conditions, more productively explained with the help of constructivist rather than primordialist methodologies. © В. Authors: Sharma S.
Title: Comparing AI and human peer feedback in assessment: Evaluating feedback quality, engagement, and learning across project-based stages
Abstract: This study compares how students experience and act on feedback when working with an artificial intelligence (AI) peer and a human peer in a project-based assessment. Conducted in upper-level data science courses, the research used a mixed-methods design informed by Feedback Literacy, Evaluative Judgment, and Learning Engagement theories. A total of 103 students completed two equivalent projects, one with a human peer and one with an AI peer, across five stages: ideation, design, coding, debugging, and reflection. Quantitative results showed that AI feedback was rated higher for usefulness, quality, uptake, and trustworthiness, while human feedback supported stronger emotional and social engagement. Qualitative findings revealed that students viewed AI feedback as immediate and practical but sometimes lacking empathy, whereas human feedback provided motivation and mutual understanding. The study concludes that AI and human peers contribute complementary strengths to assessment, with AI enhancing iterative improvement and human peers promoting reflection and collaborative dialogue in learning. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Plante T.B.; Whitsel E.A.; Aiello A.E.; Gaydosh L.; Angel R.A.; Hummer R.A.; Grago J.; Harris K.M.; Boyle R.H.; Cushman M.
Title: Laboratory methods and quality assurance in the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health Waves V and VI
Abstract: OBJECTIVES: Gerontological and population health sciences increasingly emphasize life-course, biosocial frameworks linking social environments to biological aging and disease processes, for which high-quality biological data are essential. We report on the collection, assay, and quality of aging-related biomarkers in the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health) Waves V and VI. METHODS: Staff collected blood specimens during in-home health exams, processed them locally, and shipped them to the lab for further processing, assay completion, and archiving. Analytes assessed cardiovascular disease risk, glucose homeostasis, lipids, renal function, hepatic injury, inflammation, immune system processes, and neurodegeneration. Inter-assay coefficients of variation (CVs) were estimated for sample sets. In 2% of participants, a duplicate specimen was collected within 2 weeks and assays repeated; intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) were calculated to assess short-term reliability. RESULTS: Wave V collected blood from 92% of 5,381 participants who completed the exam (mean age 38); Wave VI collected blood from 91% of 6,073 participants (mean age 44). Reliability was excellent (ICC ≥ 0.75) and highest for hemoglobin A1c at Waves V-VI and GFAP and HSV and SARS-CoV-2 serologies at Wave VI. Reliability was fair to good (ICC 0.40 to <0.75) for assays of low-abundance proteins reflecting temporally dynamic biological processes; none were poor (ICC < 0.40). CVs were desirable (<10%) for established clinical chemistry assays but less so (≥10%) for low-abundance proteins, markers of temporally dynamic biological processes, and SARS-CoV-2. DISCUSSION: High-quality biological data from Add Health Waves V and VI greatly expand the study's capacity to support life-course, biosocial research. © The Author(s) 2026. Authors: Abyaneh M.V.; Adib A.; Dehkordi A.M.
Title: Entrepreneurship Discourse in the Arabic Twitter Sphere: A Sentiment and Content Analysis
Abstract: This study investigates the structure and dynamics of entrepreneurial discourse on the Arabic Twitter (X) sphere within the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states. It examines how entrepreneurship is socially constructed amidst the transition from a rentier to a knowledge-based economy, focusing on state narratives versus public sentiment. Adopting a computational social science approach, the study analyzed a corpus of 48,841 content units harvested between June and December 2025. To ensure statistical independence and prevent double-voting bias, the research employed a Confidence-Calibrated Ensemble architecture. This pipeline integrates fine-tuned models (MARBERT) with pseudo-independent Large Language Model configurations (GPT-4 in zero-shot and few-shot settings) using calibrated tie-breaking. Techniques included Sentiment Analysis, Named Entity Recognition (NER), and demographic profiling of 1,888 active users. Descriptive analysis of the collected corpus identifies Saudi Arabia as the primary discourse locus (accounting for approximately 47% of traffic). Semantic analysis reveals a significant discursive shift from economic to cultural themes, termed ‘Entrepreneurial Nationalism,’ highlighted by a substantial growth in references to state initiatives like ‘Vision 2030.’ Within this specific dataset, the ecosystem exhibits ‘fragile positivity’ (an overwhelmingly high positive-to-negative descriptive ratio), indicating a ‘spiral of silence’ regarding critical engagement. Furthermore, user profiling uncovers an ‘elite oligarchy’ dominated by middle-aged technocrats (35–49) and highly educated individuals (e.g., PhD holders), while Generation Z remains largely marginalized. The findings suggest the Arabic Twitter sphere has evolved into a platform for ‘digital statism.’ Here, entrepreneurship functions less as a market disruptor and more as an instrument to consolidate the legitimacy of state-led modernization projects. © authors.

Authors: Chattopadhyay A.; Morris C.N.; Zubizarreta J.R.
Title: Balanced and robust randomized treatment assignments: the finite selection model for the health insurance experiment and beyond*
Abstract: The Finite Selection Model (FSM) was developed by Carl Morris in the 1970s for the design of the RAND Health Insurance Experiment (HIE), one of the largest and most comprehensive social science experiments conducted in the U.S. The idea behind the FSM is that each treatment group takes turns selecting units in a fair and random order to optimize a common assignment criterion. At each of its turns, a treatment group selects the available unit that maximally improves the combined quality of its resulting group of units in terms of the criterion. In the HIE and beyond, we revisit, formalize, and extend the FSM as a general tool for experimental design. Leveraging the idea of D-optimality, we propose and analyze a new selection criterion in the FSM. The FSM using the D-optimal selection function has no tuning parameters for covariate balance, is affine invariant, and when appropriate, retrieves several classical designs such as randomized block and matched-pair designs. For multi-arm experiments, we propose algorithms to generate a fair and random selection order of treatments. We demonstrate FSM’s performance in a case study based on the HIE and in ten randomized studies from the health and social sciences. On average, the FSM achieves 68% better covariate balance than complete randomization and 56% better covariate balance than rerandomization in a typical study. We recommend the FSM be considered in experimental design for its conceptual simplicity, efficiency, and robustness. © The Royal Statistical Society 2026. All rights reserved. Authors: Yaniasih Y.; Yoganingrum A.; Bisri A.; Marlina E.; Puspita G.C.; Maryati I.; Noorbani M.A.; Rachmawati R.
Title: Understanding self-citation: A statistical and contextual analysis of bibliographic and in-text citation in Indonesian social sciences
Abstract: Self-citation remains a contested practice in bibliometrics and is often treated as a uniform indicator, despite important distinctions between its in-text and bibliographic forms. This study examines patterns and meanings of self-citation among Indonesian social science researchers by combining quantitative statistical analysis with qualitative contextual analysis of in-text citations. A total of 3735 references from 537 Scopus-indexed articles authored by researchers affiliated with the National Research and Innovation Agency were analyzed using a custom-built citation parsing system. The system integrates four analytical dimensions (location, sentiment, function, and source role) to capture the contextual meanings of self-citation. Findings show that in-text self-citations predominantly occur in the Introduction section, mainly serving explanatory functions with largely neutral sentiment and frequently referencing prior Results sections. Statistical analysis identified significant differences between in-text and bibliographic self-citations, suggesting that in-text citation patterns may reflect contextual dimensions not captured by conventional citation counts alone. Differences in self-citation frequency were also observed across collaboration types and authorship patterns. These findings highlight the value of incorporating citation-context analysis to complement traditional bibliometric approaches and provide a more context-sensitive understanding of self-citation practices in scholarly communication. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Tutić A.; Voss T.
Title: The Covering-Law Model of Explanation in Social Science: Strengths, Limits, and Alternatives; [Das Covering-Law-Modell der Erklärung in den Sozialwissenschaften: Stärken, Grenzen und Alternativen]
Abstract: The covering-law model of explanation has long been at the center of methodological debates in the social sciences. Developed by Hempel and Oppenheim, this model posits that scientific explanations should subsume individual phenomena under general, lawlike principles. Despite its far-reaching influence, the covering-law model has faced significant criticism, particularly in the social sciences, where causal complexity and the absence of strict nomological laws fuel doubts about its applicability. This paper offers a critical assessment of the strengths and weaknesses of the covering-law model in the social sciences and engages with contemporary debates on interpretivism, functional analysis, and mechanistic approaches. We argue that, despite all criticism, the covering-law model remains a valuable point of reference for explanations in the social sciences, particularly when combined with insights from structural individualism, recent developments in action theory, and modern conceptions of causality. Furthermore, we discuss its relation to mechanistic explanations and suggest that the purported opposition between the two has been overstated. © The Author(s) 2026.
