Authors: Harris-Walls K.; Curran F.C.
Title: An Event History Analysis of the Policy Adoption of the Next Generation Science Standards
Abstract: Standards-based reform has grown in the field of education. Efforts to do so in mathematics and reading through the Common Core State Standards, while initially adopted widely, ultimately proved controversial. In contrast, the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) have been less polarizing. Using an event history analysis, we examined the state political, economic, and social factors that predicted adoption of the NGSS as well as how factors differentially related to full-scale adoption or adoption of standards based on the NGSS. Results show, while few factors predicted adoption broadly, the presence of a larger proportion of Republicans in the legislature predicted a higher likelihood of adopting standards based on the NGSS than fully adopting them. © The Author(s) 2025

Authors: Lindgren M.; Packendorff J.
Title: Homosocial and heterosocial academics in masculinity contest cultures
Abstract: Purpose – The purpose of this article is to examine how masculinities are reproduced in academic workplace cultures through homosocial and heterosocial relations in the context of neoliberal university reforms. Design/methodology/approach – Semi-structured interviews were conducted with senior lecturers across two departments of a major social science subject at two Swedish universities. We employ the analytical dimensions of Masculine Contest Cultures (MCC) to analyse gender dynamics within academic settings undergoing managerialist transformation. Findings – The study identifies patterns of harmonic versus competitive homosociality and homogenous versus fragmented heterosociality. Competitive homosociality emerges when neoliberal performance management systems disrupt traditional academic hierarchies, while harmonic homosociality persists where organisational narratives celebrate men's achievements. Women's responses vary correspondingly through fragmented heterosociality (withdrawal from traditional supportive roles) or homogenous heterosociality (maintaining collective support for men's privileges and advancement). Research limitations/implications – The study is limited to Swedish universities and senior lecturers. Future research should examine intersectional factors and conduct comparative studies across national contexts and career stages. Practical implications – Findings suggest that performance management systems can reinforce gender hierarchies when implemented without attention to homosocial and heterosocial dynamics. Universities need to provide better institutional support for middle managers, particularly women, who face contradictory expectations from multiple directions. Social implications – Understanding academic institutions as sites of masculinity contests offers insights for creating more equitable academic environments and addressing persistent gender inequalities in higher education by recognising the complex dynamics between men's competitive relations and women's varied responses to masculine workplace cultures. Originality/value – This study contributes to understanding gender dynamics in higher education by developing a nuanced conceptual framework for understanding masculinity contests in academic settings and demonstrating how seemingly similar neoliberal transformations produce different gendered outcomes across institutions through the interplay of homosocial and heterosocial relations. © 2025 Monica Lindgren and Johann Packendorff

Authors: Peterson M.E.; Miller H.A.; Hernandez P.R.; Woodcock A.; Schultz P.W.
Title: Culturally responsive teaching can protect STEM identity among underrepresented students
Abstract: While the disparity is narrowing, Hispanic/Latinx students remain underrepresented in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) majors. Prior research has shown that STEM identity is an important predictor of a sense of belonging and persistence for underrepresented minorities in STEM. Guided by social identity theory, the present study examined how culturally responsive teaching practices (CRTP) interact with negative ingroup stereotype endorsement and ethnic identification to predict STEM identification among a sample of 349 Hispanic/Latinx undergraduates across 12 Hispanic-Serving Institutions on the West Coast of the United States. Results indicated significant positive main effects of CRTP and ethnic identity on STEM identity. Additionally, CRTP moderated the relationship between students’ ethnic and STEM identities; ethnic identity was positively related to STEM identity among students reporting average or high perceived CRTP in their undergraduate courses, but not among those reporting low CRTP. Negative ingroup stereotype endorsement was negatively related to STEM identity at the bivariate level, but the association was no longer significant in the interaction model including CRTP and ethnic identity. Overall, these findings suggest that CRTP could be an identity-relevant contextual factor in which underrepresented students’ ethnic and STEM identities are more strongly aligned. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Zhang W.; Zhang L.J.; Zhu Y.
Title: GenAI-driven formative assessment for enhancing strategic competence and oral proficiency
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), exemplified by ChatGPT, is transforming language education by providing sustainable, learner-friendly and formative assessment. However, its impact on second/foreign language (L2) speaking for academic purposes, particularly on strategic competence, remains under-explored. Grounded in Dynamic Systems Theory (DST), this 20-week longitudinal mixed-methods study, a pilot study of a large project with a grant from the National Social Science Fund ofChina, examined how ChatGPT-mediated formative assessment influenced the development of strategic competence and oral proficiency among two Chinese business English majors. Data from strategic competence inventories, research journals, interviews, and oral proficiency assessments were analysed using quantitative modelling and thematic analysis. Findings reveal a nonlinear yet upward trajectory in both constructs, with individual variability in learners' strategic competence development. The four components of strategic competence, operating as four metacognitive strategies (.i.e., planning, problem-solving, monitoring, and self-evaluating) functioned both independently and interactively, with monitoring and self-evaluating showing the strongest links to oral proficiency gains. Moreover, learners reported that ChatGPT provided structured feedback, reduced anxiety, and enhanced self-regulation, though concerns about AI over-reliance emerged. These findings reinforce DST's view of L2 learning as dynamic and adaptive while also contributing to the refinement of the Strategic Competence Model of L2 Speaking (SCMLS) in AI-mediated learning contexts. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Rushemuka M.N.
Title: “I am also under pressure”: Challenges in public social protection for workers in Rwanda’s formalised small-scale mining sector
Abstract: This article examines the underexplored issue of public social protection in the artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) sector. Social protection is defined as public actions taken in response to levels of vulnerability, risk, and deprivation considered socially unacceptable within a given society and polity. Drawing on a study of ASM in Rwanda, the article identifies a range of state-led policies implemented in the sector to protect miners. These include workplace-based measures such as occupational health and safety regulations, as well as broader citizen protection programmes that are not sector-specific, including the Ejoheza pension scheme and the Mutuelle de Santé community health insurance scheme. The article draws on the concept of infrastructures of inclusion, developed in science and technology studies and anthropology, to examine the implementation challenges of these initiatives and the politics surrounding their establishment and maintenance. From this perspective, public social protection in Rwanda’s ASM is understood as part of a broader state project that seeks to render mining sites legible in order to increase mineral production while improving workers’ protection. Conceptualising the actors, institutions and relations involved as infrastructures of capitalist production places the politics of mineral production at the centre of analyses of ASM governance challenges. Authors: Yang Y.; Mashi S.A.; Nnachi N.I.
Title: Integrating Traditional Ecological Knowledge Into Forest Governance: Pathways to Sustainable Development in Protected Forest Ecosystems
Abstract: Traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) of forest communities plays a vital role in sustainable development by sustaining biodiversity, enhancing climate resilience, securing livelihoods through practices such as sacred groves and agroforestry, and supporting integrated forest management (IFM). It directly advances SDGs 1, 2, 5, 13, 15, and 16 by promoting food security, gender equality, climate adaptation, biodiversity conservation, and strong institutional governance. Despite longstanding recognition of TEK's ecological value, limited attention has been given to how it is embedded within governance systems, particularly in major protected areas where institutional and sociopolitical dynamics shape the TEK–science–governance interface. Using the social–ecological systems (SES) framework and a mixed-methods approach, this study examined four forest-dependent communities in the Okwango Division of Cross River National Park, Nigeria. Findings reveal that although knowledge holders are predominantly middle-aged men, women play critical roles in non-timber forest products (NTFPs) management and intergenerational knowledge transfer, and long-term married residents serve as key custodians of culturally embedded practices such as taboos, sacred sites, and agroforestry. However, TEK remains marginalized within centralized, state-led governance structures characterized by minimal participation, insecure land tenure, and a lack of legal recognition. The study provides both theoretical and empirical insights into how TEK can be effectively integrated with scientific forest management to advance sustainable forest policy development. It concludes that embedding TEK within inclusive, legally recognized, and participatory hybrid governance systems can strengthen resilience, adaptive management, and equity and recommends legal recognition of customary tenure, co-management frameworks, youth engagement, benefit-sharing mechanisms, and cross-sectoral partnerships to advance sustainable forest policy and conservation outcomes. © 2026 ERP Environment and John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

Authors: Awais M.
Title: Cross cultural patterns of linguistic aggression and aggressive combat content enjoyment: A computational study of PUBG reviews across six continents
Abstract: This study explores global patterns of linguistic aggression and appreciation for aggressive combat content as expressed in reviews of PlayerUnknown’s Battlegrounds (PUBG), analyzing over 18.7 million Google Play Store English language reviews from over 80 countries. Grounded in the General Aggression Model (GAM), it integrates media psychology, cross cultural communication, and computational social science to assess emotional expression in user generated content. Two indices, Aggression Score and Appreciation of Aggressive Content (AAC), were constructed using NLP, sentiment analysis, and lexicon-based tagging to capture hostile sentiment (anger) and positive reinforcement (joy, ratings, likes) in aggression-related reviews. Results reveal a significant increase in the average intensity of both scores over time, with reviews grouped under South America exhibiting higher average aggression and AAC scores within the dataset, while reviews grouped under Australia show comparatively lower levels of these measures. The study uses GAM as a conceptual lens to interpret large-scale, naturalistic expressions of aggression and enjoyment. Methodologically, it offers replicable framework for affective analysis; practically, it offers exploratory insights for game design and content moderation in digital environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Rispoli K.M.; Norman M.Z.; Ziegelmayer L.E.; Warren N.; Batistela E.
Title: Evaluating IEP Goals Addressing Social, Emotional, and Behavioral Health in Autistic Middle Schoolers
Abstract: Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) are the mechanism through which students receive special education services in schools. Little is known about the degree to which federal guidelines and science-based recommendations are evident in IEPs for autistic students, particularly those targeting social-emotional and behavioral health in middle school. Given the centrality of social-emotional and behavioral health in shaping academic success, it is critical to understand how these needs are addressed via IEPs. This study examined the quality of IEPs for 50 autistic students enrolled in grades 6 through 8, including how IEP goals related to social-emotional and behavioral health reflected quality standards established in the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act of 2006 and the National Research Council. Of 347 IEP objectives, just under half (42%) targeted social-emotional and behavioral health-related outcomes. Analysis of IEP quality indicated moderate adherence to legal standards and best practice recommendations, with variation across individual indicators of quality. Moreover, findings suggested IEP alignment with best practice recommendations was higher for children experiencing economic adversity. Results highlight opportunities for school psychologists to lead efforts in increasing knowledge and collaboration among school professionals regarding support for social-emotional and behavioral health skill development in autistic students. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Roza M.; Azhar M.; Festiyed F.; Asrizal A.
Title: Integrating Minangkabau culture into science education: preservice teachers' informal reasoning on ethnoscience for critical thinking and creativity
Abstract: This study analyzes how preservice science teachers construct informal reasoning when evaluating two Minangkabau cultural practices, namely batik tanah liek and the balimau tradition, as contexts for ethnoscience. Batik tanah liek emphasizes clay as a natural dye and fabric preservative, wheras balimau is a tradition of cleansing oneself using lime and flowers before Ramadan. This study contributes new insights by mapping the patterns of informal reasoning of preservice teachers on two traditions that have different scientific structures and religious values and linking them to pedagogical implications for ethnoscience learning. Data were collected through semi-structured questionnaires and analyzed using Braun and Clarke's inductive thematic analysis. Four categories of informal reasoning, namely personal, social, cultural, and environmental, guide how participants assess scientific relevance, cultural meaning, moral sensitivity, and learning potential. The results show that preservice teachers have stronger involvement and awareness of batik tanah liek, which provides concrete and structured scientific phenomena that trigger more rational-scientific reasoning and conceptual creativity. Conversely, balimau evokes moral-emotional reasoning due to its strong religious and socio-communal values, thus encouraging pedagogical caution. These differences indicate cultural bias and variations in epistemic access to traditional practices. Informal reasoning has been shown to play a role in training critical and creative thinking skills through evidence analysis, cultural context interpretation, and scientific solution exploration. This study emphasizes the need to integrate ethnoscience analysis into the PCK/TPACK curriculum to strengthen culturally responsive science education. © 2026 Fırtına Akademi A.Ş. All rights reserved.

Authors: Lee W.; Yoh H.; Chong S.C.
Title: Beyond faces: The effect of context on ensemble emotion perception
Abstract: The ability to judge the overall emotion of a crowd is fundamental to navigating naturalistic social scenes. However, research has typically studied such judgments using isolated faces, without any contextual information. In two experiments, this study investigates how facial expressions, background context, and observers’ emotional states jointly influence ensemble emotion perception in naturalistic scenes. In Experiment 1, participants judged the overall emotion of crowd scenes that were constructed by superimposing human figures, whose facial emotional values were quantified on a continuous scale based on naturalistic photographs, onto emotionally positive, negative, or neutral backgrounds. Bayesian model comparisons revealed that both facial emotion and background valence influenced mean judgments, with positive (negative) backgrounds biasing ratings in a more positive (negative) direction. In Experiment 2, we examined how observer mood modulates this integration by inducing positive or negative affect through an autobiographical recall task. Model comparisons revealed that observer mood also influenced judgment, extending the model of Experiment 1. Although observer mood exhibited no reliable main effect on mean ratings, it was found to significantly affect response variability: participants in a positive mood showed reduced variability, which suggests more consistent ensemble judgments. Together, these findings demonstrate that ensemble emotion perception integrates multiple sources of information beyond facial expressions; specifically, both external and internal contexts substantially influence how collective mood is perceived in social scenes. These findings emphasize the importance of studying ensemble perception in naturalistic settings. The trial-level data and analysis codes for all the experiments are available on the Open Science Framework (OSF) repository (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/B9GMQ). Authors: Mager A.; Allhutter D.
Title: Algorithmic welfare. Disaggregating semi-automated fraud detection by spotlighting human judgment in organizational practices
Abstract: This paper investigates a risk scoring algorithm used to detect social fraud in the employment sector. It draws on a case study conducted in Austria that spotlights case workers by exploring how the semi-automated fraud detection tool is embedded in, and co-produces, organizational practices in a public social insurance agency. The central question guiding this article is how case workers' roles, routines, and responsibilities are transformed by the introduction of an algorithm targeting illegal employment, social and wage dumping, and networks of bogus companies. To answer this question, the paper draws on 10 qualitative interviews, short-term ethnographic observations, and a two-day mind-scripting workshop conducted with case workers from different regional social insurance offices. Building on street-level bureaucracy research and critical data studies, the analysis shows how the fraud detection software co-produces new professional identities within welfare organizations, transforms knowledge practices of evidence-gathering, and redistributes responsibility between data science and human judgment. Finally, the paper discusses how semi-automated fraud detection ties into larger trends of welfare states, as part of a shift from care to control.  © 2026 the author(s), published by Walter de Gruyter GmbH, Berlin/Boston.

Authors: Angel D.
Title: Differential affordances in gamified learning environments: how interactive features mediate calculus understanding in higher education
Abstract: Traditional calculus instruction often limits students to passive engagement with symbolic procedures, restricting opportunities for exploration, immediate feedback, and coordination of multiple representations. Despite its foundational role in science and engineering, calculus continues to pose significant challenges for conceptual understanding and engagement among undergraduate students. Gamified digital learning environments offer potential for redesigning learner-content interactions, yet empirical evidence on their impact within short-session, curriculum-integrated higher education contexts remains limited. This study examined how the gamified learning environment CALCULUS WHIZZ was associated with first-year engineering students’ conceptual understanding of and engagement with core calculus concepts (limits, continuity, and derivatives). It specifically investigated patterns of engagement with three designed environmental affordances, immediate visual feedback, dynamic representational manipulation, and social comparison mechanisms. A mixed-methods convergent design was employed with 50 first-year engineering students across an 8-week implementation involving fifteen sessions of progressively increasing duration (15–45 min). Quantitative data included pre- and post-assessments of conceptual and procedural understanding, supplemented by platform analytics capturing 112,500 individual interactions. Qualitative data were gathered through semi-structured interviews (n = 20) and focus groups (3 groups, 4 participants per group; total N = 12) analysed via thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Conceptual understanding improved from pretest (M = 52.3%) to post-test (M = 74.1%), with a large effect size (d = 1.34) that exceeded gains in procedural fluency (d = 0.89). These gains were measured using author-developed assessments. Empirical discriminant validity between the conceptual and procedural instruments was not established. The magnitude of this difference should, therefore, be interpreted cautiously. Platform analytics revealed differential patterns of affordance utilisation: students who engaged reflectively with immediate feedback showed larger gains, while high-performing students more frequently coordinated graphical and symbolic representations. Three leader-board engagement profiles emerged (Strategic Observers, Competitive Validators, Minimally Engaged), with strategic social observation most strongly associated with positive learning outcomes. Qualitative themes highlighted reduced anxiety through iterative exploration, the value of dynamic visual metaphors for abstract concepts, and the effectiveness of short, focused sessions. The findings suggest that gamified learning environments may be associated with improvements in conceptual mathematics learning in higher education when designed around specific pedagogical affordances rather than relying primarily on motivational game mechanics. CALCULUS WHIZZ illustrates the potential for meaningful gains within short, curriculum-integrated sessions. Results provide exploratory empirical insights into how environmental affordances relate to student learning and offer tentative design principles for interactive mathematics environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature B.V. 2026.

Authors: Hussein A.; Ferede T.; Alemu A.
Title: Effects of a neuroscience informed brain based learning approach on reading attitude and self efficacy among EFL students
Abstract: This quasi-experimental study examined the impact of a Brain-Based Learning Approach (BBLA) on reading attitude and self-efficacy among English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students at Jimma University, Ethiopia. A pretest-posttest control group design was implemented with 109 first-year social science students (experimental: n = 54; control: n = 55). The experimental group received a 16-week BBLA intervention incorporating kinesthetic, visualization, collaborative, and mindfulness strategies, while the control group received conventional instruction. Reading attitude and reading self-efficacy were measured using validated questionnaires. Multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) revealed significant multivariate effects favoring the experimental group (Wilks’ Λ = 0.160, F(2, 106) = 277.808, p < 0.001). Independent t-tests showed the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group in both reading attitude (t(107) = 10.54, p < 0.001, d = 1.55) and self-efficacy (t(107) = 15.67, p < 0.001, d = 2.30). Paired t-tests confirmed significant within-group improvements for the experimental group. Results indicate BBLA strategies effectively enhance EFL students’ reading motivation and confidence. Implications for curriculum, teacher training, institutional leadership, and national policy are discussed. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Foster D.
Title: Hormonal Hinterlands: Mapping a Materialist Prehistory of Trans Medicine
Abstract: This article reexamines social histories of sex hormones in relation to critical theories of trans embodiment. It aims to foreground the entanglement of medical transition's materials in the uneven development of space, labor, and value under racial capitalism. Focusing on hormonal hinterlands—the sites and processes of primary commodity production which furnish molecules consumed to express sexed embodiments—the article draws attention to early social metabolisms of synthetic sex hormones. The article examines tensions and contradictions entailed in these hormonal social metabolisms: oscillations of spatial fixity and circulation; displacements of production from consumption; industrialized orchestrations of coerced reproduction and mass slaughter. Rereading the formative years of endocrine science alongside the consolidation of the American meatpacking industry, the article argues that, across discontinuous “prehistories,” modes of embodiment now hailed as trans have taken shape partly through assemblages of matter shaped by specific forms of human and nonhuman labor and struggle. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Gil-Ruiz P.; Martínez-Verez V.; Martínez-Hernández A.; Córdoba-Cely C.
Title: Arts Education and Cognitive and Socio-emotional Development in Early Childhood Education: A Scoping Review
Abstract: Arts education (AE) in early childhood school settings has been increasingly recognized as a pedagogical environment that supports a range of cognitive and socio-emotional processes, including creativity, critical thinking, self-regulation, and a sense of belonging. This study aims to map and synthesize recent empirical literature (2018–2024) on arts education practices integrated into early childhood education, including visual arts, music, dance, and theater. A scoping review was conducted following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, with searches performed in Scopus and Web of Science (WoS). The analysis focused on identifying types of interventions, methodological approaches, and reported cognitive and socio-emotional outcomes across studies. The findings reveal recurring patterns in the literature linking participation in AE with a variety of developmental processes, particularly in the domains of well-being, educational innovation, and socio-emotional development. However, these patterns are unevenly distributed across domains, with areas such as communication, language, and social skills remaining underrepresented. Substantial variability was also observed in intervention characteristics, including duration, intensity, and implementation. Overall, the review suggests that AE functions as a complex learning environment that may support multiple dimensions of development in early childhood. Rather than establishing causal effects, this study highlights trends, gaps, and areas for future research, including the need for clearer reporting of intervention dosage, greater methodological consistency, and increased attention to children's perspectives. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Zhang Y.; Li Y.; Ge S.
Title: Repositioning teacher authority in the age of generative AI: Insights from Chinese university teachers
Abstract: This qualitative study examines how in-service Chinese university teachers use generative AI in a policy-supportive environment and how this reshapes professional identity and authority. Semi-structured interviews with 15 teachers across the humanities, social sciences, and STEM were analyzed using NVivo-supported thematic analysis. Teachers used GenAI for lesson preparation, example generation, and feedback support, but also reported concerns about accuracy, authorship, and fair evaluation. Rather than a simple loss of authority, participants described a shift from providing information to setting standards, interpreting quality, and making ethical judgments. This shift was enacted through concrete routines, including clarifying acceptable uses, modelling transparent AI use, requiring process evidence, and using oral explanations to verify understanding. The findings show that authority in AI-mediated classrooms is being reconstituted through transparent boundary-setting, process-based verification, and human final judgment, with implications for professional development and assessment policy. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Syah M.F.J.; Fuadi D.; Suranto; Isthofa R.A.; Faiqoh N.
Title: Mapping professional identity dimensions among preservice accounting teachers
Abstract: Purpose: Research on teacher professional identity has largely focused on general or cross-disciplinary contexts, leaving subject-specific identity development, particularly in accounting education. Addressing this gap, this study aimed to empirically identify and validate the components of professional identity among first-year accounting teacher candidates in Indonesia. Design/methodology/approach: The respondents consisted of first-year students from a private university, totaling 118 participants. The data were gathered through an online self-administered questionnaire. The data analysis technique used was exploratory factor analysis (EFA). Findings: The research findings indicated the existence of five components of professional identity among first-year accounting teacher candidates in Indonesia that were statistically proven to be valid as indicators of accounting teacher identity. This analysis was based on the exploration of eight qualitative components from a previous study. These results indicate that to be able to form a professional identity in accounting teachers, they need to focus on five main components. The final components derived from the EFA analysis were identified as follows: Communication Skills, Inspiring, Diligence, Patience and Good Listener, and Active in Campus Organizations. Novelty: This study provides one of the first subject-specific EFA-based validations of professional identity components among entry-level accounting teacher candidates in the Indonesian context. By bridging qualitative findings with quantitative validation, this research advances empirical understanding of early-stage professional identity development in accounting teacher education. The findings may be applicable to accounting educators and could be extended to programs within social science education. Significance: The identified components offer a diagnostic framework for teacher education programs to assess and strengthen the foundational professional identity of prospective accounting teachers. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Hoffmann S.; Vienni-Baptista B.
Title: Training integration in science, policy and practice: insights from designing and implementing integrative teaching and learning
Abstract: Inter- and transdisciplinary (ITD) research is increasingly valued for its contribution to solving complex problems by crossing the boundaries not only of different scientific disciplines, but also those of science, policy and practice. Integration across such boundaries is widely seen as the core challenge of ITD research and critical to the success or failure of ITD projects or programs. However, there are few studies that provide insights into how to proactively lead and actively engage in integration in ITD research, teaching and learning. There are even fewer studies that provide insights into how toeffectively train integration in ITD higher education. Therefore, this article addresses two questions: (i) How can we equip students, i.e. potential future leaders and team members of ITD projects or programs, with the key competencies necessary to lead and engage in integration across the boundaries of science, policy and practice? (ii) What lessons learned can we derive from training integration in ITD higher education in order to support study directors and lecturers aiming at equipping students with the necessary competencies in integration? To answer these questions, we combine our conceptual insights from studying integration with empirical insights from leading and engaging in integration in ITD projects or programs. We derive principles for designing and implementing integrative teaching and learning and then exemplify how we apply such principles in our MSc course “Integration in Science, Policy and Practice: Inter- and Transdisciplinary Concepts, Methods, Tools” at ETH Zurich in Switzerland. We define method- and subject-specific competencies as well as social and personal competencies in integration, operationalize such competencies through competence-oriented learning objectives, outline teaching and learning activities, discuss learning outcomes and draw first lessons learned. We conclude by outlining ways forward that can support current and future study directors and lecturers in their efforts to design and implement integrative teaching and learning in ITD higher education. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Coggan A.; Shultz T.; Dyer M.; Stone-Jovicich S.; Newlands M.; Belgnaoui C.; Dean A.
Title: Putting the 'socio' in socio-ecological: Strengthening Great Barrier Reef adaptive management through evolving and elevating the role of social sciences
Abstract: The Great Barrier Reef (the Reef) is a globally significant socio-ecological system, where human wellbeing is deeply intertwined with ecological health. An adaptive management approach underpins, and shapes coordinated management of the Reef, in the face of spatial, temporal, and stakeholder diversity combined with rapidly changing climactic conditions. Social science, specifically human dimensions research, is essential for effective adaptive management of this marine environment. To examine how human dimensions research is currently applied in Reef adaptive management, and to identify barriers and enablers to its effective integration, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 30 Reef managers and social science practitioners. Overall, findings reveal increasing value placed on human dimensions research but also an uncertainty surrounding its application and significance beyond supporting biophysical science. We recommend that understanding the current challenges and the future opportunities for human dimensions to be a key player in management decision making, can be understood through a systems lens. Specifically, we suggest that shifting Reef adaptive management, from a rigid, solution-oriented hard systems approach to a more flexible, soft systems style has the potential to enable human dimensions research to move beyond contextual support for biophysical information to meaningful contributions shaping management processes and outcomes. We demonstrate the benefits of soft systems thinking for enhancing the influence of human dimensions research in environmental decision-making and adaptive management by linking empirical insights with governance literature. We conclude with recommendations to further support this transition, aiming to strengthen the resilience and inclusivity of Reef management in the face of accelerating environmental pressures. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Bagherzadeh R.; Dehnad A.; Nemati-Anaraki L.; Aghashahi M.; Malgard S.
Title: Empowering international students at iran university of medical sciences: challenges, solutions, and opportunities
Abstract: Background: Internationalization in higher education offers significant benefits for universities and host societies, yet international students frequently encounter multiple adaptation challenges. This study explored the key challenges, potential solutions, opportunities, and future prospects for international students at Iran University of Medical Sciences (IUMS). Methods: A qualitative study was conducted in 2024 with 31 international students meeting defined inclusion criteria. Data were collected using semi-structured interviews in Persian or English, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed thematically using MAXQDA 2022. Trustworthiness was ensured through credibility, dependability, confirmability, and transferability criteria. Results: Four main categories emerged: (1) challenges — including language barriers, environmental adaptation, academic overload, cultural differences, nationality-based discrimination, personal isolation, and financial constraints; (2) solutions — such as curriculum restructuring, enhanced language courses, cultural awareness programmes, improved faculty English proficiency, and institutional advisory support; (3) opportunities — encompassing high-quality educational resources, diverse institutional support services, and personal skill development; and (4) future prospects — with most students intending to return to their home countries after graduation. Conclusion: International students at IUMS face interconnected linguistic, social, educational, cultural, and economic challenges that can adversely impact academic performance and well-being. Practical, multi-level interventions are necessary to support their integration and success. The findings provide actionable recommendations for university administrators and policymakers to improve the recruitment, retention, and satisfaction of international students and to strengthen the internationalization of medical education in Iran. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Müller F.I.; Schwarz A.
Title: Take root among the stars? Emancipatory homemaking as critical worldbuilding in Octavia Butler’s Parables
Abstract: This paper draws on geographical literature on home to explore two strategies of emancipatory homemaking in the Science Fiction novels of Octavia Butler. It examines, homemaking as a strategy, first, of persistence and, second, of adaptability. Analyzing these two strategies in the way they combine, we argue, allows us to define the home as a critical place that links various geographical scales, from the most intimate to the planetary. We build our argument by tracing the ways in which the protagonists of Butler’s Parables build homes in respect of a necessary negotation between persistance vis-a-vis violence and threats on the one, and the necessity to adapt to the precarious social institutions that surround them on the other hand. Such critical, multiscalar geography of home is proposed as a middle ground between extraterrestrial escapist tendencies, and the introvert isolationism of the homely enclave. Butler’s novels help critical geographers frame the paradoxical space of the home as a productive tension: Home is as much a place of loss, instability, and uncertainty as it is a locus of political agency, counteracting violence and liberating (inter)subjective kinship. © The Author(s) 2024. Authors: Maity I.; Roy U.; Karak S.; Barry C.M.
Title: Neighbourhood ecosystem driven impacts on transition to adulthood: A bibliometric analysis of research themes and trends
Abstract: Understanding the impacts of neighbourhoods on adolescents through young adulthood is critical and meaningful. The unified ecosystem of neighbourhood certainly defines and shapes the processes of transition into adulthood that must have the recurring effect over the course of life. This study examines major themes and typologies, traces their evolution over time, and identifies key neighbourhood-related domains linked to the transition from adolescence to adulthood. A systematic bibliometric review using the Web of Science platform was carried out, incorporating 2,570 related articles. Our principal findings portray the highly diverse landscapes of neighbourhood research in the transition to adulthood, with dominant themes including health, mental health, and homeownership, and most research has been conducted in North America and Europe. Furthermore, our results show that housing and residential conditions are the dominant categories of the neighbourhood. Finally, the study highlights that neighbourhood effects are multidimensional—shaping social, spatial, psychological, cognitive, and health outcomes—and emphasises the need for comprehensive, context-sensitive geographical interventions rather than one-size-fits approaches. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Gallego-Gómez C.; Llovet C.; Dourado P.
Title: Food tourism, corporate social responsibility and environmental management: a systematic review on contributions to the sustainable development goals
Abstract: Food tourism is a growing niche within the travel industry that merges gastronomy, culture, and destination branding. Its potential to contribute to environmental sustainability and social development has gained increased scholarly interest, especially in relation to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This article presents a systematic review of 139 peer-reviewed publications (2020–2024) indexed in the Web of Science, aiming to evaluate how food tourism and corporate communication strategies—particularly public relations—intersect with sustainability objectives. The study applies bibliometric methods and the PRISMA framework to identify dominant trends, geographical hotspots, key stakeholders, and the most frequently addressed SDGs in this field. Findings reveal that most research focuses on SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure), with limited holistic coverage of all 17 goals. Furthermore, companies within the tourism and food sectors are emerging as key corporate actors implementing environmental management practices such as renewable energy use, food waste reduction, and sustainable sourcing. Public relations play a critical role in shaping stakeholder perceptions, enhancing corporate social responsibility (CSR) efforts, and legitimizing sustainability strategies. This review highlights the need for stronger integration of communication, governance, and sustainability frameworks to achieve long-term environmental and social goals in tourism. Future research should explore applied assessments of SDG implementation across tourism-related business ecosystems. © 2026 Cristina Gallego Gómez, Carmen Llovet, Pedro Dourado This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

Authors: Hughes C.
Title: Governing to make us free: towards a theory of left governmentality
Abstract: Theories of governmentality have shaped our understanding of power and rule in modern societies. A vast literature spans the humanities and social sciences, charting how ‘techniques of governance’ shape the choices and behaviours which are desirable and intelligible for free societies. But the majority of this literature is focused on liberal and neoliberal governance. How governmentality functions in the context of political projects which aspire to a radically more egalitarian and democratic society, economy, and politics, is a remarkable gap in the literature. However, in recent years, a handful of disparate interventions have begun to explore notions of ‘left governmentality’ and closely related ideas such as ‘positive biopolitics’. This article is intended to encourage the development of this nascent strand of governmentality research. It argues that previous inattention is the product of historical contingency and path dependency: governmentality is no less central to left governance than to any other form of modern governance. And, despite disciplinary, geographical, and empirical divergences, recent interventions repeat common themes: they should be understood as an emergent literature which has begun to sketch out the contours of a new research agenda. The article also suggests how emergent scholarship might be developed theoretically. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Limited 2026.

Authors: Damerau K.; Hansen K.M.; Börtitz C.
Title: Inquiry-induced Stress? Physiological Stress Levels of Lower Secondary School Students in Inquiry-based Situations in Science Classes
Abstract: In recent years, psychological strain among young people has increased worldwide due to numerous social crises. School and classroom performance requirements are primary sources of stress for students. Classroom stress emerges when the demands of a teaching situation surpass personal resources, such as self-efficacy beliefs (SEB). Scientific inquiry-based activities, including experiments or modeling, pose a significant challenge in science lessons because students have limited resources in this area, even by the end of lower secondary school. Consequently, an elevated stress level is anticipated in such situations. This exploratory study examined secondary school students' heart rate variability (n = 86 valid data sets), an indicator of physiological stress, during inquiry-based and non-inquiry-based (communication) situations in science lessons. Moreover, a hierarchical cluster analysis was conducted to investigate whether stress levels differed as a function of individual dispositions that encompassed both stress levels and scientific SEBs. Overall, no significantly elevated stress level was observed during inquiry-based situations. Nevertheless, three types of students with different physiological stress responses were identified, suggesting that individual dispositions are pivotal in guiding personalized stress prevention in science lessons. © 2026, International Council of Associations for Science Education (ICASE). Authors: Mumcu F.
Title: Exploring the Generative Gateway to Computational Thinking (EGG Model): Reversing the Perspective from Outside-In to Inside-Out
Abstract: The integration of computational thinking (CT) into science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education is often approached through external interventions, including curricula, technological tools, and policy initiatives. This study examined how teachers interpret these contextual conditions and translate their understanding of CT into instructional practice. Using a Straussian grounded theory approach, one-to-one semi-structured interviews were conducted with 13 middle-school science, mathematics, and computer science (CS) teachers in Türkiye. Data were analyzed iteratively through open, axial, and selective coding, as well as constant comparison. The analysis generated the Exploring the Generative Gateway to CT (EGG) Model, a context-specific substantive framework comprising three interconnected domains: external factors, internal factors, and learning-design factors. External factors included instructional, managerial, organizational, social, and technological contexts. Internal factors concerned teachers’ awareness, pedagogical interpretations, emotions, commitment to self-development, and risk of professional stagnation. Learning-design factors comprised the competencies and professional development processes through which teachers designed, adapted, implemented, and assessed CT-integrated STEM activities. The findings indicate that external conditions enable, constrain, or redirect teachers’ practice, while teachers’ interpretations and learning-design competence shape how they respond to those conditions. Teachers sometimes adapted activities, sought resources, collaborated with colleagues, or pursued professional learning; however, these actions mitigated particular difficulties rather than eliminating structural barriers. Sustainable CT integration, therefore, requires complementary support for teachers’ conceptual understanding and learning-design competence together with adequate curricular, institutional, collaborative, and technological conditions. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Meade M.; Jennings D.H.; Holifield R.R.; Gawronski V.T.; Hazelhoff R.; Jacobs L.C.; Melonas D.R.; Russell K.; Hayden K.L.
Title: STEMMing the tide: addressing educational inequities and environmental justice through STEM education in Africatown, Alabama
Abstract: This study evaluated early outcomes of STEMMing the Tide, a place-based STEM education initiative at Mobile County Training School (MCTS) in Africatown, Alabama, a historically Black, under-resourced community impacted by environmental injustice. The program integrated environmental justice themes into culturally responsive science and social studies middle school curricula aligned with state standards. Eight teachers from Mobile County Training School participated in the first two years of the project, reaching a total of 187 students across sixth, seventh, and eighth grades. Analysis of schoolwide science proficiency scores showed no statistically significant improvements during the study period. Historically, science proficiency scores at MCTS have consistently remained well below both county and state averages, underscoring ongoing academic inequities that persist despite the implementation of the program. Pre- and post-surveys using Likert-scale items assessed changes in participating students’ science identity and civic engagement. Although no significant differences were found between pre- and post-survey means, encouraging trends were noted. Agreement with the statement “I understand how studying science can help people fix problems” rose from 69 to 78%, and awareness of climate change increased from 62 to 86%. Modest gains were also observed in students’ recognition of community issues and collaboration skills. These findings suggest that while academic gains in science proficiency were limited, the program positively influenced students’ environmental awareness and civic perspectives. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Zaim M.; Refnaldi; Hafizh M.A.; Arsyad S.; Zakiyah M.; Waluyo B.; Zaim R.A.
Title: The hidden curriculum of journal rejection: A Bourdieusian study in Southeast Asian higher education
Abstract: Journal rejection constitutes a consequential feature of metric-driven academic publishing, particularly in systems where indexed publications govern promotion, institutional prestige, and scholarly legitimacy. Moving beyond an editorial outcome or personal setback, the study locates rejection in a hidden curriculum through which scholars learn tacit norms, hierarchies, and evaluative expectations in global publishing. Guided by qualitative hermeneutic phenomenology and Bourdieu's concepts of field, capital, habitus, and symbolic power, the inquiry involved 15 experienced social sciences and humanities scholars from Indonesia and Malaysia. Data were collected through in-depth, semi-structured phenomenological interviews guided by ten open-ended questions and analyzed through transcript immersion, reflexive bracketing, meaning-unit coding, thematic development, cross-case comparison, and Bourdieusian interpretation. Findings identify rejection as a boundary-making mechanism regulating scholarly legitimacy, an informal apprenticeship through which authors infer publishing conventions, and an evaluative encounter affecting confidence, identity, and academic positioning. Its developmental potential depended on access to linguistic, social, institutional, and experiential capital. Well-resourced scholars converted rejection into learning, whereas scholars with limited support faced prolonged uncertainty and exclusion. Participants employed regulated persistence, strategic journal repositioning, selective disengagement, and critical distancing. Clearer review criteria, post-rejection mentoring, sustained writing support, and developmental peer review are needed to reduce structural inequality in international scholarly publishing. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Sager M.T.
Title: Making Data Work: Using Conversation and Interaction Analysis to Study Data Science Education
Abstract: This article presents a methodological approach that combines conversation analysis (CA) and interaction analysis (IA) to examine how students reason with data in collaborative settings, using food justice as an illustrative case. While traditional analytical approaches in data science education often rely on individual cognitive measures or final products, this approach captures the dynamic, interactional nature of data reasoning as it unfolds in real time. By analyzing video-recorded interactions, we demonstrate how CA/IA can reveal the micro-processes through which students negotiate meaning, challenge interpretations, and engage with social and ethical dimensions of data. Though demonstrated here in a food justice context, the approach is broadly applicable to any setting where understanding the social organization of collaborative data reasoning matters, including formal classrooms, workplace teams, and community-based learning environments, and contributes both methodological and practical insights for data science education researchers. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Choi M.-A.; Park B.S.
Title: More-than-Human Mediation: Social Scientists in the Making of Environmental AI Systems
Abstract: What can social scientists contribute to the development of AI? To date, their efforts have primarily been viewed through the lens of AI's social consequences, such as offering legal and ethical guidelines and providing observation-based critiques. However, there is a growing demand for broader engagement of social scientists in AI research itself. Based on the experience of organizing and participating in two environmental AI projects, this paper aims to illuminate the unique challenges and opportunities for social scientists working with, rather than just for, engineers. Building on literature from Science and Technology Studies (STS) and anthropology on research collaboration, it shows that social scientists can take the role as mediators of AI development in three key ways: (1) connecting human and nonhuman actors across multiple disciplines and sources; (2) negotiating challenges posed by disciplinary differences and human-nonhuman distinctions; and (3) modulating the power dynamics between engineers and things in data production and interpretation. By doing so, this paper argues, social scientists can uncover the “more-than-human” dimension of AI development. © The Author(s) 2025. Authors: Li Q.; Qiao J.; Wu M.; Cai Y.; Zheng L.
Title: Leveraging digital entrepreneurship education to develop entrepreneurial competence: An innovation diffusion and regulatory focus perspective
Abstract: With the boom of digital technology, digital entrepreneurship has become an important way for young people to pursue innovation and create value. Despite its clear benefits and value, university students' digital entrepreneurship still suffers from a low success rate, which directly mirrors the marked deficiency in their digital entrepreneurial competence. In this context, exploring how digital entrepreneurship education translates into students' digital entrepreneurial competence through specific mechanisms has become a core issue to address. This study integrates Innovation Diffusion Theory and Regulatory Focus Theory and conducts a survey among Chinese university students to explore the relationships between digital entrepreneurship theoretical/practical education and students' digital entrepreneurial competence, while examining the mediating roles of relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, and perceived risk. The results show that both digital entrepreneurship theoretical and practical education exert significant positive impacts on students’ digital entrepreneurial competence. Specifically, relative advantage and perceived risk serve as common mediators for both educational pathways, whereas compatibility uniquely mediates the relationship between digital entrepreneurship practical education and competence. Unexpectedly, complexity fails to show a significant mediating effect in the full sample. Further heterogeneity analysis reveals that for humanities and social sciences students, digital entrepreneurship education significantly reduces their perceived complexity of digital entrepreneurship, demonstrating a unique psychological “demystifying” function for this group. This study enriches theoretical research on digital entrepreneurship by clarifying the transformation mechanism of digital entrepreneurship education and provides targeted insights for the curriculum design and teaching optimization of higher education institutions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Chang S.-H.; Chang Y.-Y.
Title: Generative artificial intelligence scaffolding for statistical competence in graduate nursing education
Abstract: Background: Graduate nursing students often experience significant anxiety related to statistics and have difficulty applying quantitative knowledge to clinical research practice. Although generative artificial intelligence may function as a learning scaffold, evidence supporting its structured integration into pedagogy remains limited. Purpose: To evaluate the impact of a structured generative artificial intelligence-supported self-directed learning intervention on statistical competence, learning capacity, and motivation among graduate nursing students. Methods: This quasi-experimental study employed a single-group repeated-measures design and included 15 graduate nursing students enrolled in a master's program in Taiwan. The study was conducted from September 10, 2024, to January 15, 2025, with assessments performed at Weeks 1, 10, and 18. The 18-week intervention followed a five-stage scaffolding protocol: (1) instruction in fundamental statistical concepts with instructor-guided support and demonstrations using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences, (2) independent drafting, (3) online peer collaboration, (4) generative artificial intelligence-assisted learning support, and (5) in-class metacognitive verification. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, generalized estimating equations, Pearson's correlation coefficients, and stepwise multiple regression analysis. Results: Overall learning capacity improved significantly over time (post-test estimate = 1.26, p < .001), with a very large observed effect size (Hedges' g = 3.75). Meaning construction, self-regulation, and interpersonal learning also improved significantly by the post-test (p < .001). Learning motivation increased slightly but was not statistically significant. In the stepwise multiple regression analysis, satisfaction was the only variable significantly associated with final statistics report scores (R2 = 0.61; adjusted R2 = 0.58, p = .001). Conclusions: Participants showed improvements in learning capacity following participation in the structured generative artificial intelligence-supported protocol. Learner satisfaction may be associated with higher statistical competence. These findings support the use of generative artificial intelligence as a guided educational scaffold rather than an unregulated shortcut. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Chapman B.E.
Title: Health informatics as rebellion: a framing for introducing students to an interdisciplinary domain
Abstract: Multidisciplinary fields that merge people from diverse backgrounds present pedagogical challenges for both the student and the teacher. Health informatics is once such multidisciplinary field that draws students from both clinical, social, and quantitative backgrounds. This essay explores using Freeman Dyson’s "scientist as rebel" as a framing for health informatics education to foster an inclusive and engaging introduction to the discipline. Tracing the multidisciplinary origins of health informatics, it examines the early works of informaticists Homer R. Warner and Lawrence L. Weed through Dyson’s framework. Warner’s conservative rebellion and Weed’s radical approach provide contrasting yet complementary pathways to understanding the field’s evolution and challenges. By framing health informatics as a rebellion against epistemic habits in healthcare, the essay underscores the need for intellectual freedom and creativity in navigating its intersection of science, engineering, and clinical practice. It also addresses tensions between professionalization and inclusivity. This framing aims to both introduce students to the continuing conversation of the discipline and to inspire students to challenge contemporary healthcare’s prevailing epistemic habits and to design innovative technologies that improve those habits. © The Author(s) 2025.

Authors: Twongyirwe R.; Twinamasiko S.; Ngabo V.; Adriko W.
Title: Waiting for Uganda’s first commercial ‘Pearl Sweet’ oil: Discourses on social and environmental impacts and safeguards
Abstract: Uganda discovered approximately 3.5 billion barrels of commercially recoverable oil reserves in 2006 and is poised to become a major oil producer in Sub-Saharan Africa. In assessing progress towards full–scale oil production, expected by the end of 2026, Uganda’s President referred to the country’s commercial crude oil as “pearl sweet”, highlighting its medium-to-heavy, highly waxy characteristics, relatively low sulphur content, and ease of refining. Despite the anticipated economic benefits, considerable debate persists regarding the potential social and environmental impacts of oil development and the adequacy of safeguards ahead of full–scale production. Drawing on experiences from established oil–producing countries, this paper examines how environmental and social impacts are framed, how safeguards are prioritised, and what this implies for Uganda’s emerging oil sector. Anchored in environmental justice and political ecology, the study adopts a sequential integrative design combining a systematic literature review with empirical insights from twelve purposively selected stakeholders in Uganda’s oil-producing districts and national regulatory institutions. The literature review used Boolean search strings that connected terms within conceptual blocks using OR and combined blocks using AND, following a PRISMA-guided process across Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar and institutional data bases. Of 1800 records identified, 95 key sources were retained for analysis. The findings indicate that, although Uganda has initiated several safeguards measures including oil–spill preparedness training, buffer zone enforcement, afforestation, and resettlement programs – implementation remain fragmented, under–resourced, and heavily centralised. Comparative analysis further indicates limited integration of international climate frameworks, including the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement, into national oil governance. We argue that Uganda’s challenge is not simply the absence of safeguards, but the persistence of centralised, uneven, and under–resourced governance arrangements that constrain the translation of international safeguard commitments into effective national practice. This study contributes to Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 13 (Climate Action), and SDG 15 (Life on Land), while also intersecting with SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) and SDG 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions). © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Cangero F.
Title: We Reduce, We Achieve, We Commit A Corpus-assisted Discourse Analysis
Abstract: This study explores how sustainability reports construct persuasive corporate identities that promote environmental and social responsibility. The analysis draws on a 455,000-token corpus of nine 2023 reports from companies listed in the Dow Jones Sustainability Index (DJSI), compiled and processed via Sketch Engine (Kilgarriff, et al. 2014; 2004). Methodologically, this research integrates Corpus-Based Discourse Analysis (Baker 2023; 2014; Egbert and Baker 2020), the Appraisal Framework (Martin and White 2005) and Critical Genre Analysis (Bhatia 2017; 2014; 2008) to uncover both quantitative patterns and qualitative discursive strategies. Findings reveal that sustainability reports give rise to a coherent and future-oriented narrative identity (McAdams and McLean 2013), in which the corporation emerges as an ethical, proactive and people-centred actor. First-person plural forms (i.e., we, our and us) dominate the corpus, thereby pointing to categories such as agency, collective responsibility and ownership. These frequently co-occur with material process verbs that project transformative intent (Halliday and Matthiessen 2013) and with adjectives portraying the company as sustainable, inclusive and innovative (Stibbe 2015). The discursive interplay of these features builds an ethotic argument that positions the company as trustworthy and committed. Additionally, frequent references to ‘science-based’ goals serve to contract dialogic space and reinforce corporate credibility and ethical alignment, thus reducing interpretive openness (Fuoli 2018; Martin and White 2005). While such reports are framed as informative, this analysis suggests they increasingly adopt persuasive strategies typical of promotional genres. In line with Critical Genre Analysis, they exemplify genre bending (Bhatia 2008), revealing how corporate sustainability discourse functions as a tool for identity negotiation and reputational management. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Pourhossein Parizad A.; Dehghani E.; Agha Mohammad Ali Kermani M.
Title: Data driven framework for ranking influential nodes in social networks using machine learning and neural networks
Abstract: In the dynamic and intricate domain of social networks, precise identification and ranking of influential nodes are essential for effective information dissemination, strategic decision making, and optimal resource allocation. Conventional centrality metrics frequently yield unstable outcomes due to their limited capacity to capture the multidimensional nature of influence. To address this challenge, a novel hybrid data-driven framework is introduced, comprising three integrated stages. Initially, sophisticated machine learning algorithms, namely Random Forest, XGBoost, and CatBoost, are applied to determine objective weights for six centrality metrics: The following centrality measures are examined: degree centrality, betweenness centrality, closeness centrality, eigenvector centrality, PageRank, and the global clustering coefficient-dependent degree centrality. These weights are derived from real-world data, guided by the Susceptible Infected Recovered diffusion model. In the subsequent stage, the TOPSIS method consolidates these weighted metrics to generate preliminary node rankings, thereby establishing training labels for subsequent modeling. In the final stage, a Multi Layer Perceptron neural network predicts influence scores with enhanced autonomy and precision. This network leverages structural features to rank nodes without requiring repeated TOPSIS execution. The validation of the proposed framework was conducted on four benchmark datasets: Zachary's Karate Club, American College Football, Dolphin Social Network and Bitcoin-OTC. The findings indicate that the proposed framework demonstrates superior accuracy, robustness to structural noise, and generalizability across both unsigned and signed graphs when compared to traditional single metric approaches. The outcomes underscore the framework's adaptability across diverse network structures, offering a robust instrument for advancing network science research and applications. © The Author(s) 2025.

Authors: Wentzell E.; Pajoohesh-Ganji A.; Gulati A.; Booker J.; Haywood Y.; LeLacheur S.; Carroll M.A.; Zaidi Z.
Title: Towards justice: Applying Rawlsian fairness to health professions education
Abstract: Context: Health professions education (HPE) continues to confront persistent inequities in access, opportunity and outcomes, even as diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives have become increasingly contested within institutional and public discourse. Although DEI efforts draw upon a long intellectual tradition in the social sciences, DEI research within HPE remains undertheorized, in part because the field is often siloed from broader philosophical debates about justice and fairness. While these concepts are widely valued, they are interpreted and applied differently across cultural, political and institutional contexts, contributing to misunderstanding and resistance when DEI-oriented reforms lack explicit normative grounding. Revisiting the theories that underlie DEI work is therefore important for clarifying why inequities matter in HPE and how institutions justify efforts to address them. Proposal: We highlight prioritarian moral reasoning as a foundational, though often implicit, commitment underlying DEI work in HPE. Prioritarianism holds that improving the position of those who are worse off carries special moral importance, particularly when disadvantage arises from structural conditions rather than individual choice. Within this framework, John Rawls's theory of ‘justice as fairness’ offers a lens for examining DEI in HPE institutions. Rather than presenting Rawls as a comprehensive or universally accepted theory, this paper situates his work alongside broader intellectual traditions that inform DEI and emphasizes its relevance for examining how educational opportunities are organized and justified. Conclusion: Drawing on Rawls's emphasis on fair opportunity and attention to those least advantaged, the paper highlights how justice as fairness can be used pragmatically in admissions, curriculum, assessment and resource allocation. In particular, it invites HPE to ask whether the changes being implemented are acceptable under conditions of fair opportunity and whether they would improve the position of the least advantaged. Used this way, Rawls's ideas support efforts to identify structural barriers and design policies that expand meaningful opportunity. © 2026 Association for the Study of Medical Education and John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

Authors: Larsen C.
Title: Discursive dispossession in the green transition: News media narratives on the wind-turbines on Fovsen, Norwegian Saepmie
Abstract: This article examines how Norwegian and Saami news media reported on the wind-turbine development on Fovsen from 2006 to 2023. Drawing on discourse theory, the analysis identifies four dominant narratives: economic incentives for municipalities, an ‘impending’ energy crisis and the green transition, impacts on nature and outdoor recreation, and impacts on Saami reindeer husbandry. Based on empirical material from local, regional, national and Saami news, the study demonstrates how narratives operate individually and relationally to justify, contest and negotiate the wind-turbines. The dominant narratives mobilize claims of urgency, necessity, and national interest to position wind power as a ‘crystallized’ solution to climate change and energy security in Norway. The counter narratives focus on alternative energy sources and rights-based critiques, exposing the limits to mitigation efforts and compensations proposed to Saami reindeer herders. By conceptualizing discursive dispossession, the article shows how media narratives shape the subordination of Saami livelihoods to the imperatives of the green transition. The study contributes to social science research on renewable energy development, highlighting the constitutive role of news media narratives and how renewable energy conflicts are articulated, negotiated, justified, and contested in Saepmie. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Rahimi M.; Moshiri H.; Otarkhani A.
Title: Unveiling dimensions of social security research: a comprehensive bibliometric analysis and collaborative landscape
Abstract: Purpose – This study aims to evaluate patterns, trends and knowledge networks within social security research. By using bibliometric analysis, the research seeks to provide a comprehensive perspective on the evolution of global social security research. The purpose extends to identifying significant contributors, collaborative clusters and multifaceted issues addressed in the field. Design/methodology/approach – This study uses bibliometric analysis to assess social security research trends and knowledge networks from 2015 to 2023. Using the Web of Science database, 6, 152 relevant articles are analyzed. Quantitative techniques such as coauthorship network analysis, institutional productivity rankings and keyword clustering are applied for a comprehensive understanding. Findings – The findings indicate a rising trajectory of publications in social security research, with the USA, China and Europe emerging as top contributors. Coauthorship patterns reveal collaborative clusters with focused research interests. Prominent authors emphasize key aspects like public policy, economics, health and labor dynamics related to social security. Keyword clustering identifies nine thematic clusters, ranging from inequality and poverty to retirement and disability reforms. A thematic map visualizes overarching categories, including motor themes, basic themes, niche themes and emerging themes. Originality/value – This bibliometric study offers original insights into global social security research, providing a comprehensive understanding of its evolution, significant contributors and diverse thematic issues addressed. The originality lies in the application of quantitative techniques, including coauthorship network analysis and keyword clustering, to reveal collaborative patterns and thematic clusters. The study’s value extends to facilitating evidence-based decision-making for advancing the critical domain of social security through international collaboration and impactful research aligned with societal needs. © 2024 Emerald Publishing Limited

Authors: Audikana A.
Title: Teaching (social sciences) to the police: Insights from the classroom
Abstract: Police training and education delivered by professionals and activists from outside the police field is a relatively common practice. “External” teaching can be perceived by police audiences as lacking legitimacy because of differences in professional culture, type of knowledge and skills, and background experiences. Based on a personal teaching experience to police audiences in the field of social sciences, this paper identifies several critical aspects to deal with this “externality”. The paper advocates for assuming and making good use of externality, and engaging empathetically with the variegated professional experience of police audiences. Also, it concludes that external professionals and activists in the field of social sciences need to be more conscious and critical about their own contribution to deal effectively with the “cultural gap”. © The Author(s) 2025

Authors: Patterson V.; Anderson O.S.; Garcia D.T.; Kruger J.S.; Mohammed S.; Maniar N.; Oerther D.B.; Sethi A.K.; Wapner A.; Wiss A.; Williams C.L.
Title: Public health is already working with you, and you are already working with public health. With intentional collaboration, we can do so much more
Abstract: Public health is frequently misunderstood as a field primarily responsible for outbreak response, advisories, and emergency management, a perception intensified by the COVID-19 pandemic. Yet public health's scope is far broader, encompassing the science and practice of creating the conditions in which people and communities can achieve their full potential for health. Grounded in an expansive view of health that includes physical, mental, social, economic, environmental, and structural well-being, public health applies interdisciplinary, systems-oriented approaches to prevention, policy, and population health improvement. This manuscript introduces this more complete view of public health to the National Academies of Practice (NAP) community through the lens of the Public Health Academy, emphasizing that public health is not adjacent to healthcare but a necessary partner to advance shared goals of health, equity, and impact. We situate contemporary practice within evolving public health frameworks. We describe the data and methods that drive public health: surveillance, community assessment, epidemiology, biostatistics, implementation and prevention science, and participatory approaches, and show how these tools translate evidence into sustainable, community-informed action. Finally, we argue that integrating public health into interprofessional practice and education (IPE) broadens traditional clinical teamwork to include systems thinking, cultural humility, policy literacy, and cross-sector collaboration, strengthening IPE-aligned competencies and preparing health professionals to address social determinants of health. We call for intentional collaboration across the NAP academies to advance health and wellbeing for all. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Sulehri I.G.; Rafiq M.; Arshad A.
Title: Exploring the effect of information literacy skills and digital skills on knowledge sharing and research productivity
Abstract: Purpose – Digital skills and information literacy skills (IL) are essential for teaching staff in universities that make them able to perform their academic tasks (knowledge sharing and creation) effectively and efficiently. This study aims to explore the effect of these skills on knowledge sharing and research productivity of university teachers in Pakistan. Design/methodology/approach – This study was conducted by adopting a survey research design followed by quantitative research method. Faculty members from the top three general category universities in Pakistan were the population of the study. The research participants were approached through a systematic random sampling technique. The statistical package for social sciences (SPSS) software was used to test the developed hypotheses. Findings – This study has presented novel results and portrayed significant positive effect of information literacy skills and digital skills on knowledge sharing and research productivity of universities’ faculty members. It shows that both skills are essential for teaching staff to enhance their knowledge sharing and research output. Originality/value – This study has revealed the effect of digital skills and IL skills on knowledge sharing and research productivity. This study has added a substantial amount of literature in existing body of knowledge. The study has provided pertinent implications for management bodies as well as it enhances literature on IL skills and digital skills for knowledge sharing and optimum research output. © 2024 Emerald Publishing Limited

Authors: Calvo P.
Title: The synthetic transformation of the art world: ethical tensions
Abstract: Synthetic transformation has become a disruptive force in the field of art, with profound impacts on the processes of both the generation of relevant information and applicable knowledge and the production, distribution and consumption of cultural goods and services. AI, one of its main pillars, is increasingly being used by artists and writers to complement, develop or even finish their work. But AI is also being developed to be applied and used autonomously in the production of artistic works and scientific and informational texts, i.e., without expert oversight. Using a critical hermeneutic methodology typical of the humanities and social sciences, this study aims to critically reflect on the algorithmic colonisation of the art world and its current and potential impacts. © The Author(s) 2026.
