Authors: Sárvári N.; Horváth P.; Potháczky Rácz I.
Title: Perceived gender inequalities in education and labour market entry
Abstract: Gender disparities continue to shape educational experiences and the transition to the labour market. The present study explores how women and men perceive gender inequalities in educational environments and during labour market entry. Attention is paid to perceived educational and career-related inequalities, gendered patterns in study fields and early career choices, perceived barriers to women’s career advancement, and reported experiences of differential treatment within educational institutions. The paper presents the findings of an exploratory pilot study based on a questionnaire survey. The study uses descriptive statistics and non-parametric correlation analysis to examine gender disparities, academic and career choices, and perceived obstacles to career advancement. The results show that respondents perceive labour market entry as more strongly shaped by gendered advantages favouring men than education. The results also indicate gendered patterns in academic and career choices, with women predominating in humanities and social sciences and men in STEM-related fields. Female respondents also reported experiences of differential treatment by teachers more frequently and believed that men were in a more advantageous position. The results also suggest that gender stereotypes are perceived as relevant in shaping academic and career-related expectations. The present study provides exploratory empirical evidence from a Central and Eastern European context and identifies important aspects of gender inequality that can guide future large-scale quantitative research and policy-oriented discussions on education and labour market equality. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Sirhayi L.; Boateng S.
Title: Exploring factors influencing students’ perceptions of STEM in South African schools and TVET colleges
Abstract: This study explored factors shaping students’ perceptions of Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) across South African high schools and Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) colleges, examining institutional orientation, curricular and pedagogical structures, and student socioeconomic contexts through the lens of Social Cognitive Career Theory to understand how contextual supports and barriers influence self-efficacy, outcome expectations, and career goals. The study was grounded in the interpretivist paradigm and guided the inquiry into how students construct meaning in relation to STEM learning and careers. A qualitative case study design was employed to investigate students’ lived experiences and perceptions. Four institutions, including two high schools and two TVET colleges, were selected through purposive sampling. From these institutions, three students were purposefully selected as participants. Semi-structured interviews were the primary data collection instrument. Thematic analysis was used to analyse the data and identify emerging themes. The study found that students perceived STEM subjects as both challenging and stimulating. The study also found that socio-cultural and economic factors influenced students’ attitudes toward STEM pathways. In addition, institutional challenges, including overcrowded classrooms, inadequate laboratories and insufficient career guidance, negatively affected student motivation and confidence in pursuing STEM fields. The study recommends adopting learner-centred and contextualised teaching approaches, strengthening mentorship initiatives, expanding career guidance, and expanding extracurricular STEM activities within schools and TVET colleges to increase students’ interest in STEM. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: van Panhuys M.
Title: Where’s the harm? On the argument from inductive risk in particle physics
Abstract: The Argument from Inductive Risk (AIR) explicitly calls for the consideration of non-epistemic values whenever significant non-epistemic consequences, usually understood as harms towards individuals, groups or society at large, are foreseeable. In current philosophical literature, the AIR is often assumed to have limited relevance to fundamental research, particularly in fields like particle physics which has received little attention. This paper aims to address this gap by developing experimental particle physics as a problem case for standard formulations of the AIR. I argue that, although errors in particle physics do not consistently give rise to direct socio-ethical consequences of the kind emphasized in the literature, the field nevertheless involves significant forms of epistemic responsibility arising from its technological embeddedness and broader social entanglements. Moreover, I show that the scope of the AIR depends crucially on how risk is conceptualized. While a strictly decision-theoretic framework tends to exclude particle physics by narrowing the notion of risk, alternative approaches from the ethics of technology help capture indirect and uncertain consequences. The paper therefore argues for further refinement of the AIR, rather than its simple extension, and calls for a more explicit and pluralistic account of risk in the assessment of values in science. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Huynh D.C.
Title: Multi-level governance constraints on the local science–policy–practice interface: Evidence from Ho Chi Minh City flood management
Abstract: Stronger collaboration between science, policy and practice is widely acknowledged as essential for addressing escalating climate risks, yet the governance structures shaping such collaboration are often overlooked. This study brings together Multi-level Governance and Science-Policy-Practice Interface (SPPI) scholarship to examine how vertical power relations shape the connection between climate knowledge, policy formulation and practice at the local level, through a case study of Ho Chi Minh City (HCMC)'s urban flood management. Drawing on document analysis, interviews, site visits, and news reports, the findings demonstrate that local flood management efforts are constrained by hierarchical governance procedures. The challenges include: a national preference for conventional approaches that hinders adaptive solutions at the municipal level; top-down planning that creates a mismatch between national objectives and local implementation capacity; and centralised control over budget management, technical standards, and legal reforms, which limits private sector participation and local governments' ability to respond to context-specific challenges. The paper argues that strengthening local government autonomy and enabling more flexible mechanisms for integrating diverse expertise could foster innovation and timely, context-relevant adaptation strategies. Examining the case of HCMC advances understanding of how power relations shape the SPPI and contributes to the growing global literature on the pivotal role of local governments in advancing climate change adaptation and mitigation. It calls for future studies to move beyond a single administrative level to examine how political structure influences the science-policy-practice interface in different social-political contexts. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Marvin S.
Title: Modulating the indoor–outdoor urban boundary: Inversion, reversion and extension
Abstract: This paper repositions the indoor–outdoor threshold as a neglected yet vital site of climate governance in urban studies. Examining how infrastructure modulates air, temperature, and comfort, it develops the concept of hybrid urban socio-natures as spatial assemblages formed by climate control technologies that dissolve traditional distinctions between inside and outside. Drawing on political ecology, science and technology studies, and critical urban geography, the paper proposes a typology of three governance modes, reversion, extension and inversion, that reveal how cities selectively reorganise thermal boundaries. Through comparative analysis of New York, Toronto, Ahmedabad and Medellín, it demonstrates how comfort becomes an infrastructural capacity that is unevenly governed, creating new geographies of thermal privilege and exclusion. The paper contends that modulating the indoor–outdoor boundary is a distinct aspect of urban atmospheric governance, in which comfort and exposure are politically contested. The paper highlights this boundary as a domain of infrastructural and social struggle and opens new avenues for urban climate research, placing questions of comfort and thermal justice at the core of urban studies. © Urban Studies Journal Limited 2026. Authors: Nepal H.P.; Bramblett D.E.; Benson M.
Title: Peer instruction in preclinical osteopathic microbiology education: a single-group pre–post quasi-experimental study of short-term performance outcomes and student perceptions
Abstract: Background: Peer instruction (PI) is an active learning strategy grounded on social learning theory that promotes engagement and conceptual understanding through structured peer discussion. Although implemented widely in undergraduate science education, its application in osteopathic medical education remains underexplored. Objective: This study examined associations between PI and short-term performance outcomes as well as student perceptions of PI among first-year osteopathic medical students in a preclinical microbiology course. Methods: A single-group pre-post quasi-experimental study without a control group was conducted simultaneously across both campuses of Burrell College of Osteopathic Medicine during a synchronized single 2-hour session titled ‘Infections that affect the nervous system’ in April 2025. Of 295 eligible students, 218 consented and completed all study components: PI activity involving 10 clinical based questions, a five-question exit quiz, and a post-session feedback survey on students’ perception. The PI activity included individual polling, peer discussion, re-polling, student explanation, and faculty review. Data was analyzed using IBM SPSS (version 30.0). Results: Post-PI scores (6.57 ± 1.72) were significantly higher than pre-PI scores (4.46 ± 1.75; yielding a mean gain of 2.11 points (95% CI: 1.88–2.34; t(217) = 18.18, p < 0.001) with a large effect size (Cohen’s d = 1.23). Item-level analysis showed significant improvement on 9 of 10 questions (McNemar’s test with Holm–Bonferroni adjustment for multiple comparisons, p < 0.05; improvement range: 9.2%–36.2%). Learning gains did not differ by campus location (Independent samples t-test, p > 0.05). Exit quiz scores (mean = 3.44 ± 1.18) correlated positively with both pre- and post-PI scores (Pearson correlation, r = 0.29 and 0.28; p < 0.001). Survey responses indicated favorable perceptions: 69.7% reported improved understanding, 61% rated the session good or excellent and 54.6% recommended PI for future courses. Conclusion: PI was associated with improved short-term performance outcomes and favorable student perceptions in a preclinical osteopathic microbiology course. These findings support the feasibility and potential educational value of PI as a promising active learning strategy in osteopathic medical education. Future research should explore longitudinal outcomes, controlled comparisons, and multi-institutional replication. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Yang Y.; Li Y.; Qiu Y.; Zheng R.; Qian J.; Qiu W.
Title: Factors associated with professional identity of nursing interns in China: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Abstract: Background: This study aimed to identify factors associated with professional identity among nursing interns in China. Such evidence may help inform educational and clinical mentoring strategies to cultivate and strengthen professional identity during clinical internship, and may contribute to future retention among nursing interns, thereby supporting nursing workforce stability and improving the quality of nursing care. Methods: CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, the Chinese Biomedical Literature Database, PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, CINAHL and the Cochrane Library were searched from database inception to 20 January 2026. Cross-sectional studies involving nursing interns in China and reporting professional identity and its associated factors were included. Methodological quality was assessed using the quality assessment criteria for cross-sectional studies recommended by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality. Meta-analysis was performed using RevMan 5.4, with the correlation coefficient r used as the effect size. Results: A total of 48 studies were included, comprising 41 Chinese-language and seven English-language publications. Overall, 42 factors associated with professional identity were identified; 12 were included in the meta-analysis and 30 were synthesised descriptively. The meta-analysis showed that humanistic caring ability (r = 0.77, 95% CI: 0.48–0.91), medical narrative competence (r = 0.64, 95% CI: 0.60–0.69), professional self-efficacy (r = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.49–0.72), perceived professional benefit (r = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.57–0.66), clinical learning environment (r = 0.53, 95% CI: 0.18–0.77), psychological resilience (r = 0.52, 95% CI: 0.39–0.62), social support (r = 0.52, 95% CI: 0.34–0.66), perception of hospital caring climate (r = 0.45, 95% CI: 0.31–0.57), and perceived teacher caring (r = 0.36, 95% CI: 0.22–0.50) were positively associated with professional identity. Role stress (r = -0.32, 95% CI: -0.38 to -0.25) and anxiety (r = -0.14, 95% CI: -0.19 to -0.10) were negatively associated with professional identity. The association between clinical practice behaviour and professional identity was not statistically significant (r = 0.41, 95% CI: -0.03 to 0.73). Conclusion: This study showed that professional identity among nursing interns in China was associated with multiple factors. Humanistic caring ability, clinical learning environment, psychological resilience, professional self-efficacy, perceived teacher caring, hospital caring climate, medical narrative competence, perceived professional benefit and social support were associated with higher professional identity, whereas role stress and anxiety were associated with lower professional identity. The association between clinical practice behaviour and professional identity remained inconclusive. Nursing colleges and internship hospitals should support the development of professional identity among nursing interns by optimising the clinical learning environment, strengthening clinical mentoring support, enhancing psychological resources and reducing negative emotional experiences. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Maliao R.J.; Tóthmérész B.
Title: Expert Grief: Epistemic injustice and the paradox of knowledge in social-ecological systems
Abstract: The systemic marginalization of Indigenous and Local Knowledge (ILK) creates significant blind spots in conservation science, often obscuring the affective and cognitive signals of social-ecological decay. We introduce Expert Grief, a framework describing an epistemic paradox: the cognitive fisheries ecological knowledge that underpins livelihood resilience also amplifies affective distress in response to systemic environmental decline. Using a Philippines-based model system, we analyzed multi-decadal data from 448 artisanal fishers through a retrospective cross-sectional design and Linear Mixed-Effects Models (LMMs) to link shifts in cognitive fisheries baselines with affective livelihood satisfaction. Our results reveal a significant dual erosion, where a multi-decadal simplification of the fishery's trophic structure is mirrored by a concurrent decline in livelihood satisfaction (β = −0.44, p = 0.0012). Crucially, a significant interaction between fishing experience and time explains the Expert Grief paradox. Although the ILK of veteran fishers sustains their individual catch success (β = 0.006, p = 0.01), this deeper knowledge correlates with a steeper decline in livelihood satisfaction compared to novice fishers (β = −0.001, p = 0.02). The Expert Grief framework offers two theoretical advances: mechanistically defining the cognitive drivers of Shifting Baseline Syndrome (SBS) and characterizing an affective, knowledge-mediated form of solastalgia. Exposing this grief reveals that marginalizing local expertise obscures cumulative social-ecological decay and decouples technocratic conservation from the lived realities of those at the forefront of change. Ultimately, we demonstrate that epistemic justice is not just an ethical ideal but a fundamental prerequisite for effective and equitable conservation. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Pei Z.; Guo Z.; Yu Z.; Huang Y.; Wang L.
Title: An evidence-based framework for digital intelligence-enabled urban physical examination in pandemic prevention
Abstract: Urban pandemic prevention increasingly requires digital intelligence to support evidence organization, diagnostic reasoning, and action-oriented governance. Existing studies have provided assessment tools and strategic references, yet approaches remain limited for explaining how multi-source materials can be transformed into traceable framework elements and city-specific diagnostic knowledge. Using Design Science Research, this study develops a digital-intelligence-enabled urban physical examination framework (DI-UPEF) for pandemic prevention. Policy documents, academic studies, practice reports, and expert materials are organized through a data–information–evidence transformation process, and two chains of evidence are constructed to analyze actor systems, examination objects, diagnostic methods, procedural structures, adaptive requirements, and evidence-to-action pathways. The results show that DI-UPEF involves six major actor systems and six categories of examination objects. Weak-link identification depends on a method–process structure connecting data acquisition, feature representation, model analysis, evaluation and interpretation, problem identification, and feedback loops. Adaptive capacity is reflected in anomaly triggering, dynamic adjustment, structural reconfiguration, resilience enhancement, and continuous updating, although its operational rules remain underdeveloped. Evidence-to-action translation links evidence interpretation, policy options, action design, implementation, and updating. The policy-text validation, multi-city application, and comparison with established frameworks show that DI-UPEF can organize explicit policy objectives, surface implicit methodological and operational structures, generate city-level evidence profiles, and support differentiated diagnosis across urban contexts. The framework also highlights diagnostic uncertainty and governance boundaries involving data conflicts, monitoring failures, privacy protection, surveillance risks, algorithmic transparency, social network noise, and accountability. Overall, this study provides a traceable and city-oriented diagnostic framework for evidence-informed urban pandemic prevention. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Go J.
Title: Theorist Ignored: Hubert Harrison and the Birth of Racial Capitalism Theory
Abstract: Hubert Henry Harrison (1883–1927) was an early twentieth-century writer who engaged Marxist theoreticians and conventional American sociological theory in his writings, but he remains unknown to social theorists and histories of American social science. This article shows that Harrison was a social theorist offering valuable insights into the relationship between racial inequality and capitalism. Across his writings, Harrison developed a nascent theory of racial capitalism that anticipated contemporary debates while offering distinct contributions. He conceptualized capitalist production as racially bifurcated and asserted the relative autonomy of race; he offered a structuration theory of racism and capitalist reproduction, showing how racial capitalism is a system co-constituted by racism and economic imperatives; he theorized the role of imperialism and its different forms, explaining how racism globalizes; and he explained agency and resistance as necessary outcomes of the logic of global racial capitalism. © American Sociological Association 2026

Authors: Mazzucchelli O.; Reichstein T.; Rossi-Lamastra C.
Title: Same job, different status: gender differences in societal status perception of male and female scientists
Abstract: Scientists are generally perceived as high-status individuals. This paper examines how society perceives the status of scientists in relation to their gender and context. It relies on a survey experiment conducted with 773 participants from different Italian regions who were asked to assess the status of fictional scientists of different genders. The findings reveal a gendered disparity in status attribution: male scientists are consistently perceived as high-status by both male and female participants, whereas female scientists are attributed lower status, primarily due to the evaluations made by female participants. Notably, female participants from regions with higher levels of egalitarianism attribute higher status to female scientists compared to those from less egalitarian areas, thus narrowing the status gap between male and female scientists. Our work contributes to the discourse on gender in science by demonstrating that status emerges as a distinct dimension of inequality, can be measured independently, follows a gendered pattern, and is contingent upon social contexts. © The Author(s) 2025.

Authors: Oğuz E.; Akpolat T.;  Keskinkılıç Kara S.B.;  Zafer Güneş D.
Title: Typologies of academic ethical blindness among graduate students
Abstract: Academic ethical blindness refers to the temporary inability of individuals to recognize the moral dimensions of a situation when making decisions, often emerging through rationalization, routinization, and ambiguity. Although ethical violations among graduate students have been widely documented, the cognitive patterns underlying these violations remain insufficiently understood. This study examines graduate students’ subjective perspectives on academic ethical blindness to identify the distinct viewpoints shaping their ethical reasoning. Using Q methodology, 26 graduate students enrolled in educational sciences programs at universities in Istanbul, Türkiye, sorted a Q-sample of 34 statements organized around the themes of rationalization, routine, and ambiguity. Data were analyzed in PQMethod 2.35 using principal component analysis with Varimax and judgmental rotation. A four-factor solution explaining 53% of the total variance was retained, with composite reliability coefficients ranging from 0.94 to 0.97. The findings revealed four distinct perspectives: Pragmatic Justifiers, who relax ethical boundaries in gray areas under time pressure; Procedural Purists, who adhere unconditionally to formal rules; Social Norm-Oriented, who locate ethical problems in disciplinary conventions; and Norm Seekers, who attribute ethical blindness to institutional ambiguity. The results indicate that academic ethical blindness is not a uniform moral shortcoming, but a multidimensional phenomenon shaped by the interplay of cognitive mechanisms, interpersonal dynamics, and structural conditions. These findings suggest that interventions targeting academic integrity should be differentiated according to students’ distinct ethical orientations rather than uniform regulatory approaches. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Chasen A.; Borrego M.
Title: An Exploration of the Relationships Between Science Identity and Disabled Identities in Undergraduate Science Students
Abstract: Science identity is often conceptualized through constructs such as performance, competence, recognition, and interest, with prior research highlighting the roles of race, gender, and cultural background in shaping students' experiences. However, limited scholarship has examined how disability interacts with science identity in postsecondary science education. This qualitative study explores the relationships between scientific and disabled identities among 21 undergraduate students who self-identify as disabled and have participated in lab-based science courses at a public R1 university. Through semi-structured interviews analyzed using thematic and deductive coding, we examined how students narrate the intersection of these two identities and how dimensions of the prevailing science identity framework manifest across those narratives. Nearly all participants described their identities as oppositional in at least some contexts, with performance and recognition by others, rather than competence, emerging as the dimensions most disrupted by disabling environments. Many also described interactive and parallel relationships, in which disability and science identity shaped one another bidirectionally, and in which skills cultivated through disability—resilience, adaptability, and systems thinking—transferred meaningfully into scientific practice. Fewer participants described overlapping or intersectional relationships, the latter representing the most integrated view of the two identities as mutually constitutive. Across relationship types, structural conditions consistently shaped participants' experiences including the near-total absence of visible disabled community in science spaces, and the burden of navigating disclosure. These findings extend science identity frameworks to account for disability as a key social dimension, with implications for mentorship, institutional support, and inclusive science education. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Argente-García J.E.; García A.A.; Muñoz A.C.; Caruso S.; Atucha A.M.; Gómez A.S.
Title: Combining new technologies with traditional knowledge to improve fishing efficiency and preserve the last Spanish Mediterranean Almadraba
Abstract: Mediterranean artisanal fisheries in the Region of Murcia, and more broadly, face severe economic, environmental, and socio-labour challenges that threaten their long-term sustainability and, consequently, the principles of a Blue Economy aimed at fostering growth while ensuring environmental and social wellbeing. Nevertheless, the adoption of digital technologies remains limited due to time constraints, high costs, and low technical skills. In response to these challenges, we co-developed WiSea, an early-warning and decision-support system, in collaboration with artisanal fishers from the Tonnara (Almadraba) of La Azohía and the Fishermen’s Guild of Águilas. WiSea is a prototype that integrates an underwater camera buoy with real-time data processing and transmission, thereby enabling fishers to optimise catch, monitor nets, and prevent dolphin-related damages. Importantly, beyond the technical proof of concept, the project implemented a participatory process with local artisanal fishers, actively incorporating their traditional knowledge and practices. Moreover, two multi-actor workshops involving 135 stakeholders from fisheries, science, universities, and administrations were organised to co-create solutions and explore digitalisation pathways. To complement these efforts, a questionnaire was distributed to capture perceptions on digitalisation and its role in promoting a fair and inclusive Blue Economy adapted to the Murcia region, while looking for local fishing communities. Overall, field tests during Almadraba operations and participatory evaluations confirmed WiSea’s usability and potential to enhance operational efficiency and sustainability. However, barriers such as training gaps, high costs and insufficient supportive policies persist. Therefore, unlocking the full potential of digitalisation will require coordinated technical, economic, and institutional support to ensure that innovation complements, rather than replaces, local knowledge and artisanal practices. Finally, future research should extend this approach to other Mediterranean regions to assess broader applicability and equity implications for a just Blue Economy. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Diaz J.A.R.; Montesi M.
Title: Informetric analysis of the social impact on scientific production in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, and Mexico (2016–2024); [Análisis informétrico del impacto social en la producción científica de Argentina, Brasil, Chile, Colombia y México (2016–2024)]
Abstract: In the context of recent debates on the social function of science, social impact has gained increasing prominence as a discursive category in scientific production, especially in Latin America. This article analyzes, from an informetric approach, how social impact is addressed in scientific literature produced in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, and Mexico during the period 2016–2024. The study is based on the construction of a bibliographic corpus from records retrieved from the Scopus and OpenAlex databases, used in a complementary manner to expand regional and linguistic coverage. Using co-occurrence analysis techniques, semantic network visualization, and thematic comparison between countries, the main conceptual nuclei associated with social impact are examined, as well as their relationships and national configurations. The work does not seek to measure or evaluate the effective social impact of research, but rather to identify discursive patterns, thematic regularities, and conceptual trajectories that structure its presence in indexed scientific literature. The results offer a comparative characterization of national agendas and provide insights into how social impact is configured as an object of analysis in contemporary Latin American science. © 2026 Editorial CSIC.

Authors: Isanazar A.; Abdollahee R.; Nejatifar F.; Mirfarhadi N.
Title: The relationship between social support and resilience with quality of life in breast cancer patients: a cross-sectional analytical study
Abstract: Introduction: Cancer is a condition that poses a threat to public health and adversely affects all aspects of patients’ quality of life. One strategy to mitigate the negative effects of the disease is social support. This study was conducted to determine the relationship between social support and resilience with quality of life in patients with breast cancer. Methods: This analytical cross-sectional study was carried out in the province of Gilan (northern Iran) from September 2021 to February 2022. Data were collected from breast cancer patients referred to the Hematology and Radiotherapy Department of Razi Hospital in Rasht, affiliated with the Guilan University of Medical Sciences, using four questionnaires: a demographic form, the Cancer and Davidson Resilience Questionnaire (CD-RIS), the Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (MSPSS), and the Quality of Life Questionnaire (C30-QLQ). Participants were selected through consecutive sampling. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 22, with normality assessed using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Shapiro-Wilk tests, and relationships among variables were examined using the Spearman nonparametric test. A significance level of p < 0.05 was considered for all statistical analyses. Results: A total of 89 women with breast cancer participated in the study, with a mean age of 44.15 ± 17.9 years, and more than half held a diploma or associate degree. Most patients were in stage 2 of cancer (43.8%), and chemotherapy was the most common treatment intervention (67.4%). The findings indicated that there was no significant relationship between quality of life and demographic characteristics such as age, education level, occupation, cancer stage, and type of treatment. Furthermore, Spearman’s correlation analysis revealed that the functioning score—a component of quality of life—was significantly inversely related to the total scores of social support and resilience (p = 0.041 and p = 0.028, respectively), whereas the overall quality of life score exhibited a significant positive correlation with the acceptance subscale of resilience (p = 0.007). Logistic regression analysis also indicated that family support (a subscale of social support) and personal competence (a subscale of resilience) were significant predictors of patients’ functioning and symptomatology (p = 0.05 and p = 0.019, respectively). Conclusion: The results of this study indicate that breast cancer patients require assistance in adapting to their condition. Receiving and strengthening social support from family and friends plays a crucial role in helping patients cope with and combat the disease. Enhancing perceived social support and quality of life in these patients should be given serious consideration to prevent social, psychological, and physical complications and to improve overall functioning. © The Author(s) 2025.

Authors: Yurt S.; Açıkgoz G.; Aksoy Z.; Akgun F.S.; Demirel A.; Karaca Ö.; Okuroğlu G.
Title: The effect of high-fidelity simulation on nursing students’ self-confidence and stress levels during patient intervention: a randomized controlled trial
Abstract: Background: High-fidelity simulation provides a safe and effective learning environment in nursing education, supporting the development of clinical competence and patient safety. This randomized controlled trial aimed to examine the effect of high-fidelity simulation on nursing students’ self-confidence and perceived stress levels during patient care interventions. Methods: The study included 38 senior nursing students who completed a pretest consisting of the Student Identification Form, the Self-Confidence in Intervening with Patients Scale, and the Perceived Stress Scale. The experimental group participated in a simulated shock scenario using high-fidelity simulation, while the control group received routine theoretical instruction. Posttests were administered to both groups two weeks after the intervention. The data obtained in the study were statistically analyzed using SPSS (Statistical Package for the Social Sciences) version 25.0 for Windows. The study adhered to the CONSORT 2010 guidelines. Results: No statistically significant differences were found between the experimental and control groups in posttest total scores of self-confidence or perceived stress (p > 0.05). However, within-group analysis indicated significant improvements in the experimental group’s self-confidence total score and in the subdimensions of clinical practice and psychological support (p < 0.05). These improvements demonstrate that students’ clinical performance during patient care interventions is supported. Conclusion: High-fidelity simulation training significantly enhanced nursing students’ self-confidence during patient care interventions, whereas perceived stress levels did not differ significantly within or between groups. These findings support the integration of high-fidelity simulation into nursing curricula to enhance students’ clinical preparedness. Further studies with larger and diverse samples are recommended to strengthen the evidence base. Authors: Yousefi P.; Tehran H.A.; Madani E.; Boosaliki H.; Yavari N.; Madani M.
Title: Moral character development in nursing students: a qualitative content analysis in Iran
Abstract: Background: Nursing is a moral profession requiring virtues such as compassion and integrity to deliver ethical care amid complex challenges like moral distress. Despite known influences on moral development, nursing students’ own perceptions of factors shaping their moral character remain underexplored. Therefore, this study aimed to explore nursing students’ perceptions of the factors contributing to the development of moral character. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study and conventional content analysis was used. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 16 purposive-sampled nursing students (Bachelor’s and Master’s) at Hormozgan University of Medical Sciences, Iran, between June and August 2025. Data were analysed following Graneheim and Lundman’s approach until data saturation (meaning saturation) was achieved. Trustworthiness was ensured through credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability strategies, guided by the COREQ checklist. Results: Four overarching themes emerged, encompassing 14 sub-themes: (1) inner motivations and values (four sub-themes: intrinsic motivation, personal/religious beliefs, psychological capital, self-reflection); (2) relational dynamics and communication (three sub-themes: role modeling, peer support, family/community influences); (3) moral learning in practice (three sub-themes: formal ethics education, staged clinical experiences, simulation training); and (4) systemic and organizational influences (four sub-themes: university culture, clinical ethical climate, professional norms, resource availability). Conclusion: Moral character development is a dynamic, multifaceted process shaped by personal conviction, social relationships, structured learning, and institutional contexts, underscoring the ethical significance of virtues like resilience and integrity in navigating moral distress. In this Iranian cohort, religious values and relational role models were particularly salient. These findings inform bioethics curricula and policy to strengthen moral resilience among nursing students, preparing them for ethical practice amid complex healthcare challenges. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Jiang J.; Liu J.
Title: An interdisciplinary perspective on the definition of evaluative meaning: what can linguistics learn from psychology and philosophy?
Abstract: Studies on evaluative meaning (EM) have a long history in the social sciences. Among these studies, linguistics has made significant contributions to describing the meaning and use of evaluative language. Nevertheless, distinct kinds of EMs in linguistic research overlap with each other. Although linguists have resorted to psychological and philosophical research to define different kinds of EMs, their conclusions cannot depict the relationships between those EMs. The key to identifying an interdisciplinary approach to this issue lies in comprehending current research trends and the influential theories in those two disciplines concerning the linguistic EM. Consequently, this study reviews the important and influential research on EMs shared by the three disciplines via bibliometric analysis. The co-citation analysis results indicate that psychological research, relevant to linguistic EM, primarily concerns whether EMs are generated automatically or consciously, while philosophical research, pertaining to linguistic EM, focuses mainly on the truth conditions of EM interpretation. Based on these results, we conclude two pairs of concepts (i.e., conscious vs. automatic and epistemic vs. ontological) that are likely to innovate linguistic methodology for analyzing EMs. In addition, owing to the existence of those concepts, two analytical perspectives (i.e., producer-analyst vs. addressee-analyst) are required in an interdisciplinary linguistic approach to defining linguistic EMs. The current study proposes a descriptive-explanatory perspective of linguistic EM research, which is beneficial for its definition and classification in the future. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Sezdi T.
Title: A Bibliometric Analysis of Material Deprivation: Mapping the Literature and the Emergence of Child Deprivation as a Sub-Field
Abstract: This study examines the development of the concept of material deprivation (MD) in the academic literature and the phenomenon of child material deprivation as a distinct sub-field, using bibliometric methods. The dataset, covering approximately the last 30 years, includes 805 academic studies from the Web of Science and Scopus databases, showing that academic production has increased since 2010, with the child specific sub-corpus growing at 6.82% annually. The results show that the most productive countries in this field are predominantly European countries and the United States, while the leading academic journals are those focusing on social policy and child welfare, such as the Social Indicators Research and the Child Indicators Research. Co-occurrence network analyses have identified two main focal points in the literature: poverty is concentrated on the axes of social exclusion and employment, while material deprivation focuses on multidimensional measurement methodologies. According to the study’s findings, child deprivation, addressed under the heading of child poverty in 2008, has also been examined as child specific material deprivation since 2021. This shows that the concept of child deprivation has evolved from an income-focused approach to a multidimensional approach. A complementary sub-corpus analysis using child-specific keywords reveals that 69.6% of publications on child deprivation can be found only through these terms. A preliminary content analysis of influential articles from four periods reveals a conceptual change from static measurements in the 1990’s to crisis-sensitive, dynamic frameworks. The findings also show that MD research is largely absent from mainstream economics and finance journals. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature B.V. 2026.

Authors: Dalibert L.; Groud P.-F.; Gourinat V.
Title: The Quiet Work of Prosthetic Tinkering: Disability Expertise and Everyday World-Making
Abstract: Prosthetic devices are often framed as biomedical solutions designed by professionals to restore function to disabled bodies. Drawing on ethnographic research conducted with amputees in France, the Netherlands, and Germany, this article challenges this view by examining how prosthetic users actively modify, fabricate, and reconfigure their devices in everyday life. These practices, we argue, are forms of prosthetic tinkering, that is, situated interventions through which users adjust, repurpose, or create prosthetic devices and arrangements in response to bodily sensations, environmental constraints, and social interactions. Through ethnographic cases, such as socket adjustments, homemade task-specific prostheses, alternative mobility arrangements, and aesthetic modifications, we show that these practices constitute a form of disability expertise grounded in experiential knowledge of bodies and technologies. This article shows that prosthetic tinkering allows amputees not only to improve comfort and functionality, but also to navigate ableist norms, manage the visibility of disability, and reshape social relationships. Importantly, prosthetic tinkering mainly takes place in the domestic sphere, i.e., in kitchens, garages, and living rooms, rather than in the more visible or publicised sites of technological innovation such as laboratories, engineering workshops, or fablabs. By foregrounding these often-overlooked practices, the article contributes to science and technology studies and critical disability studies debates on agency, expertise, and the politics of design, highlighting prosthetic modification as a situated practice of world-making rather than a mere technical adjustment. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Chakma S.
Title: Exoticizing the other: subaltern voices in textbooks of Bangladesh
Abstract: Education is a political construct designed to foster unity and cultivate enmity through narratives. Indigenous peoples in Bangladesh, comprising 54 ethno-linguistically diverse tribes, have historically been marginalized in educational depictions. Textbooks have been criticized for perpetuating bias and reinforcing dominant narratives that marginalize indigenous peoples. This study analyzed the representation of indigenous topics in social science textbooks for primary and junior secondary education, as outlined in the curriculum-2021 (later withdrawn). By employing Spivak’s Subaltern theory and the seven-forms-of-bias framework developed by Sadker & Sadker, this study examined a sample of six state-issued textbooks. The findings revealed that the narratives presented in the texts were riddled with biases and (mis)representation, which continue to exist in terminal competencies and textbooks, perpetuating harmful narratives. The results obtained may serve as a reference for future modifications of educational curricula and texts, with the goal of transforming the education system into a more inclusive framework that provides equitable chances for all. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Sainte-Marie M.H.; Larivière V.
Title: Any old Tom, Dick, or Harry: The citation impact of author first name genderedness
Abstract: This paper examines the relationship between the genderedness of authors' first names and citation distributions in US-affiliated scholarly production from 2010 to 2019. Merging a first name genderedness table derived from Wikidata with Web of Science publication data, we develop a relative distributional framework that compares first name, article, and citation distributions by both disciplinary group and author role along a continuous genderedness spectrum. The lexical structure of the corpus proves stable across author roles, while productivity diverges substantially by disciplinary group: physical sciences show a consistent masculine lean, social sciences a feminine one, with amplitude remaining stable across groups despite these directional differences. Once productivity is controlled for, citation analyses net of publication volume reveal a pervasive deficit across disciplinary groups and author roles: only unambiguously masculine names accumulate citations in excess of their publication volume, while feminine, neutral, and moderately masculine names all fall short of it. This asymmetry is strongest in the life sciences and weakest in the physical sciences except among middle authors, where the pattern reflects the gender composition of large collaborative teams rather than evaluative bias in citing behavior. Taken together, these results are consistent with the hypothesis that first name genderedness shapes citation recognition through implicit bias operating in low-deliberation evaluative contexts. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Sintos J.R.; Macabenta K.B.
Title: Academic engagement and resilience in undergraduate statistics programs with high involuntary enrollment
Abstract: Despite the critical role of data expertise in national development, many students enroll in statistics programs involuntarily due to university admission quotas. This study investigated the determinants of academic engagement among Bachelor of Science (BS) Statistics students using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design (N = 262). A One-Way Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA) revealed a highly significant institutional effect of Academic Year Level on the combined experiential dimensions (Pillai’s Trace = 0.15, F(12, 771) = 3.48, p <.001), establishing the presence of a distinct “Senior Year Surge” where fourth-year students exhibit significantly higher engagement and self-efficacy than underclassmen. Furthermore, a 4 × 2 Factorial ANOVA demonstrated that while initial enrollment status (voluntary vs. involuntary) significantly impacts baseline motivation, it does not interact with year level to limit final-year commitment (p >.05), proving that the “Senior Year Surge” occurs independently of initial program entry conditions. Spearman’s rank correlation matrix further indicated that Career Perception (= 0.34) and Motivation/Self-Efficacy (= 0.45) share the strongest bonds with active engagement, while institutional belongingness remains secondary. Qualitative insights from 122 participants highlighted that while students face severe “mathematical pain” and material precarity (e.g., lack of laptops), their persistence is sustained by the high perceived market utility of the degree. These findings culminate in the Statistics Student Success Framework (SSSF), a validated institutional model proving that for students in high-difficulty technical domains, instrumental career outlook serves as a more potent driver of long-term persistence than baseline interest or social integration. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Aria M.; Cuccurullo C.; D’Aniello L.; Spano M.
Title: SciK-Health: an open-data dashboard for the multidimensional evaluation of Italian academic health science centers
Abstract: Academic Health Science Centers (AHSCs) integrate research, education, and clinical care within complex organizational settings, making performance assessment inherently multidimensional. Traditional evaluation approaches based on single-source bibliometric data provide only a partial representation of this complexity, failing to capture the full translational spectrum from basic research to clinical application and societal impact. This paper presents SciK-Health, an integrated knowledge management platform designed to transform heterogeneous research data into actionable insights for multiple stakeholders. The platform addresses three key challenges: fragmentation across data sources, institutional heterogeneity requiring standardized metrics, and differentiated user needs. Methodologically, it implements a transparent three-stage workflow integrating OpenAlex (publications), Dimensions (clinical trials, patents, grants, datasets), and Altmetric (social impact), using Research Organization Registry identifiers and DOI-based cross-linking. The system operationalizes over 140 standardized indicators across five dimensions: bibliometric impact, social engagement, industrial innovation, clinical research activity, and competitive funding success. Applied to 49 Italian public AHSCs, SciK-Health adopts a user-centered design serving distinct audiences: citizens accessing institutional expertise, clinical managers supporting strategic monitoring, and policy makers conducting portfolio-level analyses. Empirical results highlight substantial institutional heterogeneity and show that single-source bibliometric approaches provide a systematically incomplete assessment of performance. Relative to existing platforms (SciVal, InCites, CWTS Leiden Open Edition), SciK-Health contributes a fully open-data infrastructure, multi-output integration, and a citizen-oriented LLM-assisted search interface. While the methodological framework is transferable, cross-national application requires substantial adaptation of data sources, institutional taxonomies, and indicator systems. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Bessai J.W.
Title: Trends in Political Science Research The Politics of Intersectionality
Abstract: Intersectionality emerged from Black feminist struggles that named how racism, sexism, class domination, and heterosexism work through the same institutions. In recent political science scholarship, the concept now organizes research on representation, social movements, bureaucracy, climate governance, and security administration. This review reads selective foundational texts alongside peer-reviewed political science scholarship published mainly between 2020 and 2024. It tracks how scholars define and operationalize intersectionality, what kinds of evidence they assemble, and how their findings travel into policy tools, bureaucratic routines, and evaluative practices. Three debates recur across this literature. The first concerns method: scholars must decide whether to model intersecting positions through surveys, interviews, comparative designs, or institutional analysis, and each choice reveals different dimensions of power. The second concerns governance: intersectionality acquires political force when categories, complaint pathways, consultation rules, and administrative records register unequal exposure to harm. The third concerns political economy: fiscal restraint, labor organization, and care infrastructures shape which commitments endure in public institutions. The review closes by arguing that durable equity practice depends on the ordinary instruments of governance, including classifications, staffing patterns, accountability routines, and data systems. © International Political Science Association 2026

Authors: Clouth F.J.; Bijlsma M.J.; Pauws S.; Vermunt J.K.
Title: Causal Inference for Latent Markov Models Using the Parametric G-Formula
Abstract: The parametric g-formula can be used to estimate causal effects of time-varying exposures on observable outcomes. It resolves intermediate confounding in such settings by specifying several parametric models, one each for every time-varying variable, and by performing micro-simulations. However, its restriction to applications with observable outcomes limits its usability for social sciences where variables of interest are often unobservable constructs. In such cases, measurement models are needed. We propose a new approach utilizing bias-adjusted three-step latent Markov models (LMMs) within the parametric g-formula. LMMs estimate the probability of membership in an unobservable state conditional on observed indicator variables. By replacing the parametric models in the g-formula with LMMs, micro-simulations are performed as usual to estimate a causal effect of the time-varying exposure. We illustrate this new approach by estimating the average treatment effect of unemployment on several unobservable mental health states utilizing longitudinal data from the Longitudinal Internet studies for the Social Sciences panel. © The Author(s) 2025. Authors: Zhao S.; Kang C.; Hu W.; Feng Z.
Title: Adoption of generative artificial intelligence in instruction: a mixed-methods UTAUT study of K-12 computer science teachers in China
Abstract: This study examines the adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in instructional practices among K-12 computer science teachers (CSTs) in China, addressing a gap in understanding how subject-specific teachers engage with emerging technologies. Grounded in Expectancy-Value Theory (EVT), the research extends the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) by incorporating Innovation Expectation (IE), Cost-benefit (CB), and Perceived Risk (PR), thereby capturing both motivational drivers and potential constraints. A mixed-methods design was employed: in the quantitative phase, survey data from 338 CSTs across 20 provinces were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM). The results showed that Performance Expectancy (PE), Effort Expectancy (EE), and IE significantly strengthened teachers’ Attitude to Use (AU), while Social Influence (SI) was not significant. Intention to Use (IU) was shaped by IE, CB, AU, and PR, with PR exerting a negative effect. IU further served as a significant predictor of Behavioral Intention to Use (BI). In the qualitative phase, 12 CSTs participated in concept map-supported interviews. Thematic analysis highlighted barriers including perceived erosion of teacher authority, student overreliance, fragmented understanding of GenAI functions, and ethical data security concerns, while underscoring the importance of targeted professional development and discipline-specific tools. Findings illustrate the multidimensional factors shaping the adoption of GenAI and emphasize the value of theoretically grounded, context-sensitive approaches in supporting teachers’ integration of emerging technologies. These findings suggest that schools and education authorities can promote the effective use of GenAI by teachers through tailored training, tiered support resources, and clear ethical guidelines. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Rimkus E.
Title: Artificial Intelligence from the Perspectives of Philosophy, Sociology and Communication; [Dirbtinis intelektas filosofijos, sociologijos ir komunikacijos požiūriu]
Abstract: The article discusses the main ideas presented at a scientific conference on artificial intelligence viewed from the perspectives of philosophy, sociology and communication. AI cannot be regarded merely as a narrow technical or computer science topic, since its development raises fundamental questions about the nature of the human mind, the cognitive capacities and creativity of the human being, and the development of society. The papers presented at the conference reveal not only the new opportunities that AI opens up for humanity, but also the risks it poses in education, media, politics, warfare, artistic creativity, social inequality, human self-understanding, and other domains. The article shows that AI’s ability to perform various tasks quickly and efficiently does not mean that it can take over what is most essential to human beings – understanding, interpretation, value orientations, the creation of meaning, and a responsible relationship with other people and with the natural and social environment. Therefore, the development of AI compels us to consider not only what technologies can do better or faster than human beings, but also what still remains beyond the reach of algorithms – lived experience, embodiment, creative intention, moral responsibility, and the capacity to reflect on the meaning of one’s actions. The article argues that AI should be understood not only as a technological system, but also as a social, cultural and political force reshaping human values and everyday life. It concludes that AI must be assessed in an interdisciplinary way, taking into account not only criteria of innovation or performance, but also its consequences for human beings, democracy, and meaningful human existence. © 2026, Lithuanian Academy of Sciences Publishers. Authors: Ćirić D.
Title: Spatial design insights for security studies: digital space for research procedures and strategic actions
Abstract: Starting from the paradigm of convergence of spatially-oriented sciences and spatial research and design, the article addresses issues related to digital environments and systems as instruments for spatial research and investigative procedures, hybrid intelligence, and provision of reliable proofs for scientific argumentation, strategic spatial decisions, actions, and interventions. It has been presumed that previously established cross-disciplinary relations could be reinvestigated in the light of the more recent techno-social and techno-scientific advancements, particularly connectivity between spatial, urban, and architectural studies and security studies. In that respect, concepts of spatiality of security and spatial security have been introduced. Next, design research methodologies have been proposed to complement the security studies, enabling them to acquire design capacities. In such reference, concepts of security design, security design research, and security design research methodology have been coined. Finally, digital spatial information and intelligence systems, or digital spatial environments and models, have been proposed as tools and formats through which stated concepts can be applied and investigated, offering new spatial and design insights for security studies. © The Author(s) 2025.

Authors: Capra G.F.
Title: Urban ethnopedology: Integrating community soil knowledge into environmental justice and urban greening policy
Abstract: Urban soils have become increasingly important for landscape and urban planning as community involvement in green space management gains prominence, yet the ways cultural diversity shapes perceptions and management of urban soils remain poorly understood. This paper consolidates urban ethnopedology (UE) into an explicit framework for analyzing how different social groups conceptualize, classify, and manage urban soils, and for integrating this experiential knowledge into environmental policy and planning. The proposal builds on existing work in critical physical geography, urban political ecology, and science and technology studies, and identifies three structural obstacles, i.e., ontological, demographic, and regulatory, that have kept community soil knowledge outside urban environmental governance. Urban ethnopedology links scattered evidence from urban agriculture, immigrant gardening, traditional ecological knowledge, community forestry, and citizen science to show that culturally based soil management practices generate systematic differences in soil quality that are largely invisible to the classification systems and regulatory thresholds on which current urban soil policies and management plans rest. Building on this, the paper proposes a four-step framework that combines ethnographic methods with field-based soil science: i) ethnographic observation and engagement, ii) systematic documentation of knowledge systems, iii) soil investigation informed by practitioner insights, and iv) collaborative interpretation with community and municipal actors. Framing urban soils as socio-ecological systems co-produced by biophysical processes and cultural practices, UE highlights how existing planning paradigms sideline the expertise of residents who already steward urban soils. The perspective argues that recognizing and mobilizing this expertise has direct implications for urban greening strategies, environmental justice objectives, and the design of more inclusive and effective soil management policies. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Osborne J.; Allchin D.
Title: Informed Trust, Epistemic Dependence, Elitism, and the Challenge of Misinformation: A Response to Potvin et al. (2025)
Abstract: In this commentary, we respond to Potvin et al. (2025), explaining the flaws we find in their critique of our vision of twenty-first -century science education (Osborne & Allchin, 2024). Principally, our response argues that they have not considered fully the social nature of knowledge, our dependence on specialized experts, or how we cope with knowledge claims that lie beyond our ability to detect all possible sources of error. We argue that reliance on the expertise of others does not foster elitism; rather, it should engender respect for others who know more than we do. This does not imply deference but rather indicates a need to educate students in science media literacy and for them to learn precisely when and why such trust is justified, or well informed. © Ontario Institute for Studies in Education (OISE) 2026.

Authors: Wu X.; Wei X.
Title: What happens to our thinking when morality marries with capital: another revolution of metaphor?
Abstract: Along the revolutionary ontological history of metaphor, this case study investigates the metaphor underpinning the theoretical discourse system of The Theory of Morality Capital and its specific interaction mechanisms. The overall findings are: the conceptual metaphor MORALITY IS CAPITAL, supporting this theory, possesses simultaneously two different interacting mechanisms between the source concept CAPITAL and the target concept MORALITY. One is the surface conventional metaphorical mapping mechanism in which the source CAPITAL is the basis for understanding the target MORALITY, and the other is the inner influencing mechanism in which the target MORALITY has the function of restraining, guiding, and coordinating the source CAPITAL. These two mechanisms motivate two sets of novel concept systems for supporting The Theory of Morality Capital, and at the same time provide two ways of understanding these emerging concepts. The present study designates this unique bidirectional interaction within the same conceptual metaphor as “the understanding-influencing interaction between CAPITAL and MORALITY”. By nature, it differs from the bidirectionality of metaphorical mapping discussed in the previous studies, which are based on two distinct interpretive grounds and undergo semantic shifts. These findings provide four implications for metaphor research and, in conjunction with the existing studies on bidirectional metaphorical mapping, may potentially pave the way for fostering another breakthrough understanding of metaphorical thinking in the future. Meanwhile, this study may offer insights into cognitive mechanisms for constructing an innovative theoretical discourse system in humanities and social sciences. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Demirdöǧen B.; Uzuntiryaki-Kondakci E.; McAlpin J.D.; Lewis J.E.
Title: Self-Regulated Learning and Chemistry Mindset as Predictors of General Chemistry Performance: Evidence from Natural Sciences and Engineering Majors in Turkey
Abstract: Introductory chemistry courses present significant challenges for undergraduate students, and understanding the factors that support or hinder performance remains an active area of inquiry. This study examined the construct validity of the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) and investigated the extent to which self-regulation strategies and chemistry mindsets predict exam performance among natural sciences and engineering majors enrolled in general chemistry courses at a large research-intensive university in Turkey. A total of 871 students completed a 45-item version of the MSLQ and the Chemistry Mindset Instrument (CheMI) during the Spring 2024 semester. Confirmatory factor analysis supported a four second-order factor structure: individual learning strategies, metacognitive self-regulation, social learning strategies, and effort and environment regulation strategies. Regression analyses revealed that prior exam performance was the strongest predictor of subsequent achievement in both of the course contexts. Among the MSLQ factors, social learning strategies were uniquely predictive for students enrolled in the course for natural science majors, while effort and environment regulation strategies were uniquely predictive for students enrolled in the course for engineering majors. The chemistry mindset did not contribute unique predictive variance beyond prior performance in either group. These findings underscore the context-dependent nature of self-regulated learning in chemistry and suggest that targeted instructional supports such as peer learning programs for students in the course for natural science majors and time management interventions for students in the course for engineering majors may better align with students’ distinct regulatory needs. © 2026 American Chemical Society and Division of Chemical Education, Inc.

Authors: Frank D.
Title: Cultural Evolution Theory – Bridging Which Gap?
Abstract: Since the 19th century, numerous approaches have been developed to determine the relationship between Charles Darwin's theory of evolution and humans as cultural beings. All reductionist approaches, from Social Darwinism and its normative claims to Sociobiology and Memetics, have been subjected to considerable criticism, such as that of being subject to a naturalistic fallacy or assuming a simplifying and empirically untenable genetic or otherwise biological determinism. In more recent approaches, such as the Cultural Evolution Theory (CET), this criticism has been considered to the extent that culture is recognized as a distinct sphere with its own principles. Nevertheless, CET is also still intended to be a naturalistic approach, aspiring to bridge the gap between the natural sciences and the social sciences. In this paper I will (I) analyse what kind of naturalism underlies the CET approaches, (II) consider how this naturalistic claim relates to the thesis of unification and (III) argue that CET is not a bridge to the social sciences, but at least in some respects a social science itself. The quest for a bridge between the natural sciences and the social sciences is reasonable for the purpose of intensive cooperation, but not in the sense of an ontological or methodological naturalization. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: van Rossum M.
Title: De ‘jongens’ van Bontekoe? Over nut en noodzaak van mondiale geschiedenissen van kolonialisme en arbeid
Abstract: This text is the inaugural lecture given by Professor Matthias van Rossum for the professorship by special appointment on Global Histories of Labour and Colonialism at the Radboud University. The professorship is established by the International Institute of Social History (IISH), part of the Royal Dutch Academy of Sciences (KNAW), where he works as senior researcher since 2016. Van Rossum is involved in several large research and infrastructure projects addressing the history of slavery, slave trade, labour, and colonialism. In his inaugural lecture, he argues for the need for source-based global social and labour histories to critically revisit lingering dogmas that stem from colonial legacies and elite history writing, and to reconstruct narratives of the past that can shape our understanding of the world and build bridges. © (2026), (Netherlands Institute of International Relations). Authors: Myrogiannis S.; Repapis C.
Title: The reception of economic thought by Greek-speaking intellectuals in the early 19th century
Abstract: This paper offers a novel account of the historical conditions that led Greek-speaking intellectuals to read Political Economy texts before the creation of the Moden Greek state. In the period up to the Greek War of Independence, Modern Greeks were an important economic force within the Ottoman Empire and around the Eastern Mediterranean due to their trading activity. Focusing on archival material and testimonials on reading and publishing, we construct a novel understanding about the relationship between economic thought, statecraft and institutional framework, during a period of revolutionary activity. Our focus is on the reading and reception of Political Economy works as texts read through the eyes of intellectuals that were motivated by specific interests and objectives. The use of the framework of Speech Acts offers a new understanding on how economic texts are interpreted in a motivated way and, thus, offer an explanation on open research questions on the reception of economic thought during this period. We argue that in the mind of Greek-speaking intellectuals, this new science can achieve multiple goals: (1) educate Modern Greeks and bring them closer to the European mind-frame, (2) ennoble the position of traders within the social polity and, (3) discuss statecraft and therefore the institutional framework that the new Modern Greek state should have. It follows that for Modern Greeks, Political Economy texts were read, at least in part, as statecraft manuals. This shows the importance of context to understand reader reception and text interpretation during a specific historical period. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Authors: Baker D.P.; Adeel A.B.; Moradel-Vásquez J.J.; Macasaet B.T.; Powell J.J.W.; Prieto J.; Dusdal J.; Pang J.; Fu Y.C.
Title: Deepening and broadening knowledge after the PISA scientific event: bibliometric, semantic network, and expert analyses of scientization in education research
Abstract: The intensification of science as a social institution—known as scientization—is a hallmark of post-industrial society, characterized by deepening research within primary fields and expanding into new ones. While computational analyses of large bibliometric datasets reveal historical trends in the growth of science, their scale misses underlying dynamics. Conversely, qualitative accounts of specific discoveries provide context but fail to capture broader processes driving scientization. This paper introduces a middle-range approach to studying the expansion of science, focusing on scientific responses to significant scientific events (“S-events”) within specific fields over fixed periods. By combining bibliometric data with natural language processing analyses of semantic networks and expert assessments, this approach sheds light on the development of epistemic communities and their role in deepening, broadening, and interacting to foster scientific progress. The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) event generated discovery by facilitating a fluid epistemic community of interconnected scientific papers, journals, and scientists. The accumulation of PISA papers appeared not only in directly relevant journals, but also in those at cognitive distance from educational learning science. A dynamic of new ideas broadened the main conceptual core network, while other ideas formed short-lived distal conceptual cores. This case study highlights the strengths and limitations of this middle-range approach for investigating scientization processes. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Maneenut P.; Prayai N.; Prasittichok P.
Title: Shaping citizens for the Future: A needs assessment of active citizenship among undergraduate students in Bangkok
Abstract: In today's interconnected world, the role of active citizenship has become increasingly significant in responding to complex societal challenges that transcend national borders. However, studies assessing the needs required to foster active citizenship remain limited. This study aimed to identify and rank the priority needs related to key components of active citizenship among undergraduate students, while also examining the gaps between students' expectations and the existing conditions of these components in Bangkok, Thailand. A total of 421 undergraduate students were selected through a stratified random sampling procedure, representing three principal fields of study: Humanities and Social Sciences, Applied Sciences and Technologies, and Health Sciences. Data on social responsibility, civic literacy, and civic participation were collected using a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire assessing both current and desired conditions. The data were subsequently analyzed using descriptive statistics, including frequency, percentage, mean, and standard deviation, together with the Modified Priority Needs Index (PNImodified). The findings identify social responsibility as the most critical area requiring improvement, followed by civic literacy and civic participation. The study concludes that current higher education practices remain insufficient in fostering active citizenship, particularly in strengthening students' sense of social responsibility. Thus, the study recommends that universities should reconsider and redesign both curricular and co-curricular programs to incorporate contextually relevant learning experiences that promote ethical reasoning, civic engagement, and social awareness. The study provides specific guidelines on how universities can better prepare graduates for participation in civil society while remaining responsive to local institutional and cultural contexts. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Maria Vijay M.; Vijaykarthigeyan K.T.; Maria Evelyn Jucunda M.; Sivakumar D.; Rekhapriyadharshini A.
Title: The role of financial technology and financial literacy in driving financial inclusion among the women workforce in the informal sector
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Financial Inclusion is directly related to economic growth and is an integral factor in achieving sustainable development goals. As India plans to achieve Viksit Bharat by 2047, which calls for inclusive growth, the role of women and their participation in the economy becomes a significant factor in its achievement. Women have long been suppressed by patriarchal norms in a country like India, which prohibits them from availing formal financial services. However, with the development of financial technology, the gap between underserved populations and formal financial services can be reduced if used effectively. This study attempts to unravel the importance of urban financial advancements in driving financial inclusion of women’s workforce in the informal sector. METHODS: This study adopted a confirmatory quantitative survey method using Structural Equation Modeling to explore the mediating role of financial literacy between fintech and financial inclusion among women in Chennai’s informal sector. Data were collected over eight weeks through snowball sampling, using both online and in-person surveys administered in Tamil. A structured questionnaire with a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree) was used. Responses were coded by researchers, data consistency verified with an independent sample t-test, and analyses conducted using the Statistical Package for Social Sciences and Analysis of Moment Structures. FINDINGS: The findings of the study indicate that financial technology and Financial Literacy have a significant positive impact on Financial Inclusion. The study also finds that Financial Literacymediates the impact of financial technology on Financial Inclusion. Partial mediation exists in the relationship between financial technology, Financial Inclusion, and Financial Literacy, and the impact of financial technology on Financial Literacy is strengthened with a beta estimate of 0.481 after Financial Literacy is introduced as a mediating variable as compared to 0.347 before mediation. This suggests that financial technology can provide access to financial services, but utilization of these services effectively depends on Financial Literacy. CONCLUSION: This study highlights the complementary roles of financial technology and literacy in advancing inclusion among women in India’s informal sector. While fintech improves access to services, its impact is greater when users have financial knowledge and skills. The findings emphasize the need for integrated policies combining digital tools with financial education, supporting India’s inclusive growth goals under Viksit Bharat 2047. These insights are valuable for policymakers, regulators, fintech providers, and agencies working to close gender and financial gaps. ©2026 The author(s). Authors: Perron B.E.; Victor B.G.; Qi Z.
Title: Evolution of Social Work Knowledge Production Over 35 Years: An AI-Enabled Analysis of Trends in Empiricism, Methodology, Collaboration, Citation Patterns, and Output
Abstract: Purpose: This study developed a comprehensive bibliographic infrastructure addressing systematic coverage gaps in social work literature indexing and examined disciplinary knowledge production patterns from 1989 to 2025. Method: Article metadata was compiled from Web of Science, Scopus, Directory of Open Access Journals, and web scraping. A small language model performed classification and extraction tasks on abstracts. Results: Analysis of 62,602 scientific articles from 88 journals (1989–2025) revealed 4.9% annual growth. Empirical research increased from 43% to 72% of publications. Methodological composition shifted from quantitative dominance (69% of empirical studies in the 1990s) to methodological pluralism (47% qualitative, 44% quantitative in the 2020s). Author collaboration increased, with mean authors per article rising from 1.85 to 3.35. Citation analysis shows 17.5% of articles remain uncited. Discussion: Findings document exponential growth alongside substantial increases in empiricism, coauthorship, and qualitative methods. Persistent challenges in citation database coverage systematically disadvantage scholarship published outside mainstream commercial indexing systems. © The Author(s) 2026
