Authors: Bogenbayeva A.; Orazbayeva F.; Rauandina A.; Kumisbekova Z.; Imankulova M.
Title: Technology-Enhanced Language Learning in Multilingual Environments: A Linguistic Review of Socio-Pedagogical and Neurolinguistic Frameworks
Abstract: This research is a qualitative systematic review examining technology-enhanced Kazakh language teaching in multilingual educational environments through socio-pedagogical and neurolinguistic frameworks. In this context, the Web of Science (WoS) and Scopus databases were searched within the framework of the PRISMA protocol; of the 449 studies identified, 32 studies published from 2015 onward were included in the analysis because they met the inclusion criteria. The findings are presented around four research questions. First, it was determined that social media tools and digital platforms reinforce students' Kazakh language use practices and facilitate identity repositioning. Regarding the second research question, gamification, artificial intelligence-based dialogue systems, and personalized learning models were found to have positive effects on language outcomes, although these effects vary according to the type of tool and pedagogical context. The TPACK framework stands out as a determining variable in teacher-student interaction and the effectiveness of scaffolding strategies. In addition, the number of direct studies using neurolinguistic methods is very limited; indirect findings obtained through cognitive lexicology and personalized learning environments provide a strong basis for future research in this field. Future research is recommended to use neuroimaging methods and longitudinal designs, conduct multilingual systematic reviews that include publications in Kazakh and Russian, integrate TPACK into teacher training, and include user-experience evaluations in technology-based tools. © International Journal of Technology in Education and Science (IJTES).

Authors: Çobanoğlu N.; Çelik O.T.; Abdulbaki Karaca M.
Title: Leadership in special education: A bibliometric and thematic review
Abstract: Effective leadership is critical for advancing inclusive practices and improving outcomes for students with disabilities. However, the scholarly landscape of leadership in special education remains fragmented and lacks a comprehensive structural synthesis. This study mapped the development, intellectual structure, thematic content, methodological characteristics, and leadership focus areas of 77 publications indexed in Web of Science and Scopus by combining bibliometric analysis with full-text thematic content analysis. Bibliometric methods and content analysis were used to assess the development of research on leadership in special education and identify thematic areas. The findings show that interest in leadership within special education has increased in recent years, with social justice leadership and inclusive education as the primary research areas. Within the WoS and Scopus dataset analyzed, international co-authorship links are most visible around the USA. Additionally, it was concluded that qualitative methodologies are predominantly used in research, with various research themes clustered around key concepts such as leadership, social justice, and disability. In recent years, approaches like distributed leadership and collaborative leadership have gained prominence, and limited leadership frameworks have been discussed in special education. Future research could explore the effects of social justice leadership and inclusive education in more detail, focusing on practices in different countries or education systems. The study also suggests placing more emphasis on the diversity of leadership models, with a focus on approaches such as distributed leadership and digital leadership in special education. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Lopes L.F.; de Fátima Rodrigues Pereira M.
Title: Technology and teaching work: reflections on human emancipation in the light of Marx, Vieira Pinto, and Marcuse; [Tecnologia e trabalho docente: reflexões sobre emancipação humana à luz de Marx, Vieira Pinto e Marcuse]; [Tecnología y trabajo docente: reflexiones sobre la emancipación humana a la luz de Marx, Vieira Pinto y Marcuse]
Abstract: This literature- and document-based study provides a critical and reflective analysis of the development of technique and technology. It adopts a qualitative and exploratory approach, with its analytical procedures informed by Ricoeur's (1989) hermeneutics. The study examines the origin of the term "tekhnē"; the notion of technique as human mastery over nature; the impact of technology on the expansion of capital and its consequences for teachers' work; and, finally, the utopian vision of emancipation through work. Given the complexity of the history of technology and the social and economic changes that have shaped it, the theoretical framework draws primarily on the contributions of Vieira Pinto (2005a), Marx (2010), Pasquinelli (2023), and Marcuse (2019b). The documentary analysis relies primarily on the Summary of the Global Education Monitoring Report, published by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO, 2023), and the Brazilian Artificial Intelligence Plan, issued by the Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation (MCTI) (Brazil, 2025). The findings indicate that, as a dimension of human existence, technology is ambivalently both an instrument of domination and a potential vehicle for emancipation. This study seeks to contribute to the academic debate regarding the historical role of technology and its implications for teachers' work in contemporary society. © 2026, Universidade Estadual de Ponta Grossa, Editora. Authors: Kaymaz Ç.K.; Uçan N.S.
Title: Beyond the classroom: mapping the motivational landscape of science tourists in a UNESCO global geopark
Abstract: Despite the growing significance of science tourism, empirical research on visitor motivations within UNESCO Global Geoparks (UGGp) remains limited. This study investigates the demographic profiles and travel motivations of tourists visiting the Kula-Salihli UNESCO Global Geopark, Türkiye. Adopting a mixed-methods approach, data were collected from 373 participants to analyze the interplay between demographic variables and motivational dimensions, specifically excitement-adventure, active enjoyment, learning-knowledge, and social interaction. The findings reveal distinct visitor segments driven primarily by intellectual curiosity and nature-based experiences. These insights provide a critical framework for destination managers to design targeted sustainable tourism strategies that effectively balance recreational demand with the imperative of geoconservation. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature B.V. 2026.

Authors: Almayez M.
Title: ​Cognitive and emotional predictors of preference for emotionally intelligent speaking assessment among Saudi EFL learners: a structural equation modelling approach
Abstract: This study examined Saudi English learners’ perceptions of Emotionally Intelligent Speaking Assessment (EISA) through a structural equation modelling approach informed by Expectancy-Value Theory (EVT) and the Control-Value Theory of Achievement Emotions (CVTAE). A total of 754 undergraduate students from Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) and non-STEM disciplines completed the validated EISA Questionnaire, developed to explore the emotional, cognitive, and fairness-related dimensions of speaking assessment. Although emotional intelligence has received growing attention in language education, little empirical research has investigated how learners perceive emotionally responsive speaking assessments within the Saudi context, where evaluation remains predominantly product-oriented. The results showed that the perceived importance of emotional expression, fairness, self-confidence, and usefulness significantly predicted learners’ preference for EISA. Mediation analysis revealed that fairness, self-confidence, and usefulness mediated the link between perceived importance and assessment preference, while moderation analysis showed effects of gender, academic field, and speaking proficiency. Rather than treating cognitive appraisals as a distinct construct, the study investigated how learners’ motivational and emotional perceptions jointly shaped their preferences for emotionally intelligent assessment. These findings indicate the importance of integrating emotional and social dimensions into speaking assessment to foster more equitable, authentic, and communicatively relevant evaluation practices. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Cevallos-Vallejos M.; Sánchez de Céspedes I.-S.; Núñez-Pérez J.; Pais-Chanfrau J.-M.
Title: Education for sustainable development through waste valorisation research projects: training sustainability competencies in agro-industrial engineering students during the COVID-19 pandemic
Abstract: Purpose – This paper aims to examine how education for sustainable development (ESD) can be effectively implemented within higher education institutions through authentic waste valorisation research projects, even under the challenging circumstances of the COVID-19 pandemic. This study demonstrates how final-degree projects (FDPs) focused on circular economy principles can develop key sustainability competencies in agro-industrial engineering students while contributing to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 4 and 12. We analyse how integrating problem-based learning, project-based learning, learning-by-doing and research-based learning approaches creates synergistic effects for competency development. Design/methodology/approach – A multiple-case study methodology was used to analyse three FDPs focused on agro-industrial waste valorisation (coffee residues, goat milk whey and cocoa pod husks) conducted between March 2020 and March 2022 at a public university in Ecuador. Quantitative data from 229 graduates across seven engineering programmes were integrated with qualitative analyses of pedagogical strategies and competency development indicators. Findings – Despite severe pandemic restrictions, including laboratory closures and mandatory confinement, 229 students completed their research theses during the study period. The cohort achieved a 13.1% publication rate (30 publications from 229 theses), with 46% of journal articles published in Q1- and Q2-ranked journals. The three detailed case studies resulted in publications in high-impact journals, demonstrating novel approaches to waste valorisation. Students developed measurable sustainability competencies, including systems thinking, anticipatory competence, normative competence, strategic competence and interpersonal competence. Research limitations/implications – This study is limited to a single institution in Ecuador and focuses specifically on agro-industrial engineering programmes within the Faculty of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences Engineering. The pandemic context, while providing unique research opportunities, also constrained specific methodological approaches. However, the methodology demonstrates transferability to other disciplines and institutional contexts where waste valorisation and circular economy concepts are relevant to local sustainability challenges. Because the case studies were selected for success, conclusions about competency development should be interpreted as demonstrating what the model can achieve under favourable conditions rather than as representative of all FDP outcomes. Practical implications – The findings provide a replicable model for integrating ESD into higher education curricula through authentic research projects addressing real sustainability challenges. Social implications – By training future researchers and pre-professionals in waste valorisation and circular economy principles, this educational approach helps build local capacity for sustainable development in developing countries. Originality/value – This paper provides novel empirical evidence on how ESD can be effectively implemented through waste-valorisation research projects in Latin American universities. The study’s principal originality lies in its artefact-based approach to competency evidencing: rather than relying solely on self-report instruments, competency claims are triangulated with observable indicators drawn from thesis documents, logbooks and published articles, thereby providing a replicable assessment methodology for ESD in research-intensive programmes. © 2026 Marcelo Cevallos-Vallejos, Ima-Sumac Sánchez de Céspedes, Jimmy Núñez-Pérez and José-Manuel Pais-Chanfrau.

Authors: Le Coze J.C.
Title: Half a century of Safety Science (1976–2026). Divergence and convergence in the field
Abstract: This article celebrates the 50th anniversary of the journal Safety Science. Taking this opportunity, it reflects on the journal’s foundations, drawing on Rasmussen’s influential sociotechnical systems view. The success of this influential safety model is based on its combination of three key facets: (1) cross-disciplinarity; (2) political, economic, social, and technological change; and (3) safety as a multilevel phenomenon. Following an introduction to the emergence of safety research in the 1970 s, the article discusses these three facets in turn. First, it argues that a key issue in safety is divergence, a kind of “ Tower of Babel ” syndrome that, over time, creates divides between disciplines and research traditions. The controversy between the “ new view ” and “ behaviour-based safety ” serves as an example of this. The article then argues that Rasmussen’s contribution requires a strategy of convergence, the opposite of divergence. Second, the article demonstrates the value of this strategy when applied to the question of change and illustrates how the use of different disciplines can help to understand its multidimensional nature, its contemporary global scale. Third, the article highlights the interest of this strategy in characterising the complex patterns of interactions across levels, a thorny empirical topic in safety research since Rasmussen’s proposition. In conclusion, the article explains that fifty years after the institutionalisation of safety as a scientific field, there are five challenges that must be addressed to reinforce its foundations. These challenges range from establishing a historical and conceptual identification of research traditions to establishing their empirical and practical connections. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Hancock P.A.
Title: Science for the People: The Life and Contributions of Mark Chignell
Abstract: The present work provides both assessment and appreciation of the profound and deeply human contributions of the scientist Mark Hume Chignell. His varying conceptual, methodological, and applied innovations are set within a career chronology that features a focus on his humanity as much as it does on his science. Having assimilated the disparate, yet still coherent scientific disciplines of both psychology and engineering, it is of little surprise that Chignell’s oeuvre featured a Human Factors/Ergonomics emphasis in which he might well be considered the quintessential engineering psychologist. Whilst making crucial contributions to the theoretical formulations concerning adaptative and expert systems, Chignell was never content to be isolated in the experimental laboratory but felt obliged and even mandated to carry progress being made therein out into the world of users. His later work on assistive medical technologies for the elderly typified these concerns and embodied his lifelong dedication to the improvement of humanity. This characteristic, whether expressed through his far-reaching science or in his immediate professional and social presence, ran as a golden thread throughout his lifetime, and now beyond. © 2026 The Author. Authors: Enemuwe C.A.; Okine J.O.; Gyau S.A.
Title: The organised crime of kidnapping in Nigeria: a quantitative study of the factors influencing its severity
Abstract: The extant literature in the social sciences often employs qualitative methods to capture the contextual nuances of the nature, manifestations, and impacts of issues of importance today. This is the case for studies looking at kidnapping in Nigeria, where perception-based surveys are often neglected. We argue that these qualitative approaches alone are inadequate for thoroughly comprehending the structural factors and public opinions that explain the occurrence and severity of kidnapping in Nigeria. This study extensively analyses the seriousness of kidnapping as a critical security issue in contemporary Nigeria, seeking to explore the factors contributing to this phenomenon through a quantitative survey based on citizen perceptions, as they endure the impacts of kidnapping within their communities. Using logistic regression, this study examined the 2022 Afrobarometer data to determine the factors influencing kidnapping in Nigeria. The findings indicate that, as the frequency of kidnapping is rising, poor police handling of kidnapping cases, worsening economic conditions, community safety concerns, ethnic marginalization, and low ethnic trust significantly predict the perceived severity of kidnapping in Nigeria. In contrast, perceptions of government handling crime (although associated considerably at the bivariate level) and corruption were not statistically significant in the multivariate analysis. Highlighting the severity of kidnapping in Nigeria contributes to the body of knowledge in security studies, development studies, and governance by illustrating how economic hardship, institutional failure, and social crisis influence the frequency and perceived seriousness of kidnapping. It points to the need for more collaborative, networked governance that puts people at the centre of policies and actions to tackle kidnapping in Nigeria. © The Author(s) 2025.

Authors: Skardhamar T.
Title: Black Ships: What Kind of Martial Art Is Sociology?
Abstract: Pierre Bourdieu described sociology as a martial art but never specified what kind. The kind matters. The Japanese martial tradition offers a typology he did not draw: -jutsu, oriented toward defeating a real opponent; -do as competition, oriented toward internal scoring within a closed tournament; and -do as formation, oriented toward cultivating the practitioner rather than testing any claim against reality. I use this typology as a diagnostic framework. Sociology is predominantly -do. The costs are visible and cumulative, and they follow a pattern of slow response to external challenges: the credibility revolution, open science, and now AI. Open science and AI reshape what counts as rigorous work across methods, quantitative and qualitative alike. In 1853, Commodore Perry’s Black Ships arrived at Edo Bay, and the Shogunate discovered that two centuries of internal competition had not prepared it for an external force indifferent to its rules. The political order it had sustained did not survive the encounter. Sociology faces a comparable moment. I argue for a -jutsu imperative: not for any particular method, but for pressure-testing by standards the discipline does not control — a standard sociology has already committed to by claiming to produce knowledge about the social world, whether it acknowledges this or not. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Hahn M.; Samhammer D.; Tretter M.; Dabrock P.
Title: An actor-network-theory informed normative framework for the governance of AI-systems in medicine
Abstract: The impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on clinical decision-making has become a focal point within a multitude of ethical, legal, and social discussions. Examining concrete use cases reveals that the introduction of an AI-system as a new actant in clinical practice changes the whole context with its relationships, roles, and routines. To better understand these changes, an interpretative framework can help to trace such transformations and uncover their ethical implications. In Science and Technology Studies (STS), a well-known approach is the application of Actor-Network-Theory (ANT) to concrete phenomena, including in the field of medicine. We aim to build on this established approach by developing a normative framework informed by ANT. To this end, we derive evaluation questions from Latour’s four meanings of mediation: translation to ask what goals should be pursued, composition to evaluate who should be involved, reversible blackboxing to specify how the different actants should be involved, and delegation to reflect on who should be responsible. These questions can thus inform the governance of AI-systems in medicine and contribute to their responsible implementation. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Casaña Mohedo J.; Beltran-de-Miguel B.; Esteve-Claramunt F.; Kiosses S.; Sandri E.
Title: Eggs as gastronomic memory: A qualitative content analysis of intergenerational culinary transmission, health perceptions, and sustainability in Spanish households
Abstract: This study examines the role of eggs as a vehicle of gastronomic memory and cultural identity within the Mediterranean Diet, focusing on their place in the intergenerational transmission of culinary culture in Spanish households. Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory and Food Literacy frameworks, a qualitative content analysis (Graneheim & Lundman) was applied to open-ended survey responses from 169 participants, isolating a subsample of 49 who explicitly discussed egg consumption. Analysis yielded three overarching categories and ten subcategories. Eggs emerged as a powerful emotional anchor to childhood, transmitted primarily through maternal and, occasionally, paternal figures as agents of culinary socialization. Despite being valued as a nutritionally dense, fast, and affordable "lifesaver" food, a "time paradox" was identified: younger generations increasingly replace homemade preparations with precooked alternatives, reflecting an erosion of basic culinary skills. Eggs were also framed as a "democratic" and sustainable food, linked to Km0 and local-origin consumption. These findings position the egg as a strategic bridge between culinary heritage and contemporary lifestyle constraints, offering a concrete pedagogical resource for public health strategies promoting home cooking and food literacy. This work extends existing food-science literature on eggs, predominantly nutritional and clinical in focus, toward a gastronomic and sociocultural understanding of everyday food practices. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Basumatary B.; Verma M.K.
Title: Unearthing the misconduct and inaccuracies in social science research: a trend analysis of retracted articles based on retraction watch database
Abstract: Purpose – The purpose of this study is to comprehensively analyze the research article retractions in social sciences over the past decade (2014–2023). Design/methodology/approach – The study used scientometric methods to evaluate the prevalence, patterns and factors contributing to social sciences article retractions. Bibliographic data of retracted articles were collected from the Retraction Watch Database under an agreement signed with the database. Further, citations of the retracted articles were collected from Scopus and Google Scholar. The analysis encompasses performance assessment and citation-based analysis to reveal the trend of retraction and scrutinize the impact of retracted articles. Findings – Over the past decade, article retractions have shown dynamic trends, with notable fluctuations in recent years. Further, investigating the time taken for article retraction reveals the urgency of addressing issues identified soon after publication. Scientific misconduct and publication-related concerns emerge as primary factors leading to retractions. Countries such as Russia, the USA, China and publishers such as Elsevier and Taylor and Francis led in the retractions of social science articles. A significant portion of retracted works had garnered academic attention prior to retraction and even after retraction. Originality/value – This study can contribute to a better understanding among scholars and stakeholders of the trends and reasons for retractions of research articles in the social sciences. © 2024 Emerald Publishing Limited

Authors: Welderufael S.; Gidey T.; Gebreslassie H.; Hishe M.; Gebrehiwet H.
Title: Crop biocultural trait diversity and its contribution to post conflict seed system resilience in Laelay Mychew district Northern Ethiopia
Abstract: Understanding crop biocultural trait diversity is crucial for sustaining agricultural resilience and guiding recovery in conflict-affected farming systems. This study examined the dimensions of crop biocultural trait diversity and its contribution to post-conflict seed system resilience in Laelay Mychew district, northern Ethiopia, one of the districts most severely affected by the 2020–2022 Tigray conflict. Data were collected from 378 households through surveys, key informant interviews, and crop diversity inventories across seven staple crops; sorghum, teff, wheat, barley, maize, finger millet and faba bean. Using a 12 biocultural traits framework, the study integrated agronomic, culinary, sociocultural and economic dimensions to assess how farmers value, select, and manage their crops. Results showed that farmers maintained 54 varieties of the seven staples, of which 70.4% were farmers’ varieties, underscoring the persistence of traditional knowledge and cultural attachment to local crops despite wartime disruptions. Sorghum, barley, and finger millet exhibited the highest varietal richness, reflecting the interplay of ecological adaptation and cultural heritage. Adaptive strategies such as crop diversification, informal seed sharing, mutual support, and community-based seed multiplication remained central during and after conflict, reinforcing local seed system resilience. The findings demonstrate that biocultural practices are foundational to agricultural recovery and social cohesion. By bridging agronomy, anthropology, and resilience science, this study highlights the need for post-conflict agricultural policies to move beyond productivity-driven models toward biocultural frameworks that integrate ecological, cultural, and social dimensions. Such approaches can foster inclusive, sustainable, and resilient livelihood restoration in Tigray and similar conflict-affected regions. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Thomson D.; Newton A.S.; Hartling L.; Caine K.J.; Hand L.; Oetomo A.; Ebi K.L.
Title: Normalising a climate lens in two Canadian provincial health systems: An assessment using implementation science
Abstract: Rationale As climate change intensifies, health systems must integrate climate resilience and decarbonisation as core functions. This requires a climate lens to coordinate diverse climate-related initiatives across all system functions (e.g. public health, clinical care, facility management and system management). Objective We compared the adoption of a climate lens in the health systems in two Canadian provinces (British Columbia and Ontario), to identify the contextual and social/cognitive factors influencing implementation and normalisation processes. Methods Drawing on 428 documents and webpages and 41 semi-structured interviews, our exploratory analysis used Normalization Process Theory and implementation science frameworks to assess how social and cognitive processes influence implementation. Results We found that normalisation is an emergent, socially constructed process shaped by system architecture, leadership, resource allocation and relational networks. In British Columbia, formal accountability mechanisms streamlined implementation; in Ontario, local leadership and relational networks drove progress despite lacking provincial mandates. Ultimately, individual staff members sustain climate-health policies and programs by deploying policy capacity to bridge gaps and boundaries in formal system structures. Conclusions These findings offer a roadmap for health systems to support and advance sustained climate action, highlighting how progress can be achieved through both formal policy mandates and local leadership networks. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Fotopoulos D.; Kleanthis N.; van den Berg N.J.; Pearce B.J.; van Vuuren D.P.; Flamos A.; Stavrakas V.
Title: Combining storylines of energy citizenship with narratives of future-world evolutions to design transformative and socially informed energy transition scenarios
Abstract: Despite a growing body of research seeking to integrate social sciences into scenario-based research and modelling, climate policy analysis remains largely dominated by top-down approaches that underrepresent the sociopolitical dimensions of the energy transition, particularly at the local level. In this context, the concept of energy citizenship has gained increasing attention as a means of fostering more inclusive, democratic, and equitable energy systems. However, significant gaps exist regarding its conceptual clarity, operationalisation, and systematic integration into scenario-based research and modelling practices. This study addresses these gaps by presenting a novel interdisciplinary framework for transformative scenario design that explicitly links social innovations of energy citizenship with alternative future-world evolutions. We deconstruct energy citizenship into distinct patterns and trends and translate them into people-centred storylines that capture diverse forms of individual and collective engagement in the energy transition. These storylines are embedded within three future-world narratives inspired by the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways, while describing alternative long-term pathways in which citizen agency, social practices, and collective action play the central role. We construct a multilayered scenario space that enables systematic exploration of decarbonisation pathways informed by empirical research clarifying the concept of energy citizenship, while also testing the robustness of transition strategies under contrasting sociopolitical conditions. Overall, the proposed framework advances understanding of how energy citizenship can shape mitigation pathways, while also providing less stylised and more transparent assumptions for scenario-based modelling. It also offers a platform for continued exchange between modelling communities, policymakers, and practitioners, supporting more inclusive climate action. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Shahabadi A.; Davarikish R.; Omidi V.
Title: Impact of sustainable competitiveness on migration and brain drain
Abstract: Migration and brain drain are considered key factors influencing the economic dynamism of countries. By reducing the skilled workforce, they can have significant negative effects on economic performance. The objective of this study is to investigate the impact of sustainable competitiveness components, including natural capital, resource intensity and efficiency, intellectual capital, governance capabilities, and social capital, on the migration and brain drain index across 60 selected science-producing countries over the period 2014–2023. The study employs the Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) and classifies countries into two groups: The selected Advanced Economies and Emerging and Developing Economies. The results show that, in both groups, governance capabilities, natural capital, resource intensity and efficiency, and social capital have a negative and statistically significant effect on migration and brain drain, whereas intellectual capital have a positive and statistically significant effect. The findings indicate that strengthening the components of sustainable competitiveness can play an effective role in reducing migration and brain drain. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature B.V. 2026.

Authors: Su J.; Lyu Y.; Zhao Y.; Wang Z.; Wang R.; Wang X.; Zhou Q.; Peng C.; Li Y.; Hu W.
Title: The longitudinal relationships between scientific motivation and critical thinking disposition: A cross-lagged panel network analysis
Abstract: Based on self-determination theory (SDT), meta-theory of personality (MTP), and social cognitive theory (SCT), scientific motivation (SM) and critical thinking disposition (CTD) may be reciprocally linked, yet longitudinal evidence remains limited. This study used cross-lagged panel network analysis to examine SM-CTD associations among 3898 students across upper elementary, junior high, and senior high schools. The overall network revealed bidirectional relationships between intrinsic motivation and personal relevance (IMPR) and inquisitiveness (INQ), IMPR and self-confidence (SC), and self-efficacy (SE) and SC. Upper elementary networks showed reciprocal links between IMPR and INQ, and between IMPR and SC. Junior high networks retained these and added bidirectional paths between IMPR and analyticity (ANA), and SC and SE. Senior high networks uniquely revealed a reciprocal link between SE and systematicity (SYS). These findings highlight IMPR and SE as potential intervention targets. Furthermore, stage-varying reciprocal relationships suggest that educational interventions should be tailored to specific developmental stages. Educational relevance statement: Understanding the co-development of scientific motivation and critical thinking disposition is vital, as modern educational frameworks increasingly demand the integration of motivational drivers and critical thinking dispositions. While traditional instructional models often assume a unidirectional influence between motivation and critical thinking dispositions, our findings suggest that they function as a mutually reinforcing, bidirectional system. Specifically, we identified intrinsic motivation and personal relevance (IMPR) and scientific self-efficacy (SE) as the core functional hubs driving this co-development. Consequently, rather than dispersing efforts across all cognitive traits, educators may achieve broader impact by focusing interventions on these specific targets. Connecting science curricula to students' real-world experiences (boosting IMPR) and designing achievable inquiry tasks (building SE) can naturally activate other critical thinking dispositions. Importantly, our cross-stage findings indicate that these dynamics are not uniform across age groups. Therefore, interventions should ideally evolve alongside students' development. Such efforts should begin by fostering foundational curiosity and self-confidence in elementary school, build upon this foundation to cultivate analytical thinking in junior high school, and ultimately shift toward systematic reasoning within autonomy-supportive environments in senior high school. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Batra R.; Kim L.; Mandel I.; Kwatra A.; Jane L.E.; Jackson S.J.; Roumen T.
Title: (De)composing Craft: An Elementary Grammar for Sharing Expertise in Craft Workflows
Abstract: Craft practices rely on evolving archives of skill and knowledge developed through generations of craftspeople experimenting with designs, materials, and techniques. Better documentation of these practices enables the sharing of knowledge and expertise between sites and generations. However, most documentation focuses on the linear steps leading to final artifacts, neglecting the distinct tacit knowledge, improvisational actions, and situated adaptations needed to meet the unique demands of each craft project. This omission limits knowledge sharing and reduces craft to a mechanical endeavor, rather than a sophisticated and contextual way of seeing, thinking, and doing. Drawing on expert interviews and literature from HCI, CSCW and the social sciences, we develop an elementary grammar to document improvisational actions of real-world craft practices. We demonstrate the utility of this grammar with a MLLM-powered interface called CraftLink that can be used to analyze expert videos and generate documentation to share material and contextual variations of practices with other knowledgeable but non-master craftspeople. Our user study with expert crocheters (N=7) evaluates our grammar’s effectiveness in capturing and sharing expert knowledge with other craftspeople, offering new pathways for computational systems to support collaborative archives of knowledge and practice across time, space, and skill levels. We conclude by showing how our grammar addresses four key tensions of the craft learning environment: personal and shareable documentation, fragmented and discoverable expertise, linear and iterative practices, and data privacy and ownership. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Authors: Shi X.
Title: A comparative study of history of science, philosophy of science, and combined instruction on students’ understanding of the nature of science in a Chinese high school context
Abstract: Despite the empirical evidence for the role of the history and philosophy of science in science education, the independent effects of history and philosophy of science courses have not been comparatively studied. Hence, this study implemented three elective courses—philosophy of science, history of science, and history and philosophy of science—in Chinese high schools to explore their impact on students’ understanding of the nature of science, as conceptualized in the Family Resemblance Approach. It addresses the following question: to what extent do these courses influence students’ scientific perceptions in both cognitive-epistemic and social-institutional systems? Pre- and post-course questionnaires were used to assess changes in students’ views and compare the effects across the three instructional approaches. The results of this study showed that the philosophy of science course helped students improve their cognitive-epistemic systems. Meanwhile, students who took the other two courses improved their understanding of the nature of science in terms of both cognitive-epistemic and social-institutional systems. The results of this study provide valuable insights into the connection between the history and philosophy of science in the teaching process and offer practical implications for science education. However, given the small sample size and the non-random assignment of instructional groups, the findings should be interpreted with caution and warrant further investigation in more diverse and representative contexts. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Zheng J.; Wu P.; Pan L.
Title: TECP: Insight into hybrid propagation factors from prompt-based LLMs for comprehensive cascade prediction
Abstract: Cascade prediction aims to forecast the future scale of post propagation on social networks. Existing models primarily rely on cascade sequences observed after a specific propagation period, overlooking the intrinsic influence of the text and metadata of source posts on the propagation scale, thereby limiting their ability to provide early-stage predictions and reducing interpretability. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) can extract propagation-related factors by analyzing source post text and metadata, experiments show that they often fail to adaptively select useful insights from these factors. To address these limitations, we propose a Textual Enhanced Cascade Prediction Model based on Large Language Model (TECP). Specifically, TECP utilizes LLMs to analyze the text and metadata of source posts and extract key factors influencing post spread from three aspects rooted in communication theories: topic, content, and audience. To selectively extract meaningful insights from these factors, a Text-Factor Collaboration module is proposed for propagation-aware textual representation. By leveraging multi-task learning, TECP can predict the future cascade level using only textual representations, which can also be seamlessly integrated into existing sequence-based cascade models to predict cascade scale. Experiments on Weibo and Twitter datasets demonstrate the model’s superiority. It achieves a 15.6% higher Macro-F1 for cascade level prediction without relying on cascade sequences. Moreover, as a plug-and-play module, it reduces the average MSLE by 5.24% for sequence-based models in cascade scale prediction. The source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TECP-DFB9/. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Namwase J.; Maling S.; Opolot I.; Kyomya J.; Ouma R.O.; Favina A.; Nakkazi S.; Turyamusiima R.; Semuwemba J.; Nakirya L.; Wakida E.K.
Title: Social determinants of academic performance among undergraduate health professional students at Mbarara University of Science and Technology, Uganda
Abstract: Background: Academic performance among health professional students is influenced by social determinants. This study assessed factors associated with academic performance among undergraduate health professional students at Mbarara University of Science and Technology (MUST), Uganda. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional survey among 335 undergraduate students using a self-administered questionnaire. Academic performance was categorized as poor or good. Bivariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors independently associated with poor academic performance. Results: Of the 335 students (mean age 23.86 ± 6.4 years), 70.8% demonstrated good academic performance. In multivariable analysis, female students had significantly higher odds of poor academic performance compared with male students (AOR = 1.95; 95% CI: 1.01–3.78). Third-year students were more likely to have poor academic performance than fifth-year students (AOR = 4.27; 95% CI: 1.06–17.20). In contrast, students with high online social media engagement had significantly lower odds of poor academic performance compared with those with low engagement (AOR = 0.30; 95% CI: 0.12–0.74). Conclusion: Female gender and being in the third year of study were associated with higher odds of poor academic performance, while high online social media engagement was associated with lower odds of poor academic performance. Targeted academic support for vulnerable student groups and structured approaches to online engagement may help improve academic outcomes. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Uzel A.S.
Title: Semi-rural fringe as a distinct smart territory: Proximity, institutional mediation, and the conditions for durable technology adoption around Bristol
Abstract: Rural social science has long grappled with the uneven geography of technological change, yet the semi-rural fringe remains analytically neglected: neither fully captured by smart city frameworks nor adequately represented by remote rural development models. This article investigates how the territorial characteristics of accessible fringe communities around Bristol, the United Kingdom, shape the conditions under which digital transformation becomes durable. Drawing on a qualitative case-study design combining semi-structured interviews with 20 participants, field observations, and ward-level census indicators, the study develops and applies the Semi-Rural Technology Adoption and Support (SRTAS) framework, integrating Diffusion of Innovations Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model with Digital Transformation Theory. Three findings appear to emerge: proximity to Bristol may generate awareness and trial opportunities through commuting and professional networks; infrastructure gaps, affordability barriers, and weak onboarding may prevent exposure from converting into stable use; and durable adoption appears to depend on institutional mediation — defined here as the delivery-side capacity of public, quasi-public, and publicly regulated or commissioned private actors, operating across five specified dimensions — rather than on individual disposition or capability. These findings suggest that the semi-rural fringe may constitute a proximity-structured territorial category requiring place-sensitive rural and peri-urban policy, while also reframing digital inequality as a governance challenge that may extend well beyond the urban core. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Grant C.; Ripoll S.; Waldman L.
Title: Bridging divides: The role of social science in operationalising transdisciplinarity for epidemic preparedness in sub-Saharan Africa, 2012–2023
Abstract: This paper investigates the role of transdisciplinarity, social science, and communities’ knowledge in epidemic and pandemic preparedness and response in sub-Saharan Africa. It addresses how social science contributions have evolved over the past decade, explores the ways in which transdisciplinary approaches have been implemented and developed and analyses how social science can help to operationalise transdisciplinarity. The research applies a conceptual framework focusing on the intersection of power, knowledge, and crisis, and adopts a definition of transdisciplinarity that emphasises multi-actor collaboration and the integration and bridging of academic and non-academic knowledge. Three empirical case studies are presented: neglected zoonoses (2012–2014), the West Africa Ebola outbreak (2014–2016), and the COVID-19 pandemic (2020–2023). This paper argues that attention to the politics of knowledge and power dynamics in research and policy implementation is key to understanding how social science and transdiciplinarity can be a catalyst for knowledge integration and bridging into effective epidemic preparedness and response systems. The paper identifies three main areas of social science contribution. The first of these is how social science serves as a catalyst, translating, bonding, and connecting diverse disciplinary perspectives. Secondly, social science functions as a nexus, facilitating connections and collaboration across academic and societal boundaries to address complex challenges. Thirdly, the operationalisation of innovative social science methods, such as transdisciplinary modelling, participatory research, rapid response studies, and social media analysis, offers opportunities for generating actionable, context-specific knowledge that bridges science, policy, and practice. The findings advance theoretical and empirical understanding of transdisciplinary approaches, and assess progress towards more contextually-responsive, integrative and bridging strategies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Nazarovets S.
Title: Poor bibliometric studies do not make bibliometrics poor science: a response to Ellegaard
Abstract: This commentary responds to Ellegaard’s (2026) critical evaluation of bibliometric analysis, particularly his suggestion that some bibliometric studies may be more appropriately published as policy briefs, institutional reports, or working papers rather than in scholarly journals. While agreeing that the rapid growth of bibliometric publications has been accompanied by an increase in low-quality and purely descriptive studies, I argue that this problem should not be conflated with the scientific value of bibliometric research as a methodological tradition. Contemporary bibliometrics extends far beyond mapping the scholarly literature and contributes to the study of researcher mobility, scientific collaboration, open access, research integrity, science policy, and other aspects of science as a social institution. The bibliometric community has also developed methodological guidance, reporting recommendations, and evaluation frameworks aimed at improving the quality, transparency, and reproducibility of bibliometric research. The central challenge, therefore, is not the legitimacy of bibliometric studies as a scholarly genre, but the uneven adoption of quality standards across disciplines and journals. © Akadémiai Kiadó Zrt 2026.

Authors: Wang X.
Title: Research on the Characteristics and Evolution of China’s Artificial Intelligence Standard Collaboration Network
Abstract: Standard development is a critical activity that facilitates innovation collaboration, regulates industrial development, and ensures the safety of science and technology. In response to the era of artificial intelligence, China is accelerating its AI standard process, giving rise to an AI standard collaboration network characterized by multi-stakeholder synergy among government, industry, academia, and research institutes, as well as broad participation from the entire industry. To analyse the stage-specific characteristics and evolutionary patterns of the AI standard collaboration network, this research extracts 1,658 drafting organizations from 271 AI standards and applies social network analysis to construct collaboration networks across three periods: the stable start and pilot exploration period (pre-2017), the top-down design and strategic layout period (2017-2024), and the comprehensive empowerment and systematic advancement period (2025-present). The findings are as follows: First, during the stable start and pilot exploration period, AI standards were few in number, narrow in scope, and limited in type. Standard drafting was carried out by a handful of specific actors, with little collaboration among them, and thus no standard collaboration network formed. Second, during the top-down design and strategic layout period, the number of AI standards increased significantly, their content gradually matured, and their types became diverse. A firm-led standard collaboration network began to take shape, with notable changes in network size, number of ties, density, average path length, clustering coefficient, and other indicators. A core-periphery structural pattern became evident, with Beijing Baidu Netcom Science Technology Co., Ltd., Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., and the China Electronics Standardization Institute occupying advantageous positions within the network. Third, during the comprehensive empowerment and systematic advancement period, the “AI+” action has deeply integrated AI into numerous industries. The dominance of core standardisation organisations has further strengthened, emerging industry actors have risen rapidly, the influence of universities has somewhat diminished, and the network structure displays a one core with multiple strong players characteristic. Fourth, the effects of transitivity and geographic homophily on the standardisation collaboration network have weakened, whereas the influence of organisational homophily has strengthened, and the mediating effect exerts a negative influence. © The Author(s) 2026. Authors: Heijens M.J.M.
Title: Enabling emancipation: How school climate and teacher autonomy relate to critical-thinking practice via socio-emotional skills
Abstract: Emancipatory education aims to foster learners’ critical engagement with knowledge, often by implementing classroom critical-thinking practice. Socio-emotional skills can support this process by creating trusting, dialogic, and responsive environments which enable critical reflection. This study examines how school climate and teacher autonomy shape this mechanism. This analysis includes 54,310 teachers from 18 countries from the 2024 TALIS dataset. Four moderated mediation models were estimated to test whether socio-emotional skills mediate the relationship between school climate and autonomy and critical-thinking practice, and whether these pathways differ between teachers active in social sciences and other subjects. Results show that school climate and autonomy are positively associated with critical-thinking practice, with socio-emotional skills acting as a partial mediator. For teachers with social science education, the indirect effects are stronger. The findings suggest that emancipatory teaching depends not only on teacher beliefs and classroom practices, but also on supportive institutional conditions and subject-specific preparation. © 2026 The Author. Authors: Dyer K.D.; Fine M.; Foster B.
Title: Disciplinary Systems Theory: A Bibliometric Review of Scholarly Interdisciplinarity in Human Development and Family Science
Abstract: Interdisciplinarity in human development and family science (HDFS) is difficult to define because the boundaries demarcating the discipline are ambiguous. We introduce disciplinary systems theory (DST), which, like family systems theory, is a variant of general systems theory. DST describes how disciplinary systems and subsystems create boundaries of variable permeability. We use bibliometric review techniques to explore boundary permeability to describe interdisciplinarity in HDFS. We reviewed 278 articles published in Child Development, Journal of Marriage and Family, and Family Relations in 2014. The disciplinary affiliations of the first three authors of each article were identified. The papers referenced in those articles, and the papers that later cited those articles were identified and classified by discipline using Web of Science categories. We found stubbornly impermeable subdisciplinary boundaries between developmental science and family science, but a very strong suprasystem connecting developmental science to its root discipline of psychology. Authorship and citation patterns indicate less permeable boundaries between HDFS and the related disciplines of education and social work. © 2026 National Council for Family Relations.

Authors: Burbano D.V.; Foley P.; Adjei M.; Wiber M.G.
Title: Exploring social dimensions of sustainability: A review of lobster fisheries research in Atlantic Canada
Abstract: International fisheries management increasingly calls for holistic, interdisciplinary approaches that integrate institutional, economic, and socio-cultural dimensions. Yet, incorporating diverse social data, particularly from the social sciences, into decision-making remains a persistent challenge. This paper uses Atlantic Canadian lobster fisheries as a case study to assess how social dimensions of sustainability have been addressed in research and to identify barriers to their integration into policy and management. Guided by the Canadian Fisheries Research Network’s full-spectrum sustainability framework, this scoping review synthesizes 23 peer-reviewed social science studies on lobster fisheries in Atlantic Canada. The review finds that governance themes, such as access rights, co-management, and regulatory frameworks, receive the most attention, while labour conditions, economic viability, intergenerational access, and cultural identity are comparatively underexplored. Regional imbalances are also evident, with most case studies concentrated in Nova Scotia and limited research from other Atlantic provinces. Persistent knowledge gaps relate to institutional responsiveness, alternative governance models, intra-community differences, occupational health and safety, and spatial conflict. The reviewed studies illustrate the interdisciplinary nature of the literature, portraying lobster fisheries as complex social-ecological systems shaped by legal, cultural, institutional, and economic forces. Findings underscore the need for more interdisciplinary, equity-centered, and context-sensitive research to support holistic and adaptive fisheries governance. Greater integration of social dimensions into fisheries policy may support more sustainable and inclusive governance Atlantic Canadian lobster fisheries. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Eren Bozdoğan K.; Bozdoğan E.; Toprak F.; Pulat E.
Title: A qualitative analysis of empathy and awareness of digital violence among high school students
Abstract: This study investigates the perceptions of digital violence, empathy levels, and coping strategies among Generation Z adolescents, specifically within a high-achieving academic context. Adopting a qualitative case study design, data were collected from 20 students attending a Science High School in Turkey, utilizing the “vignette technique” based on real-life scenarios and semi-structured interviews. The findings reveal a significant gender divide in digital experiences: while female students exhibit high “affective empathy” and prioritize social support mechanisms (e.g., sharing with family), male students tend to display “indifference” or “anger,” favoring technical or retaliatory solutions (e.g., blocking, confronting). These results suggest that generic prevention strategies are insufficient. The study concludes that interventions targeting high school students must be gender-sensitive --focusing on emotional regulation for males and technical empowerment for females– and validates the vignette technique as an effective tool for uncovering latent attitudes in digital well-being research. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Nagel J.
Title: Causal Explanation in History: An Analysis of Research Practices; [Kausales Erklären in der Geschichtswissenschaft: eine Analyse von Forschungspraktiken]
Abstract: (How) do historians infer causality? Comparing two typical bodies of research literature—the dispute over the Anglo-American “Great Rapprochement” after 1895 and that over extreme violence in colonial warfare—I analyze to what extent historians use causal language, establish causal–intentional explanations, analyze unintended consequences, and use causal theories, comparisons, and counterfactuals. I conclude that historical research practice defies the clarity of methodological dichotomies such as “explaining vs. understanding,” though it is best described as vaguely causal–analytical. Given the disconnect between methodological discussions (of both the social sciences and history itself) and research practice, historians do not appear to be either “natural allies” in the struggle of anticausalist social scientists or easy sparring partners for methodological exchange with causalist social scientists. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Wang L.; Mat T.Z.T.; Mansor S.M.
Title: The Social Architecture of Green Technology Governance: Digital Transformation, Labor Stratification and Green Digital Education in China’s High-Tech Sector
Abstract: Against China’s dual carbon strategic agenda and the deep integration of digital economy and real manufacturing, green technological innovation has long been framed as an industrial economic driver for high-tech sectors. Yet insufficient scholarly attention has been paid to its intertwined social, labour and educational repercussions—core domains of social science research. Digital transformation and environmental regulation jointly reshape corporate green innovation incentives, while simultaneously restructuring labour markets, widening inter-regional social inequalities, and exposing systemic gaps in public green digital literacy education. Drawing on balanced provincial panel data covering 30 Chinese provincial-level high-tech industries from 2012 to 2022, this study constructs multi-dimensional composite indicators of digital transformation and environmental regulatory stringency via the entropy weight method. It empirically estimates the baseline impact of industrial digitalisation on green innovation, and systematically unpacks the moderating social mechanisms embedded within environmental policy enforcement. Heterogeneity analyses are implemented across high-tech sub-sectors and three major geographic zones (Eastern, Central, Western China). Macro panel findings are triangulated with micro firm-level questionnaire data, and three robustness strategies (variable substitution, instrumental variable estimation, lagged variable processing) mitigate endogeneity bias. The empirical results reveal three interlinked economic-socio-educational outcomes: (1) Digital transformation significantly raises both the quantity and quality of green patents within high-tech industries by reducing information frictions and optimising cross-regional innovation resource allocation, yet it exacerbates labour skill stratification and creates uneven access to digital green training resources across regions; (2) Environmental regulatory intensity positively moderates the digitalisation-green innovation linkage, consistent with an extended Porter Hypothesis contextualised to digital societies; stringent environmental compliance pressures push firms to invest in digital low-carbon upgrades, but simultaneously erode employment security for low-skilled workers and highlight underinvestment in vocational green technology education; (3) Pronounced industrial and regional social heterogeneity exists: synergies between digital transformation and environmental governance (alongside associated labour and educational pressures) are most salient in electronic information manufacturing and Eastern coastal provinces, whereas aerospace manufacturing and Western inland regions fail to realise equitable green transition outcomes due to inadequate digital infrastructure and under-resourced public environmental education systems. This paper reconceptualises digital-green industrial dynamics through sociological stratification theory and public policy education frameworks, expanding the theoretical scope of the Porter Hypothesis into social science discourse. Beyond industrial policy recommendations, it delivers transferable global insights for inclusive labour governance and green digital curriculum design, offering cross-national lessons for social scientists and education practitioners studying sustainable industrial transitions. © 2026 Wang et al.

Authors: Leggerini C.; Bannò M.
Title: Women in STEM on twitter (now X): symbolic equality or structural change in Italian public discourse?
Abstract: Purpose – This study examines how public discourse on women in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) evolves over time and across Italian regions, assessing whether increased online visibility reflects substantive cultural change or primarily symbolic inclusion. Drawing on Role Congruity Theory, it explores how digital narratives may promote inclusion while reproducing gendered expectations. Design/methodology/approach – The study analyses 76, 448 Italian tweets published between 2014 and 2022. A mixed computational approach combines sentiment analysis, emotion recognition and topic modelling comparisons to investigate temporal trends and emotional framing in discussions about women in STEM. Findings – Results show a growth in public attention, primarily driven by event-based and institutional communication. Sentiment is predominantly positive or neutral, with minimal overt negativity. However, this positivity may reflect celebratory dissemination rather than critical engagement with structural inequalities. Trust and surprise emerge as dominant emotions, indicating the relevance of role models while suggesting that women's presence in STEM is still perceived as culturally “exceptional”. Visibility often depends on a limited number of symbolic women actors. Research limitations/implications – The analysis is limited to Twitter (now X) and the Italian context, suggesting opportunities for cross-platform and cross-country extensions. Practical implications – Visibility-based initiatives should be complemented by strategies addressing gendered expectations and structural barriers in STEM. Social implications – Symbolic inclusion risks masking persistent inequalities, underscoring the need for more transformative approaches to gender equality in STEM. Originality/value – The study provides novel empirical evidence on symbolic inclusion in digital discourse by integrating large-scale social media analysis with Role Congruity Theory. © 2026 Chiara Leggerini and Mariasole Bannò

Authors: Guarrella C.; Cohrssen C.; Lilley N.
Title: Uncovering Science Education in Australian Early Childhood Teacher Qualifications
Abstract: Despite the existence of a national Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) education agenda highlighting the importance of science education in the years before formal schooling, guiding documents for early childhood curricula and practice in Australia continue to lack systematic integration of science teaching and learning. Without clear guidance on how science (or science as an element of STEM) can be enacted in early childhood education, there is similarly limited guidance for the integration of science in initial teacher education (ITE). A social research audit of publicly accessible course handbooks was used to understand how science is positioned within Australian early childhood ITE programs. Findings suggest that preparation to teach science is highly variable, ranging along a continuum from none at all, through exposure to science within an integrated STEM or STEAM subject, to the development of discipline-specific science pedagogical content knowledge. This variability has implications for future research, policy and practice. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Cook R.A.
Title: Dynamic programming for calculating the triad census
Abstract: Triad census is a popular static analysis technique that summarizes topology and triadic behavior in a network. However, traditional static methods for counting triad motifs do not scale for dynamic analysis on large event logs of digital trace data increasingly used in computational social science. Further, tracking triad evolution over time can provide insights into behavioral elements such as information brokerage not captured in static analysis. We propose Dynamic Triad Census (DTC), a dynamic programming algorithm to calculate the triad census procedure efficiently over time. Formal analyses of the correctness and computational complexity of the proposed method are supported by numerical experiments that demonstrate its accuracy and improved efficiency over existing static counting methods. We show how efficient computation and storage of census motifs enables dynamic network analysis of triad transition and brokerage behavior in longitudinal networks by using motifs as covariates in other dynamic techniques and as their own objects of inquiry. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: McCormick-Huhn J.
Title: A PSYCHOLOGICAL EXPLANATION FOR REINSTATING PRECLEARANCE UNDER THE VOTING RIGHTS ACT
Abstract: The Voting Rights Act (VRA) was signed into law nearly sixty years ago. But in 2013, the Supreme Court’s Shelby County v. Holder opinion effectively gutted the VRA’s preclearance requirement, which required states with a history of discriminatory voting laws to submit proposed voting law changes for federal approval. The Supreme Court determined that the formula for determining the “covered jurisdictions” subjected to preclearance was outdated and unnecessary in light of “progress” and how the VRA “proved immensely successful at redressing racial discrimination and integrating the voting process.” This Article is the first to analyze Shelby County and preclearance from a psychological perspective. Specifically, this Article presents psychology research from the past decade that has documented the conditions under which white Americans experience status threat in light of the looming racial demographic shift in the U.S. population—a shift from majority-white to majority-minority. Psychology research has also documented backlash to racial progress, specifically the election of President Barack Obama. The discussed psychology research is complemented by other findings in political science and sociology. Taken together, the psychology research and social science findings provide strong support for reinstating preclearance to prevent reactionary steps taken by states to suppress voting by growing minority group populations. Moreover, the research warns that the “progress” championed by the majority in Shelby County comes at a cost—another reason to reinstate preclearance. By using the current psychological findings—and embarking on new avenues of psychological research—we can also better tailor the “covered jurisdictions” formula to put in place voter protections during periods of time surrounding “racial-shift events,” such as when a jurisdiction’s voter-eligible population shifts to majority-minority. © 2026 Temple University. Authors: Chapman S.; Roy D.; Baker W.; Hotko K.; Hamilton A.; Burke K.
Title: Supporting initial teacher education student creativity and critical thinking using active constraints in assessment: A scoping review
Abstract: Assessment design plays a critical role in shaping student learning in higher education, particularly in disciplines where creativity is both a learning outcome and a pedagogical approach. In Initial Teacher Education (ITE), this role is intensified, as assessment tasks often function as the primary site of learning for time-poor students and simultaneously model pedagogical practice for future teachers. While constraints are frequently embedded within assessment tasks, their role in supporting creativity remains under-theorised and inconsistently articulated in the literature. This scoping review examines how constraints are used within assessment tasks that aim to foster creativity and/or critical thinking in social sciences, humanities, education and creative arts courses in higher education in order to consider implications for enhancing creativity through assessment tasks in ITE. Using a scoping review framework, 28 empirical studies published since 2000 were identified and analysed thematically. Six key themes emerged: the role of prior experience, constraints as catalysts for creativity, task design and flexibility, rubrics and scaffolding as support structures, the domain-specificity of creativity, and the presence of “invisible architectures” in task design. Findings indicate that constraints function as powerful pedagogical mechanisms when they are intentionally designed, aligned with disciplinary practices, and calibrated to student readiness. However, many studies prioritise creative outcomes without sufficiently detailing the task conditions that shape them. Drawing on these findings, the paper positions constraints as active contributors to assessment design and introduces a design-oriented framework to support educators in making constraints explicit and pedagogically purposeful. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Thein C.
Title: Is Antisemitism a Blind Spot of Critical Social Theory?
Abstract: Even if theoretical and empirical research on antisemitism has been making further progress in recent decades, the findings associated with this expertise in social sciences do not represent a specific point of reference for contemporary approaches to Critical Social Theory. This assessment is surprising for at least two reasons. Firstly, with the intention to shed light on the internal relationship between manifestations of antisemitism and the structures of modern liberal or fascist societies the early tradition of the Frankfurt School had explicitly placed a critical analyzation of it at the center of its research program in the 1930s and 1940s. Secondly, it can be stated that intersectional approaches as well as the critique of structural forms of racism have already come into focus of interest for Critical Social Theory. However, this has been largely done without critically addressing antisemitism as a specific and relevant phenomenon of contemporary societies. In the following, this article shows that this non-thematization can be explained by highlighting some misdirected premises in the newer critical conceptions concerning the social structures of domination and oppression as well as to reductionists approaches to racism which miss to address the specific characteristics of antisemitism. © The Author(s) 2025

Authors: Brezovec E.; Zelić M.; Zagode A.M.
Title: Stabilizing truth in educational sciences: a systematic review of generative AI in education
Abstract: Purpose – This paper examines how the scientific system, particularly the educational sciences, observes and communicates the phenomenon of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education. Drawing on Luhmann’s social systems theory, the purpose is to reconstruct how scientific communication stabilizes truth by framing AI through distinctions such as augmentation, automation, and hybrid models. Design/methodology/approach – A systematic literature review was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 framework, using Scopus to cover the period 2020–2025. Out of 1, 105 initial publications, 110 studies met the inclusion criteria. Quality was assessed with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Findings – Educational sciences primarily frame generative AI as augmentation (71.8%), with automation (18.2%) and hybrid models (3.6%) secondary. Higher education dominates as the site of observation (65.5%), while primary and vocational education remain marginal. Ethical concerns focus on privacy, bias, accountability, and teacher autonomy. The scientific system reduces uncertainty by coding AI as supportive rather than disruptive. Research limitations/implications – The review relied on Scopus, English-only full-text sources, and citation-based selection, which may bias findings. Practical implications – The study enriches systematic review methodology by integrating systems theory, showing how reviews can serve not only as syntheses but also as tools for second-order observation of scientific communication. Originality/value – By combining systematic review with systems theory, the study demonstrates how science programs its communication about AI, offering a transferable model for analysing emerging technologies in other social systems. © 2025 Erik Brezovec, Marija Zelić and Ana Marija Zagode

Authors: Phillipson J.; Steins N.A.; Raakjaer J.
Title: The European Social Science Fisheries Network: a retrospective
Abstract: In this paper we delve into the history of fisheries social sciences in Europe. We reflect, on the 30th anniversary of its start date, on the works of the European Social Science Fisheries Network (ESSFiN) and its contribution to the development and integration of social science expertise and research within fisheries management. In the late 1990s, ESSFiN succeeded in plugging the institutional gap, providing an opportunity to demonstrate the extent, breadth and relevance of the social sciences' potential to an understanding of issues in the organisation and governance of marine fisheries in Europe. It helped change the course of fisheries social sciences and became the standard bearer for an applied social approach to fisheries governance and management, and its value to the growing focus on multi-disciplinary research. ESSFiN had long lasting contributions in terms of substantive insights and agendas, capacity building within the marine social sciences and policy impacts, but crucially also potentially offers insights relevant to current and future challenges in the field. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Sabbagh-Khoury A.
Title: Decolonizing Epistemological Violence: Settler Colonialism and Intracommunal Violence and Crime in Palestinian Society in Israel
Abstract: This paper critically examines production of knowledge about intracommunal violence and crime within Palestinian society in Israel, highlighting the relationship between power structures and epistemological frameworks. It centers the ontological relationship of power to settler colonial structures, interrogating how knowledge is shaped within domination and resistance. The paper identifies two paradigms: the first, a cultural/pathological paradigm that frames violence as a manifestation of cultural or social dysfunction; the second, an ethnic-minority/liberal paradigm, which attributes violence to inequality and social stratification, positioning Palestinians as a marginalized minority within a liberal state. It then introduces a third burgeoning paradigm, the settler colonial and apartheid paradigm, conceptualizing violence as a consequence of structural dispossession, systemic neglect, and “organized colonial abandonment.” Drawing on a systematic review of academic, NGO, and journalistic reports in Hebrew, Arabic, and English, the paper demonstrates how certain paradigms reinforce dominant narratives that stigmatize Palestinian society in Israel while obscuring the Israeli settler state's role in sustaining violence and Jewish supremacy. It further highlights the key role of Palestinian NGOs, activists, and journalists in challenging two hegemonic frameworks and producing counter-knowledge. By advocating anti-colonial epistemology within social sciences, the paper calls for centering counter-hegemonic knowledge production, affirming indigenous struggles for epistemological and material decolonization. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Götz F.J.; Heineck P.M.; Böckler A.; Eder A.B.
Title: Dimensional asymmetries in social attention: Dynamic head movements elicit opposite attentional biases in vertical versus horizontal dimensions
Abstract: Abstract: When observing a person with direct gaze but a horizontally averted head posture, attention often shifts opposite to head direction (overshoot effect). We investigated whether this effect generalizes to vertical head movements and whether it depends on gaze direction information. Across four experiments, centrally presented faces shifted dynamically to averted head positions before a target appeared at a location congruent or incongruent with head direction. Vertical head movements (Experiments 1 and 2) produced head-congruency effects, which were stronger when the eyes were closed. In contrast, horizontal head movements (Experiments 3 and 4) produced classic overshoot effects, which surprisingly were amplified when the eyes were closed. Thus, direct gaze attenuated head-cueing effects but did not alter their direction. Overall, these findings reveal dimensional asymmetries in social attention and demonstrate that gaze-head integration considers spatial context. Implications for hierarchical, holistic, and predictive cue-integration accounts are discussed. Open Practices Statement: All four experiments were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; Experiment 1: https://osf.io/qds4x; Experiment 2: https://osf.io/d6rwe; Experiment 3: https://osf.io/xe9a6; Experiment 4: https://osf.io/3pq49). Materials, experimental scripts, stimuli, raw data, and analysis scripts underlying the reported results are publicly available at https://osf.io/aq7zf/ and https://osf.io/j96fx/ © The Author(s) 2026.
