Authors: Ruiz-García A.; Hernández-Leo D.
Title: How Does Technical Background Shape Teachers' Epistemic Framings, Reflection, and Conceptualisation of Digital Competence?
Abstract: As digital technologies increasingly shape education and social life, teachers are expected to exercise Teachers' Digital Competence (TDC) as professional agency across pedagogical, organisational, and ethical dimensions. While policy frameworks such as DigCompEdu articulate this breadth, how teachers interpret and enact these dimensions in reflective practice remains insufficiently understood. This qualitative study examines how teachers with and without an undergraduate computer science background conceptualise TDC by mapping how their distinct disciplinary backgrounds act as epistemic lenses through two guided reflective interventions: the SELFIEforTEACHERS (SfT) self-assessment tool and a subsequent collective reflection focused on ethical and socio-technical issues. Moving away from a linear skill-accumulation model, this study uses an expertise-informed analytical lens to analyse differences in knowledge organisation, reflective orientation, and metacognitive engagement. The findings suggest that disciplinary enculturation shapes the reflective trajectory and epistemic framings of TDC. While SfT supports structured, multidimensional reflection aligned with policy intentions, deeper developmental engagement (particularly with ethical judgement) is strengthened when reflection foregrounds socio-technical complexity. The study contributes to conceptualising TDC as epistemic resilience within evolving educational systems. © 2026 The Author(s). European Journal of Education published by John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

Authors: Castillo I.A.; Klaeson K.; Ekelund A.-C.; Tengelin E.
Title: Norm-critical elements in nursing and healthcare education: a scoping review
Abstract: Background: Access to healthcare is a fundamental human right that is often influenced by social norms and power structures. Implicit biases in society, healthcare, and education contribute to health inequalities. Incorporating equity and social justice into nursing and healthcare education, through norm-critical pedagogy can empower learners to address and promote social justice and health equity in patient care and community health. Methods: The aim of the study was to describe characteristics and recurring elements of norm-critical literature in published research. This study followed Arksey and O’Malley’s scoping review framework and adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis extension for scoping reviews to report the findings. A search was conducted in across five scientific databases – CINAHL, APA PsycINFO, ERIC, Medline, and Web of Science – limiting results to English language articles. Two authors independently screened, extracted, and analysed the data, guided by selected key concepts based on the population, concept, and context framework. The included articles were condensed according to specific characteristics and analysed thematically. Results: Sixteen articles were included in the review, and all published from 2017 onwards, primarily in nursing journals. Most of these articles employed qualitative methodologies. A thematic analysis generated three themes: ‘Redesigning education toward norm-critical pedagogy’, ‘Redefining one’s positionality as a teacher’, and ‘Transforming education for a norm-conscious sustainable healthcare future’. Conclusions: This scoping review concludes that the characteristics of norm-critical literature, primarily centred on Western nursing education, has limited applicability in other healthcare educations. The literature describes key challenges in integrating norm-criticism into educational structures, often placing undue responsibility on individual teachers to adopt a norm-critical pedagogy. This review calls for further empirical research on norm-criticism to advance its use as a pedagogical model in nursing and healthcare education. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Busch C.A.; Meuler M.; Theobald E.J.
Title: National biology learning objectives and assessment questions often overlook science’s connection to society
Abstract: Making connections between science and societal or cultural issues in biology courses may lead to increases in students’ engagement, ability to recognize the potential for biology to advance social change, and ultimately their retention in the discipline. One common way to make these connections is via the incorporation of socioscientific issues. Using a rubric we created and refined, we evaluated learning objectives and practice assessment questions from 16 national biology education frameworks and assessments (n = 2890) for the presence of these connections to societal or cultural issues. As tools to support instructors to design their courses at both the college-preparatory and undergraduate levels, we contend that whether content is connected with societal or cultural issues will, in part, depend on whether these connections are prioritized via inclusion in learning objectives and assessment questions. We found connections between science content and societal or cultural issues in only 7% (n = 213) of the items reviewed. Further, these connections were often implicit, rather than explicitly stated. The items where these connections were made most often related to topics such as ethics or public health. Nearly 40% (n = 83) of the items that made these connections did so by relating to a socioscientific issue. The dearth of connections between biology content and societal or cultural issues highlights an opportunity for growth in promoting sociopolitical consciousness in biology curricula and the lack of prioritization in these biology education resources. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Forte D.L.
Title: Ecolinguistics and the multimodal reorientation of language studies
Abstract: This paper examines the place of ecolinguistics within the broader discipline of linguistics, arguing that it constitutes a transversal paradigm with the potential to redefine language as an ecological phenomenon (Steffensen et al., 2024). Tracing the historical development of linguistic thought from Saussurean structuralism to contemporary cognitive and critical approaches, analysis highlights how dominant paradigms have been constrained by anthropocentrism and a monomodal conception of language centred on the verbal dimension (Perniss, 2018). Ecolinguistics, emerging from the broader ecological turn in the social sciences, allows a challenge of this foundation by integrating the more-than-human world into linguistic inquiry. The paper posits that ecolinguistics as theoretical framework provides tools to deconstruct human exceptionalism in linguistic studies, shifting the focus from what makes language uniquely human to how it situates communicative beings within a shared ecosystem. To fully realize this reorientation, I advocate for the adoption of a multimodal approach to language. By recognizing meaning as constructed through the integration of diverse semiotic resources—gesture, posture, facial expression, vocalization, and image—this framework deconstructs the barrier between human language and animal communication. Reviewing evidence from cognitive science and zoo semiotics, including the syntactic alarm calls of prairie dogs, the cultural performativity of birdsong, and the embodied cognition of octopuses, the argument establishes a communicative and multimodal continuum across species. This perspective reveals that many species employ complex, context-dependent combinations of modalities, suggesting that human linguistic distinctiveness is one of degree and combinatorial emphasis, not of kind (de Waal, 2016). Ultimately, the paper contends that a multimodal ecolinguistics fosters a critical epistemology essential for a world in socio-ecological crisis. It moves linguistics from an anthropocentric monologue towards an ethics of dialogic participation within a living, semiotic web. By analysing how discourses construct human–environment relations, ecolinguistics can become a vital tool for deconstructing narratives of domination and fostering ecological kinship, humility, and responsibility. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Faria C.
Title: Potentialities of a Local Job Shadowing Experience in Initial Science Teachers' Training
Abstract: This paper describes a “job shadowing” initiative developed in the context of initial teacher education to promote awareness of the different dimensions present in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) relationships. Ten pre-service teachers participated in this initiative, visiting three different contexts: A museum integrated within a school, an oceanarium, and a research center. After each visit, participants completed a learning diary and a checklist, designed to promote participants’ metacognitive thinking about the job they were observing and to identify the experienced utility of each visit. This experience seemed to have promoted a broader, more critical, and more integrated view of education, impacted participants’ motivation, professional awareness, and social commitment, and contributed to the strengthening of the vision of education as dynamic, interdisciplinary, and socially relevant, and of educational careers as flexible, multifaceted, and constantly evolving. This has important implications for STEM teacher education and professional development, highlighting the value of incorporating non-formal and research-based experiences into training programs to better prepare educators for the complexities of contemporary educational landscapes. © 2026, International Council of Associations for Science Education (ICASE). Authors: Jakab M.
Title: Conspiracy Thinking in Psychotherapy: A Narrative Review Integrating Topical Research on Conspiracy Beliefs and Process-related Common Factors
Abstract: Despite growing interdisciplinary work on conspiracy beliefs, explicit psychotherapy research on these phenomena remains limited. This review first outlines this research gap and then examines how conspiracy thinking may affect the construction of meaning and other common factors of the psychotherapeutic process. The narrative review was chosen because literature integrating psychotherapy- and conspiracy-related themes was assumed to be scarce. In a first step, such literature (general and orientation-specific) was identified (and scarcity confirmed). In a second step, topical conspiracy research from psychology, philosophy and the social sciences was identified by adding emergent keywords and then integrated with process-relevant common factors. Sufficiency was assumed when a consistent narrative could be substantiated and further search brought up mainly sources already identified. Research directly linking conspiracy thinking and psychotherapy is rare and often limited to etiological dimensions. Integrating findings across disciplines, conspiracy thinking emerges as an intervening factor in meaning-making, alliance, narrative flexibility and social embeddedness in therapy. Generalized, trait-like epistemic mistrust can undermine credibility, while state-like conspiracy-related mistrust may signal repairable alliance ruptures. Conceptual tools such as negative capability suggest that interventions should emphasize restoring interpretative freedom rather than confronting conspiracy narratives. Apart from these process-related dimensions, also clinically relevant correlations with anxiety, paranoid ideation or personality disorders are described in literature. The therapeutic significance of conspiracy thinking appears to lie less in specific beliefs than in their relational and epistemic consequences for therapy. Psychotherapy science could benefit from further integrating research from sociology, political- and communication science and study of religion, and vice versa. Further research is needed on how therapists’ own epistemic positions and demand for authentic presence interfere with client’s conspiracy beliefs, and how practice can better understand epistemic distrust without pathologizing contextually grounded skepticism. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Authors: Mbowe A.E.; Anselimus S.M.
Title: Barriers to preparing pre-service science teachers for inclusive education of pupils with visual impairments in Tanzania
Abstract: Inclusive science education for learners with visual impairments (VI) is still a significant challenge in Tanzania, despite progressive policy frameworks and teacher education reforms. This study investigated the challenges faced by tutors and pre-service science teachers in preparing to teach pupils with VI, focusing on curriculum design, pedagogical practice, resource availability, and practical training. A qualitative approach was employed, utilising a single-case study of a teacher training college. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, and classroom observations with 28 purposively sampled participants, including tutors, the head of the science department, and pre-service teachers. Thematic analysis revealed four major challenges: absence of a VI-specific curriculum, shortage of specialised tutors, scarcity of teaching and learning materials, and limited duration and structure of teaching practice. These gaps undermine the practical competence, confidence, and self-efficacy of pre-service teachers, constraining the quality of science education accessible to VI learners. The findings show an urgent policy and institutional imperative that without targeted curriculum adaptations, investment in assistive technologies, and enhanced tutor capacity, learners with VI risk continued exclusion from meaningful science education, perpetuating inequities in STEM access and achievement. The study emphasizes the relevance of Universal Design for Learning and the Social Model of Disability in guiding inclusive pedagogy. Recommendations include development of structured VI-specific curricula, recruitment and professional development of specialised tutors, extended and supported practicum experiences, and systemic resource allocation. Future research should examine the effectiveness of these interventions on both teacher preparedness and learner outcomes. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Xu J.; Lu X.; Abdi N.M.
Title: Re-centering the role of humans in AI-assisted writing scoring: A scoping review from a critical perspective
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been used to assess the academic writing of English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) university students. This scoping review synthesized empirical studies comparing AI-assisted and human scoring of EFL academic writing from perspectives of Critical Language Testing (CLT) and Critical Digital Pedagogy (CDP). Following PRISMA-guided procedures, this review searched Web of Science, ERIC, and PubMed for empirical studies published between 2015 and 2025. Twelve studies met the inclusion criteria of peer-reviewed empirical studies comparing AI-assisted and human scoring in EFL university learners’ academic writing and were further analyzed through thematic synthesis guided by theoretical frameworks of CLT and CDP. The results revealed that AI-generated scores generally showed moderate alignment with human-created scores, particularly for surface-level linguistic features, but demonstrated lower agreement for higher-level writing aspects. AI tools were also frequently reported to be stricter than human raters and to be affected by prompting design. From a CLT perspective, fairness-related issues were underexplored, while assessment transparency and social implications were unevenly illustrated across the reviewed studies. From a CDP perspective, most studies reflected critical awareness of using AI and emphasized human oversight over AI-assisted scoring but rarely explained how teachers can practically and critically use AI to support dialogic assessment processes. The findings highlight the need for future studies to integrate technical validation of AI-assisted writing assessments with considerations of fairness, transparency, human agency, the critical use of AI, and dialogic pedagogies. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Wu J.; Zhang T.; Liang J.
Title: Understanding linguistic accommodation in science and literature: professional norms reshape gendered discourse
Abstract: Language use is shaped by societal norms surrounding gender identities, reinforcing gendered stereotypes in linguistic expression. However, recent research suggests that individuals may adopt counter-stereotypical language styles to achieve specific communicative purposes, particularly in professional settings where occupational demands take precedence over social expectations. This study examines professional environments as a distinct case in which individuals engage in linguistic accommodation that may challenge socially constructed gender norms. Focusing on science and literature as two contrasting disciplines, we investigate how professional norms interact with social norms and may shape patterns of linguistic performance. Through an analysis of autobiographies and speeches, we find that scientific discourse predominantly favors a logical and categorical language style, aligning with the professional expectations of precision and objectivity. In contrast, literary discourse exhibits greater linguistic diversity, suggesting that this discipline prioritizes creativity and personal expression rather than adherence to rigid norms. By incorporating both gender identity and disciplinary context into the analysis of language use, we show that professional norms can reshape gender-linked linguistic patterns, moderating and in some cases counteracting stereotypical associations between gender and language. Furthermore, our findings reveal that emotional language is more prevalent in speech than in writing, indicating that the communicative context also plays a crucial role in shaping language use. These findings not only advance theoretical understanding of gender and discourse but also have practical implications for fostering more inclusive professional communication across disciplines. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Capizzo L.; Lenhardt S.; Nzau T.
Title: Ungrounding public relations theory: Conceptual scholarship as rigor and refuge
Abstract: Public relations has a rich history of meaningful, generative scholarship performed through the construction of conceptual essays—non-empirical articles designed to develop new theories or to question, probe, or extend existing ones. Guidance for theory building in public relations has largely come from the social sciences, such as Broom’s (2006) open system approach, connecting theory and model construction to primarily quantitative methodological investigation. This article provides a guide to crafting a wide range of conceptual essays, empowering theorists across the epistemological and methodological spectrums, with a focus on making the work of theory building more accessible, globally representative, and decolonial. The clearer the path toward the robust construction and diligent contextualization of new theory, the more inclusive public relations theorization has the potential to become. This article offers the framework of ungrounding and presents structured approaches for conducting conceptual research in public relations—promoting conceptual theorizing as a methodological practice. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Schnettler S.; Huinink J.
Title: Refitting the Lower Decks of the Coleman Boat: A Biosocial and Evolutionary Expansion of the Standard Model of Sociological Explanation; [Erweiterung der unteren Decks des Coleman-Boots: Eine biosoziale und evolutionäre Erweiterung des Standardmodells der soziologischen Erklärung]
Abstract: In this article, we argue that the standard model of sociological explanation can be substantially improved by systematically integrating insights from biosocial and evolutionary research. Building on Coleman’s macro–micro–macro model, we propose an extension of this framework that adds a “covert” inner-individual micro level beneath the traditional “overt” micro level. This “lower deck” of the “Coleman boat” comprises genetic variation and epigenetic, hormonal, neural, and other physiological processes that affect individual behavior, mediate and moderate the impact of social contexts on behavior, and, in aggregation, shape macro-level outcomes. Using examples from biosociology, neurosociology, and sociogenomics, we illustrate how ignoring these processes can bias estimates of social effects, leave central sociological mechanisms underspecified, and thus ultimately yield incomplete explanations. We further draw on evolutionary sociology and the evolutionary behavioral sciences, including cultural evolution approaches and evolutionary psychology, to show how evolved psychological mechanisms and evolved dispositions for prosocial, selfish, and antagonistic behavior, as well as evolutionary mismatches, shape contemporary social behavior and macro-level dynamics. On this basis, we argue for an interdisciplinary action theory that incorporates both automatic and reflexive processes and is informed by biological and evolutionary findings while retaining the analytical primacy of sociological explanation. We provide the extended Coleman scheme as a heuristic for scholars to locate when and how inner-individual mechanisms matter in sociological analyses and for guiding empirical research on patterned interactions between nature and nurture. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Magallón M.-D.-M.; Sáenz J.
Title: Revealing Hidden Impact: Social and Solidarity Economy Enterprise Networks and Sustainable Development in Developing Countries
Abstract: The Social and Solidarity Economy (SSE) offers strong potential for sustainable development in low-income regions, yet its enterprises often operate with scarce resources, weak monitoring systems, and limited visibility. These constraints hinder both their capacity to demonstrate contributions to sustainable development (SD) and their own progress toward greater sustainability. Support networks can play a decisive role in overcoming these limitations. This study develops a Sustainability Assessment Framework (SAF) specifically designed for vulnerable SSE initiatives supported by international networks. Following a Design Science Research approach, the SAF was co-created through a participatory, multi-stakeholder process grounded in SSE principles. Adaptable across sectors, it enables comparative evaluation, strengthens learning processes, and supports continuous improvement. Applied to 21 social business initiatives in 7 countries, facilitated by 9 Latin American NGOs, the SAF reinforces the legitimacy of support networks and enhances understanding of SSE's contribution to SD. The findings offer actionable insights for NGOs, policymakers, and scholars. © 2026 The Author(s). Sustainable Development published by ERP Environment and John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

Authors: Pulchny A.; Gallagher-Mackay K.; Robson K.
Title: When Protection Becomes Prevention: The Impact of the Ethics Review Process on Graduate Researchers
Abstract: This article presents results from a national online survey on the unintended effects of research ethics board (REB) processes on research, teaching, and learning in the Social Sciences and Humanities across Canada (N = 620). Focusing on student responses (n = 93), key findings reveal how REB proceduralism, inconsistent risk assessments, and ethics creep disproportionately burden graduate students and restrict innovative, culturally responsive research. Students indicate that REB processes prioritize institutional liability over meaningful ethical engagement, often resulting in delays, emotional strain, and reduced academic motivation. Using DiMaggio and Powell’s framework of institutional isomorphism, the authors identify a paradox: while ethics processes are intended to be standardized, their implementation varies significantly across institutions. The authors recommend reducing barriers for low-risk studies, streamlining multi-institutional reviews, and enhancing REB transparency and cultural responsiveness, alongside offering student-informed strategies for reforming ethics review to better support early-career researchers. © The Author(s) 2026. Authors: de Juana-Ortín C.
Title: From pigments to pixels: Continuity, transition, and challenges of color in the digital preservation of heritage
Abstract: Color constitutes a key dimension of cultural heritage, encoding technical, symbolic, and social knowledge beyond its aesthetic role. This paper examines color as a continuous epistemic and technical phenomenon, from prehistoric material practices to contemporary digital environments. The study aims to establish an integrated conceptual framework that links archaeological evidence with current spectral, multispectral, and virtual technologies. Adopting an interdisciplinary approach, it analyses core processes including color acquisition, spectral-to-color conversion, metamerism, virtual restoration, and chromatic data management under FAIR principles. The discussion integrates recent research in archaeology, heritage science, and digital humanities, while addressing challenges related to calibration, reproducibility, and perceptual variability. The main contribution of the paper lies in articulating a structured framework that connects material, perceptual, and digital dimensions of color. It argues that the transition from pigment to pixel represents not a rupture, but a technologically mediated continuity in the human experience and preservation of color. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Blanco Sequeiros S.
Title: Explaining evidential discordance
Abstract: Evidential discordance, or the situation where scientific evidence supports contrary hypotheses, claims or theories about a given phenomenon, is common in scientific inquiry (Franklin, 2002; Boyd, 2018; Stegenga, 2009, 2012). Although in many ways useful for scientific progress, discordance also poses distinct epistemic and methodological challenges for science, as it hinders building consensus and causes problems for decision making (Collins, 1985; Hey, 2015a; Maziarz, 2024; Reijula and Blanco Sequeiros, 2024). To address these challenges, philosophers of science have discussed episodes of disagreement in scientific evidence and presented strategies for dealing with discordance (Bokulich, 2020; Ohnesorge, 2021; Reijula & Blanco Sequeiros, 2024). Despite this discussion, the concept of evidential discordance itself has remained overlooked. In this paper, I clarify the concept of discordant evidence, and propose a novel explanation for the emergence of evidential discordance into scientific evidence. I argue that evidential discordance can be explained by disagreement between inferences from data to phenomena between various lines of evidence. The data-to-phenomenon inferences conflict because of how they conceptualize the causal tracks of the phenomenon of interest within data. This explanation for discordance is useful because it unifies a variety of empirical explanations for discordance, including error, noise and bias. I use examples from the social sciences to showcase my arguments but the lessons extend to other areas of philosophy of science as well. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Oechsler B.; Cleary Y.; Closs S.
Title: Piloting Kenya’s First Master’s Program in Technical Communication: Digital Innovation, Intercultural Challenges, and Lessons for Higher Education in the Global South
Abstract: About the case: This case study examines the curriculum development and pilot phase of Kenya’s first master’s program in technical communication, at Pwani University, developed with Karlsruhe University of Applied Sciences (Germany). The pilot tested a hybrid, mostly online, curriculum aimed at introducing applied technical communication education in Kenya’s traditionally theory-based higher education system. Situating the case: Kenya’s higher education system, shaped by its colonial legacy, remains theory-focused despite economic growth and digital expansion. National strategies prioritize curricular modernization for job-ready skills. Situated within broader technical and professional communication scholarship and international efforts, the new master’s program addresses this goal through digital, practice-oriented education with international instructors. Methods/approach: Standardized online surveys collected quantitative and qualitative feedback through two evaluations: a student-only survey on course contents, and a general survey with students and instructors after the first semester, focusing on organization, virtual learning environment, social/technical aspects, international context, motivation, practice-oriented content, and challenges/improvements. Results/discussion: Students valued practice-oriented teaching, international instructors, and flexible formats, but faced unstable internet, device access issues, and limited peer interaction. Instructors noted challenges engaging students online and managing coordination within an international, rotating teaching team. Conclusion: The pilot demonstrated feasibility and strong demand while revealing intersectional technical, social, and cultural barriers. Planned improvements for the full master’s program include enhanced technical support, equipment loans, in-person onboarding, and local capacity building. This pilot provides transferable insights into introducing a new discipline in the Global South while implementing digital, practice-oriented education in a theory-oriented environment, emphasizing that sustainable success requires technological infrastructure, holistic support, and collaborative adaptation. © 1988-2012 IEEE.

Authors: Evangelista-Silva P.H.; Ramos J.K.N.
Title: Unraveling the enigma of digestion: a digital educational activity as a tool for teaching digestive system physiology
Abstract: Human physiology is challenging for undergraduates due to its abstract nature. The summer course "Human Physiology: Practicing and Discussing Physiology" offered by the Institute of Biomedical Sciences at the University of São Paulo has fostered innovative teaching strategies for over two decades. In 2022, due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the course was offered remotely, requiring adaptation of practical activities to a virtual environment. We developed a virtual didactic activity called "Unraveling the Enigma of Digestion: Digital Marathon" using Google Forms integrated with social media. Designed as a board-game-like experience, each stage involved online games, storytelling, puzzles, crosswords, and interactions with fictional characters, addressing macronutrient digestion and absorption. Progression required applying concepts from classes. This report describes the structure and implementation of the digital marathon in a remote teaching context. The proposed approach represents a flexible and low-cost strategy to support engagement and active learning in remote or hybrid physiology teaching. NEW & NOTEWORTHY We present a novel teaching approach in the form of an innovative digital marathon that integrates active learning strategies with widely accessible social media platforms to support the remote teaching of digestive system physiology. This approach illustrates how interactive, low-cost digital tools can be structured to facilitate engagement and discussion of theoretical content in virtual or hybrid learning environments. Authors: Lorimer K.; Sime P.; McMillan L.
Title: When class silences disclosure: Working-Class women, sexual violence and classed gender stigma in healthcare
Abstract: Feminist sociology has illuminated how sexual violence both reflects and reproduces gendered inequalities, yet its intersection with social class remains comparatively under-theorised in health research, particularly in relation to healthcare and disclosure. This study advances critical social science research on health and healthcare by theorising classed gender stigma as a mechanism through which class and gender intersect to shape working-class women's willingness to disclose sexual violence within healthcare encounters. Drawing on episodic interviews with working-class women in Scotland, the analysis focuses on disclosure within healthcare and related professional support context, including specialist mental health services and third-sector provision. The findings show how classed histories of dismissal, material constraint and respectability norms shape women's expectations of being believed and their assessments of whether healthcare encounters are safe spaces for disclosure. Disclosure within healthcare emerges as a socially organised process shaped by classed relations of care and institutional practices, including appointment structures, referral pathways and access to paid support. The analysis develops the concept of classed gender stigma to show how healthcare encounters shape whose disclosures are recognised as credible and deserving of care following sexual violence. The paper advances understanding of how health inequalities are reproduced through silence within healthcare contexts and highlights the importance of integrating analyses of class and institutional practice into health-focused research on sexual violence disclosure. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Dash T.; Sahoo C.K.
Title: Exploring the Nexus Between Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainable Development: A Bibliometric Analysis
Abstract: This study presents a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of corporate social responsibility and sustainable development (CSR–SD) research spanning 2003–2025, examining the intellectual, thematic, and geographical evolution of the field in the context of global sustainability agendas. A total of 2099 peer-reviewed journal articles were retrieved from the Scopus and Web of Science databases to ensure broad coverage and methodological robustness. The dataset was analyzed using the Bibliometrix package in the R programming language. Co-authorship, co-citation, and keyword co-occurrence analyses, complemented by thematic evolution and strategic mapping techniques, reveal five developmental phases reflecting the progression of CSR–SD scholarship from early normative discussions toward governance-oriented and performance-driven sustainability frameworks. The findings highlight the growing prominence of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) reporting, sustainability reporting, sustainable finance, innovation, and stakeholder engagement, indicating the increasing integration of CSR–SD into corporate strategy, governance systems, and capital markets. China and Spain emerge as leading contributors to the literature, while the geographical distribution of publications reveals opportunities for broader participation from underrepresented regions. Theoretically, the study draws upon Stakeholder Theory, Legitimacy Theory, and the Triple Bottom Line framework to interpret evolving research clusters, intellectual structures, and thematic shifts. By providing a longitudinal, dual-database assessment of CSR–SD scholarship, this study contributes a theoretically grounded and methodologically rigorous understanding of the field's evolution and offers valuable insights for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers seeking to advance sustainability-oriented corporate strategies and inclusive sustainable development transitions. © 2026 ERP Environment and John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

Authors: Li Z.; Cheung K.F.A.; Lei L.
Title: Telling academic tales: The role of narrative structure in shaping research impact across disciplines
Abstract: Narrative structure, also known as the shape of stories, refers to the way a story is organized and presented from a semantic progression perspective. In academic writing, high-quality research articles are often metaphorically described as well-told academic stories, as narrative devices can present complex ideas in a clear and engaging manner. However, the role of the narrative structure in academic writing remains underexplored. To address the issue, we examined the narrative structure in research articles and its relationship with citation counts from three dimensions (i.e., speed, volume, and circuitousness) and in different disciplines. The results revealed significant cross-disciplinary differences in the narrative structure of research articles. Specifically, articles in medical and life sciences exhibited the highest levels across all three dimensions, while those in social sciences demonstrated the lowest speed and volume, and articles in applied sciences showed the lowest circuitousness. Furthermore, speed was negatively related to citation counts, whereas both volume and circuitousness were positively related to citation counts, except that volume showed a negative relationship in medical and life sciences. To the best of our knowledge, this study is probably the first cross-disciplinary investigation of the narrative structure in academic writing. Possible explanations for the findings were discussed. Implications for researchers and instructors of academic writing were also provided. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Squire R.; Byron C.; Legroux N.; Peters K.
Title: Towards Oblique Engagements With ‘Tipping Points’: A Critical Geography for Redirecting Debates
Abstract: This intervention brings debates about tipping points into conversation with critical geographical thinking to suggest a more ‘oblique’ engagement with the concept. Such an approach is vital for rethinking the normative discourses and established imaginaries that dominate in the application of ‘tipping’ to understandings of environmental change. The use of the term ‘tipping point’ has grown exponentially over the last two decades within environmental sciences to describe accelerated, self-amplifying and often irreversible changes to environmental systems. It has also garnered significant momentum in policy debates. Yet it is far from a universally lauded concept, with widespread concerns in the sciences about the validity and usefulness of defining such catastrophic points of no return and within the social sciences and humanities about the politics and ethics of tipping points. This intervention argues that human geography has a key role to play in this complex landscape in furthering critical engagements with tipping points as the concept continues to unfold and take hold. It calls for an unfixing of dominant understandings and framings through key geographical ideas: space and scale, time and temporalities and a/effect. These geographical ideas permit a redirection in current debates, especially around governance. Much is at stake in such a critique where tipping points may be productively questioned, imagined as something otherwise, or even outright refused as a guiding concept of our times. More equitable enquiries may emerge as a result. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Woodward M.; Powell A.; Dixon-Woods M.; Burt J.; Winter C.; Lattey K.; Draycott T.J.; van der Scheer J.W.
Title: Design and context of use of postpartum haemorrhage kits in the UK: a qualitative study combining human factors and social science analysis
Abstract: Effective management of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) – a leading cause of maternal mortality – depends on rapid access to critical equipment and medications. PPH emergency kits support timely care, but their design and practical use remain largely unexamined. We combined human factors and social science analysis – drawing on photographs, field observations, and 19 interviews with maternity professionals – to examine kit designs, usability, and contextual factors in six UK maternity units. Many design features, including kit format, item grouping, item visibility, and portability, varied substantially across units. Usability was shaped by factors including labour room and storage constraints, medication access, staff skill mix, and restocking procedures. Some designs risked delays or confusion in emergencies. While standardisation may improve kit safety and efficiency, rigid solutions could risk misalignment with local workflows. A modular approach combining standardised core components with adaptable elements, designed collaboratively with end-users and grounded in ergonomic principles may provide an effective solution. Authors: Chien N.W.; Yujie G.; Udin U.; Zhi T.
Title: Analysis of the factors influencing consumers’ intention to purchase green food
Abstract: Background and Objectives: With sustained socio-economic development, problems such as resource constraints, ecological damage, and food safety have become increasingly prominent and have become important factors constraining sustainable development. To address these challenges, this study applies the stimulus-organism-response framework to examine key factors that shape consumers' green purchase intention in the food industry in China. Green advertising, environmental attitude, product attributes, and social media influence are conceptualized as external stimuli, while customer perceived value represents the internal psychological mechanism driving behavioural intention. Methods: A total of 371 valid survey responses were analysed using Statistical Package for Social Sciences software (version 27.0) and Analysis of Moment Structures (version 28.0) to conduct reliability testing, factor analysis, structural modelling, and mediation analysis. Findings: All four external variables significantly increase customer perceived value, which in turn strengthens green purchase intention. Mediation results show that customer perceived value partially mediates the effects of green advertising and product attributes, and fully mediates the effects of environmental attitude and social media influence. Conclusion: The study demonstrates that customer perceived value plays a central role in transforming external green marketing stimuli into purchase intention. These findings provide theoretical insight for stimulus-organism-response-based green marketing research and practical guidance for food enterprises seeking to promote sustainable consumer behaviour. ©2026 The author(s). Authors: Azizi M.; Chlebek N.; Dewsbury B.
Title: The Intention–Implementation Gap: Micro-Cycles and Contextual Factors in First-Year STEM Students’ Self-Regulated Learning
Abstract: First-year students in STEM programs face significant academic and personal challenges that can undermine retention and success, particularly for those navigating new institutional environments without prior college experience. While self- regulated learning (SRL) theory offers a well-established framework for understanding how students plan and reflect, less attention has been paid to the performance phase, the stage where students must translate plans into action amid real academic and social demands. This qualitative study examines the experiences of 15 first-year life science students across three institution types, a Hispanic-Serving Institution, a predominantly white institution, and a liberal arts college, to investigate what plans students formed at the end of their first semester and what factors facilitated or hindered implementation during their second semester. Using thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews, three major plan themes emerged: help-seeking, internal academic adjustments, and managing social and emotional well-being. Facilitating factors for these plans included small class sizes, anonymized participation tools, approachable instructors, peer and family support, counseling services, and structured planning tools, while hindering factors included fear of judgment, high instructor-student ratios, scheduling conflicts, academic burnout, and unsupportive living environments. The findings reveal that plan implementation depended on the interplay of intersecting psychological, social, and structural factors, which created unique conditions that influenced whether students were able to enact their plans. Importantly, the findings reveal that plan implementation unfolded not as a linear process but through nested micro-cycles of forethought, performance, and reflection within the performance phase, triggered by specific events throughout the semester. These findings have implications for how institutions design learner-centered support for STEM students not only at key transition points, but also throughout the semester, to address the conditions that influence whether students are able to successfully implement, adapt, or abandon their regulatory efforts. © 2026 by the authors.

Authors: Yang H.; Jeon H.
Title: The effect of the small school revitalization act on academic achievement: evidence from a regression discontinuity design in South Korea
Abstract: This study evaluates the impact of South Korea’s Small School Revitalization (SSR) policy on eighth-grade academic achievement in Jeonnam Province, a rural province experiencing significant population decline. The SSR policy, targeting schools with fewer than 60 students, aims to prevent student attrition by enhancing education quality. Examining data from the Jeonnam Student Longitudinal Study (JELS) and employing quasi-experimental research methods such as regression discontinuity design and propensity score matching, we find significant positive impacts of the SSR policy on academic achievement in eighth-grade math and science but limited effects for Korean language and social studies. These findings suggest that targeted support for small schools can be an effective alternative to closure and can help promote rural school revitalization. This study contributes to policy discussions on improving small rural schools, offering evidence for contexts facing similar challenges. © Education Research Institute, Seoul National University 2025.

Authors: Chávez-Galeana D.; Navarro Méndez A.S.; Ramirez-Gutierrez C.F.
Title: SDG-focused research at Mexico’s leading universities (2015–2023): a bibliometric analysis of structure, growth, collaboration, and specialization
Abstract: The deadline for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is fast approaching in 2030, yet progress in many areas remains slower than expected. The knowledge generated by universities plays a central role in meeting these goals within the established timeframe. In this context, analyzing how universities perform in producing relevant knowledge for the SDGs becomes critically important. However, there is still limited empirical evidence on how universities are contributing to this agenda, particularly in middle-income countries such as Mexico. This study examines publication and specialization patterns in SDG-related scientific output across 15 of Mexico’s most productive universities from 2015 to 2023. Using SciVal (based on Scopus), a set of bibliometric indicators was developed to assess dimensions such as impact, citation, collaboration type, and relative specialization. The findings indicate that publications related to the SDGs have increased at a faster rate than total scientific output across all institutions. These universities specialize in a diverse range of SDGs, with particular emphasis on SDGs 2 (Zero Hunger), 14 (Life Below Water), and 15 (Life on Land). Additionally, new cases of specialization and extraordinary growth were documented in a group of SDGs referred to as “social” due to their alignment with social science disciplines (e.g., SDGs 1, 4, 5, 8, 10, and 16). These results provide valuable evidence for science policy and highlight the importance of strengthening the role of universities as key actors in addressing global and local sustainability challenges. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Kubota H.; Caine V.; Clandinin D.J.
Title: Conceptualizing the Relational Work of Narrative Inquiry as Spaces of Appearance
Abstract: While Arendt’s theoretical work is now widely taken up in social science research, it has not been taken up in qualitative research methodologies. We use Arendt’s distinction between the private and public through the creation of a space of appearance to show how we can understand participants’ and researchers’ experiences in narrative inquiry. We show how a relational space co-created with each participant shaped a space of appearance. In this article, we draw on one participant’s, Ama, experiences to make visible how we conceptualize research conversations as spaces of appearance. © The Author(s) 2025. Authors: Aloyo E.
Title: Forecasting-informed foreign policy decision-making: the case of jus ad vim
Abstract: How should decisions be made regarding instances in which force-short-of-war might be used? This article argues that such decisions can and should be improved by drawing on empirical social science findings on forecasting from scholars such as Philip Tetlock. Integrating evidence-based forecasting methods into decision-making procedures can help counter cognitive biases that can lead to suboptimal decisions. The article illustrates the argument with examples, including the United States’ arming rebels and conducting limited strikes in Syria during the civil war in that country, and shows how such forecasting is useful to assess whether a key jus ad vim principle, that of escalation, would likely be met. Furthermore, including forecasting in decision-making may decrease the risk of just war theory principles in general—and jus ad vim principles specifically—being abused by powerful actors, because providing accurate forecasts would provide the probability of failure of jus ad vim, and other, policy options. © The Author(s) 2026. Authors: Hiltner S.
Title: Limited Attention to Climate Change in U.S. Sociology
Abstract: Climate change is increasingly recognized as not only a biophysical and technological problem but also a social one. Nonetheless, sociologists have expressed concern that sociology has paid relatively little attention to climate change. This deficit threatens to limit the frames available to understand and imagine solutions to the climate crisis. In this paper I report the most up-to-date and expansive empirical assessment of attention to climate change in sociology in the United States (U.S.). I find little to no mention of climate change across leading sociology journal articles (0.89%), conference sessions (1.5%), and faculty biographies (2.8%) and course listings (0.2%) in the 20 top-ranked departments in the U.S. Two leading journals, the American Sociological Review and American Journal of Sociology, have cumulatively published just three articles focused on climate change to date. This level of disciplinary attention appears low compared to the field’s engagement with other important social problems. My findings thus suggest that climate silence is persistent and pervasive in U.S. sociology. I discuss the implications of this silence and outline opportunities for sociologists, funders, journalists, and policymakers to embrace social science perspectives in climate change teaching, research, and policymaking. © The Author(s) 2024.

Authors: Rakhoveio P.S.; Gill R.; Veimy M.
Title: Role of Traditional Games in Shaping Cultural Identity and Strengthening Community Cohesion
Abstract: Traditional games in the Poumai Naga culture are integral to festivals and social life, symbolising unity and fostering community cohesion. Common games, such as wrestling, kabaddi, and tug-of-war, offer a platform for youth to demonstrate physical strength while promoting camaraderie and preserving cultural heritage. These games also serve to build relationships and teach essential life skills. This study uses a qualitative approach, employing semi-structured interviews with community members from four Poumai Naga villages, Phuba, Tungjoy, Saranamai, and Koide, to explore the cultural values embedded in these traditional games. The research explores how traditional games shape cultural identity and strengthen community cohesion. The research highlights the ongoing practice of traditional games in the Poumai community, despite the influence of modern sports. Through thematic analysis of primary and secondary data, the study underscores the significance of these games in preserving their identity, while also acknowledging the global appeal and shared traits of traditional games across cultures. Additionally, the study emphasises the potential for educators to incorporate traditional games into teaching social science concepts, as these games serve as lived expressions of social norms, community organisation, cooperation, and identity. The embedded rituals and symbolic elements of the games provide rich context for understanding topics such as tradition, authority, communal values, and intergenerational knowledge transfer. The integration of such games in both formal education and community development initiatives reflects their dual function as instruments of learning and preservation. The continued practice of traditional games in the Poumai Naga community represents a rich blend of recreation, ritual, and social function, reinforcing values of strength, respect, and tradition in shaping the identity of future generations while offering contemporary relevance in educational and developmental frameworks. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025.

Authors: Romanello M.; Lamprianou I.; Michaelides M.
Title: Who lost the most? COVID-19 school closures, PISA achievement, and socioeconomic gaps
Abstract: This paper examines how COVID-19 school closures were associated with student achievement and social inequalities using data from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) for 2018 and 2022. The analysis examines how different remote learning methods were associated with the relationship among school closures, educational inequality, and learning outcomes in mathematics, science, and reading. To estimate both direct and indirect associations, the study employs a Generalized Structural Equation Model (GSEM) and a Triple Difference-in-Differences approach. This method enables the simultaneous estimation of correlates of remote learning modality usage and their associations with proficiency outcomes, while accounting for students' socioeconomic backgrounds. The results show clear differences between advanced and emerging/developing economies. In advanced economies, school closures were associated with moderate average learning losses, but a significant increase in social inequalities. In emerging/developing economies, school closures were primarily associated with larger average learning losses rather than with increased socioeconomic gaps. This may be due to the limited spread of digital learning technologies that could help create advantages. In summary, the results suggest that school closures were associated less with a uniform disruption to learning and more with a redistribution of educational opportunities along socioeconomic lines, with the type of remote learning available to students associated with much of who lost the most. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Durocher M.
Title: What's in the Blood? Temporalities at Play in Diet-Related Risk Management Testing Practices
Abstract: In this paper, I look at two different sets of practices that are part of the risk management apparatus in place in Québec & Canada to apprehend and control risks associated with food consumption. More specifically, I contrast diabetes and chemical contaminants risk management testing practices, so as to compare how both frame and approach risks, in a context where recent research in social sciences, epigenetics and environmental sciences increasingly points to “environmental” pathways of disease causation while many chronic conditions remain highly individualized in public and health discourses. The analysis pays close attention to the different temporalities discursively created, considered, and neglected in these practices in order to understand how risk is approached and worked on. This highlights the power relations that inform how we care (or not) for (certain) bodies, inflecting in particular ways their—uneven—becomings. I argue that the Canadian biotechnological apparatus of testing practices meant to apprehend and control diet-related risks contributes to foreclosing the temporalities of health and illness considered and acted upon. As such, the apparatus contributes to (re)producing inequalities, here mostly health related ones, as well as creating differentiated biological materialities. © The Author(s) 2024. Authors: Chen Y.-Y.
Title: Everyday culinary practices and the socio-cultural significance of domestic cooking: A conceptual analysis
Abstract: Gastronomy research has traditionally centered on professional kitchens, culinary innovation, and publicly visible food cultures, leaving everyday domestic cooking conceptually underexplored. Although household food preparation is widely recognized as culturally significant, it is often framed as routine or instrumental labor rather than as a site of gastronomic knowledge production. This paper addresses this analytical gap by repositioning domestic cooking as a foundational domain of gastronomy and food science. Drawing on theories of tacit knowledge, cultural capital, and practice-based learning, the study introduces Culinary Home Economics Capital (CHE Capital) as a conceptual framework for analyzing how everyday domestic cooking generates, stabilizes, and circulates culinary knowledge. CHE Capital conceptualizes domestic culinary competence as a form of capital grounded in embodied and tacit knowledge, social articulation, relational embedding, and processes of accumulation and circulation beyond the household. Rather than relying on professionalization, market exchange, or symbolic distinction, CHE Capital highlights how gastronomic value emerges through repetition, care, informal learning, and intergenerational transmission. Through a conceptual analysis informed by scholarship in gastronomy, food sociology, and food science, the paper demonstrates how domestic cooking functions as a primary environment for sensory calibration, procedural judgment, and adaptive culinary skill development. By foregrounding tacit and relational forms of knowledge, CHE Capital expands the conceptual boundaries of gastronomy and offers a framework for systematically examining everyday cooking as a generative site of gastronomic, cultural, and educational value. The study contributes to ongoing debates on social gastronomy, informal food learning, and culinary knowledge circulation, and provides a theoretical foundation for future empirical research on domestic cooking, food education, and sensory development across the life course. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Lin C.; Wojkowski S.; Quach S.
Title: Trends and changes in interprofessional education readiness and perceptions across the Faculty of Health Sciences at McMaster University over 6 years: A cross-sectional analysis
Abstract: Background Interprofessional education (IPE) prepares pre-licensure health sciences students to deliver team-based, patient-centered care, but its effectiveness depends on students' readiness to engage. In 2019, the Program for Interprofessional Practice, Education and Research at McMaster University, launched a quality improvement initiative to assess health sciences students' IPE readiness. This study characterized students’ IPE readiness at program entry from 2019 to 2024, spanning a novel transition from in-person (pre-COVID) to online (during COVID) and hybrid (post-COVID) delivery formats. Methods This repeated cross-sectional study invited incoming first-year health sciences students to complete a voluntary survey, including demographic questions and the Likert-version Readiness for Interprofessional Learning Scale (RIPLS). Descriptive statistics characterized the sample. Total and subscale RIPLS scores were compared across program specializations, disciplines and time periods using Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney U tests. Analyses were conducted using STATA 18.0 B/E, with p ' .05 considered statistically significant. Results Two thousand fifty-six students completed at least one RIPLS subscale between 2019 and 2024. Respondents had a mean (SD) age of 22.1 (4.4) years and were mainly women-identifying (n = 1494, 72.7%). Graduate Professional students demonstrated a high IPE readiness compared to Undergraduate General (p ' .001) and Undergraduate Professional students (p ' .001). Students from Social Work, Midwifery, Nursing and Bachelor of Health Sciences reported lower RIPLS scores compared to the other disciplines (all p ' .05). Total RIPLS scores were lowest during COVID compared to the pre- and post-COVID periods (all p ' .001). Conclusions This study provides insights into IPE perceptions across six years. These findings can inform IPE programs in refining their IPE offerings to better align students’ learning needs. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Nguyen D.
Title: Comparing the use of linking adverbials in academic writing by L1 and L2 English student writers: A corpus-based study
Abstract: This study investigates the usage of linking adverbials (LAs) and their semantic types in the academic essays of L1 and L2 English university students in the British Academic Written English (BAWE) corpus across four academic levels (e.g., first-year, second-year, third-year undergraduate, master) and three disciplinary groups (e.g., Arts and Humanities, Social Sciences, Life and Physical Sciences). Findings show that L2 writers employed more LAs in their academic essays than their L1 counterparts, although both groups relied predominantly on a limited subset of this linguistic feature in academic writing. Configural Frequency Analysis (CFA) reveals another important finding: while disciplinary variations in LA usage were observed for both L1 and L2, there was no significant difference in the use of LAs across academic levels. Notably, L1 students showed a preference for adversative adverbials (e.g., yet, however), whereas L2 students tended to use additive adverbials (e.g., moreover) more frequently. The findings offer insights into the differential cohesive strategies employed by L1 and L2 writers. Ultimately, these findings have important implications for targeted academic writing instruction aimed at enhancing essay cohesion for undergraduate students in diverse disciplinary contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Schrauf R.W.; López de Victoria Rodríguez P.C.
Title: On ‘doing being moral’ in the research interview
Abstract: Abstract – In qualitative research interviews, participants sometimes relate vivid, ethically charged accounts of their lifeworlds. However, the genre constraints of the interview discourage interviewers from expressions of direct affiliation (agreement, approval, disapproval) with the interviewee’s moral stances and rather encourage expressions of conversational alignment (attention, interest, comprehension) to keep the information flowing. Interviewees for their part may prefer and make a bid for more engagement from interviewers. We examine the affordances and constraints of the research interview and the discursive practices available to interviewees for ‘doing moral action’ in the interview: constructing their moral identities, describing their moral worlds, evaluating others, and attempting to more fully engage their interviewers. In the latter, interviewees employ a discursive ‘recruitment to action’ exercised subtly and indirectly by linguistically calibrating the space-time of their moral narratives to accord with the space-time of the interview and indexing their stories to transcendent norms and timeless truths. Authors: Géring Z.; Tamássy R.; Frányó Z.; Knúlné Pál E.; Rakovics M.
Title: More focus on society, less on student development – mission-change of Hungarian higher education institutions between 2017 and 2023
Abstract: In a constantly changing world, universities have to make considerable efforts to legitimise themselves both as higher education institutions (HEIs) and as important and future-oriented institutions that serve society. These legitimacy claims can be detected in mission statements, which are commonly used communication tools to reach stakeholders. Accordingly, this research aims to investigate the change in mission of Hungarian HEIs between 2017 and 2023. We analysed 35 Hungarian HEIs’ publicly available mission texts from their official websites and distinguished 38 mentioned social roles and responsibilities. The longitudinal approach made it possible to identify the unchanging social roles and, at the same time, to identify the emerging and disappearing roles and stakeholders. The results show that the ‘Education’, ‘Science, research’, ‘External relations’, ‘High quality’, and ‘Traditions, values’ role groups are stable throughout the years. We perceive them as legitimating role groups in that their mention seems to be continuously present. There is only one role group, which showed an increasing tendency: the roles indicating services to and well-being of society. However, this heightened focus on society’s demands seems to be reached at the expense of student-centredness because the frequency of mentioned roles and responsibilities concerning the students significantly decreased. The question arose whether these changes can be connected to the transformation in higher education governance and the spreading of new managerialism, or rather mirror the HEIs’ attempts to react to the challenges and changes in the international and national environment and address the difficulties of mission overload. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Boglev G.
Title: Seven Decades of Demographic Trends at the Hugo Awards From 1953 to 2023: How the Award Recipients Reflect Actual and Aspirational Demographic Trends in Society
Abstract: This study analyses the demographic trends at the Hugo Awards, with a focus on the authors' genders, languages, nationalities, and uses of pseudonyms. This research uses publicly available information published by the World Science Fiction Society and the Hugo Awards to determine demographic trends in nominated and winning authors for the Best Novel category over 7 decades. Several years of controversies around manipulation of the voting, and how these controversies themselves reflect and represent social changes, have also been considered. This analysis shows that trends for some of the demographic features of authors have changed significantly over the decades and done so largely in line with corresponding societal changes and changes to the publishing industry and science fiction. However, some demographic categories have remained stable over the years, despite external sociocultural and changes and changes to the operation of the awards themselves. The changes in demographic trends at the Hugo Awards observed in this paper have been slow, inconsistent, and met with multiple occasions of backlash. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Laidlaw P.
Title: Integrating professional ethics in environmental science education: bridging codes of conduct with educational practice
Abstract: This study explores the critical intersection of professional ethics and environmental science education, highlighting the urgent need for coherent, integrated ethical frameworks in this inherently interdisciplinary field. Environmental scientists increasingly face complex ethical dilemmas involving trade-offs between economic development, ecological preservation, and social justice. Yet, ethics remains inconsistently embedded in environmental science curricula. Through thematic analysis of 28 Australian environmental professional codes and comparison with leading international frameworks, this research identifies seven core ethical principles: integrity, scientific objectivity, environmental stewardship, public accountability, justice, transparency, and ethical courage. The analysis reveals significant curricular gaps, particularly in areas such as Indigenous co-governance, sustainability commitments, and climate advocacy, where Australian standards fall short of global benchmarks. Drawing on educational theory and transdisciplinary ethics, the paper presents practical, evidence-informed strategies for embedding ethics education across four domains: curriculum development, pedagogical design, faculty support, and professional partnerships. Recommendations include integrating ethics into learning outcomes, adopting experiential and cross-disciplinary teaching methods, forming student-led ethics committees, and fostering collaboration between universities and professional bodies. By equipping graduates with the ethical competencies needed for professional practice, this approach strengthens public trust in environmental science and supports more just, responsible, and sustainable outcomes for ecosystems and communities. © AESS 2025.

Authors: Thornton M.
Title: Resisting disinformation: theorising whole-of-society and sociotechnical resistance
Abstract: How can states resist transnational disinformation campaigns? Analyses in the field of International Relations (IR) have offered a variety of explanations which index the harms of disinformation to state power, yet state resistance to disinformation remains underexplored and under-theorised. Through the concept of a ‘mobilisation of resistance’ and based insights from Social Theory and Science and Technology Studies (STS), this article posits a social-processual framework to explain whole-of-society resistance to transnational disinformation and the role of sociotechnical systems in facilitating this resistance. This approach emphasises the agency of civil society actors and sociotechnical systems in articulating resistance to transnational disinformation alongside the state. The article specifies four processes through which a mobilisation of resistance to disinformation can be expressed through technology: enframing, co-production, legitimation and humour. As a country at the forefront of combatting disinformation from China, Taiwan presents a valuable empirical site through which resistance to transnational disinformation can be understood. Taking Taiwan’s open-source governance (OSG) and algorithmic co-governance (ACG) as paradigmatic cases of whole-of-society sociotechnical resistance, I seek to illustrate how these four processes have been materially enacted to resist Chinese disinformation campaigns on the one hand while promoting a democratic social order in Taiwan on the other hand. © The Author(s) 2025. Authors: Heikkinen A.; van Gerven M.; Koulu R.
Title: From Discretion to Calculation: How Analog Automation Shaped Digitalization of Finnish Social Assistance
Abstract: Automation in public administration is often seen as a recent, purely digital phenomenon that transforms decision-making and governance. This article challenges that view by elucidating a historical continuum in the automation of administrative decision-making. It introduces the concept of analog automation to highlight how complex social, organizational, legal, and historical factors have impacted decision-makers' discretionary space and paved the way for digital automation. Drawing on public administration, science and technology studies, and sociolegal scholarship, the article uses analog automation to study the gradual yet significant change of automation in Finland's social assistance system over four decades. Analysis of legislative and policy documents shows how discretionary space has been gradually restricted by changes in organizational structures and practices and their adoption into legal obligations. The article provides historical context to current debates on digital transformation, showing how long-standing institutional developments enable automation and how standardization and discretion have become increasingly intertwined. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Sociophonetic Markers in English Majors: How Urban Jordanian Identity Shapes Consonantal Substitutions
Abstract: This study examined English pronunciation errors among 50 Jordanian English majors at the Faculty of Educational Sciences and Arts. Data were collected via a 190-item word-list reading task, focusing on frequency and complexity. Recordings were transcribed using IPA and analyzed via Praat, with inter-rater reliability confirmed at 0.85. The research investigated seven consonants (i.e., /dʒ/, /tʃ/, /θ/, /ð/, /ʃ/, /ʒ/, and /ŋ/) across various positions. Analyzed through Contrastive Analysis, Markedness Theory, and Sociophonetics, findings revealed a systematic hierarchy of phonological complexity. Primary deviations included deaffrication (/dʒ/→/ʒ/), stopping (/ð/→/d/), and nasal epenthesis (/ŋ/→ [ŋg]). Notably, applying Al-Wer’s (2004, 2019) framework, substitutions of /z/ for /ð/ and /g/ for /dʒ/ reflect dialectal prestige and urban identity rather than mere mistakes. Results suggest that teaching should prioritize articulatory features and functional intelligibility over native-like accuracy. Educators need to recognize that pronunciation reflects cultural identity and Jordanian dialects, supporting learners by relating linguistic rules to social contexts. © 2026 Alkarazoun, Smadi, Al-Hawamdeh, El-kanash, Sayyed, and Aledwan.

Authors: Tenenberg J.
Title: Computing Education’s Superbug: Interrogating the Computer-Mind Metaphors
Abstract: In one of the significant results from early computing education research, Pea identifies a computer-as-mind metaphor that novices use in ascribing mental properties of personhood to the computer, which causes students considerable conceptual confusion. In characterizing this as students’ superbug, Pea uses a mind-as-computer metaphor, the converse metaphor to the one that students use. In doing so, he makes visible a metaphor that has become one of the predominant metaphors of mind in mid- to late-20th century theorizing in psychology and the cognitive sciences. I take both of these metaphors (computer-as-mind and mind-as-computer) to be the superbug that plagues not only student attempts to program but also computing education more broadly. The purpose of this article is to argue that these computer-mind metaphors are a steady undercurrent that runs from the cognitive sciences through computing education and the research on it, what is problematic about these metaphors, what causes this metaphorical affliction, why we might want to cure ourselves from it, and how we can do so. Key to this cure is to counter disembodied views of human reasoning and action, epitomized in first generation cognitive science, with embodied and enactive theoretical perspectives, epitomized in second generation cognitive science and in multimodal and embodied approaches to the social sciences. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Authors: Tavakkoli Z.; Hui T.; Ghaemmaghami P.
Title: Teacher Educators as Sustainability Change Agents: Identity, Agency, and Disciplinary Cultures in EFL and Social Sciences Programmes
Abstract: Sustainability education (SE) is increasingly recognized as a critical aspect of higher education and teacher education due to global environmental, social, and economic challenges. However, limited research has examined how teacher educators in developing countries, including Iran, conceptualize and implement sustainability in their teaching practices. This qualitative narrative study explored how Iranian English as a Foreign Language (EFL) and Social Science (SS) teacher educators interpret and enact sustainability through the Identity–Agency–Disciplinary (IAD) framework. Twenty semi-structured interviews were conducted with teacher educators from four public universities in Iran, and thematic analysis was performed using NVivo software. Findings indicate a complex, recursive relationship between sustainability literacy and sustainability implementation. EFL teacher educators exhibited strong awareness of sustainable practices' outcomes but reported limited integration of sustainability into their professional identity, enacting only partial sustainable practices. Conversely, SS teacher educators demonstrated conceptual understanding of sustainability but experienced identity fragmentation and resistance to practical implementation. Across both disciplines, identity tension and constrained professional agency exceeded institutional constraints, while disciplinary culture both facilitated and hindered transformative practices. Overall, the study reconceptualizes teacher educators as conditionally empowered actors who implement sustainability only when identity, agency, and disciplinary culture align. These results highlight that effective sustainability reforms in teacher education require systematic support for professional identity development and opportunities for agency, rather than reliance solely on policy mandates. This study contributes to literature on teacher identity, professional agency, and disciplinary culture, offering theoretical and practical insights for fostering transformative, sustainability-oriented pedagogical practices in diverse educational contexts. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Dey S.; Rangarajan K.
Title: Sustainable Development and Inorganic Growth: A Bibliometric and NLP Driven Review of ESG in Mergers and Acquisitions (1982–2024)
Abstract: Achieving the UN Sustainable Development Goals by 2030 requires firms to embed sustainability into core strategic decisions. Mergers and acquisitions (M&A), a primary vehicle for inorganic growth, are increasingly shaped by Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) considerations. However, the ESG–M&A intersection remains fragmented and theoretically underdeveloped. This study systematically maps the intellectual architecture of this emerging field, identifies latent thematic frontiers, and derives theoretically grounded directions for future research. Following a PRISMA-guided selection protocol, 1225 articles from the combined Web of Science and Scopus databases (1982–2024) were analysed using a three-method triangulation design. Bibliometric analysis—including citation, co-citation, bibliographic coupling, and keyword co-occurrence—identified dominant scholars, journals, countries, and research themes. Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA, k = 11) and BERTopic (k = 13) were applied to extract latent semantic structures and uncover nuanced thematic clusters beyond the reach of conventional co-word methods. Existing literature on M&A as strategy revealed dominant streams such as valuation, corporate governance, and performance. However, ESG integration remained underexplored. NLP-driven models provided novel insights, uncovering emerging clusters on green logistics, skills and social development policy, gender and biodiversity, ethical consumption, and psychological drivers of green finance—topics overlooked by conventional methods. Combining bibliometrics with NLP techniques offers methodological novelty, exposes new thematic frontiers, and informs future scholarship and practice in sustainability-driven corporate strategies. This study presents the largest assembled corpus at the ESG–M&A intersection to date, uniquely combining classical science mapping with transformer-based semantic clustering to map four decades of interdisciplinary scholarship. © 2026 ERP Environment and John Wiley & Sons Ltd.
